Elsternwick|Prep|How We Express Ourselve.d: Students create a short class book for How We Express Ourselves, with each child adding a page to a shared story. This supports the line of inquiry Imagining stories together and shows that stories are shared in different ways. Children draw a picture, add a simple sentence with teacher help, and record themselves reading their page aloud. Book Creator’s pages, drawing tools and voice recording make a finished digital book the class can read and listen to together.

Students use ScratchJr to make two characters act out a simple beginning, middle and ending for a story in How We Express Ourselves. This connects to Ways stories are shared by turning a spoken idea into a short coded animation. Children choose a background and characters, then join movement, speech and start blocks to make each scene play. They test and fix their block sequence before presenting the animation to a partner.

Small groups use Stop Motion Studio to retell a familiar story for How We Express Ourselves with classroom toys or playdough characters. This supports Connecting with stories as children choose an important moment and explain why it matters to them. They move the characters a tiny amount, take a frame, and repeat until they have recorded a short scene. The app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback turn their movements into a shareable stop-motion film.

Students use ChatterPix Kids to let a character from a shared story speak about what happened in How We Express Ourselves. This develops Connecting with stories because children talk from the character’s point of view. Each child photographs their drawing, draws a mouth line, and records a short message such as what the character saw, wanted or felt. The talking-mouth and voice-recording features create a brief character video to show the class.

Students use Beebots to retell a simple story across a teacher-prepared floor grid showing key settings from How We Express Ourselves. This links to Ways stories are shared because the story is presented through movement and spoken narration. In pairs, children press the directional buttons to program the Beebot to visit the pictures in story order, then say what happens at each stop. They test, clear and correct the sequence before presenting their moving story path to the class.

Elsternwick|Prep|How We Organise Ourselv.d: Students view the streets around Elsternwick in Google Maps and use Street View to find places such as the school, library, shops and emergency services. They discuss who works in each place and connect this to the line of inquiry, “Connections in my community.” In pairs, students present a short Street View walkthrough showing a route between two familiar community places. The map search, zoom and Street View features let them explore these real locations without needing a student login.

Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a teacher-prepared floor map of the local community, stopping at places such as the school, park, library and fire station. At each stop, they explain one role a person plays there, linking to the central idea, “Everyone has a role to play in the community.” Students enter directions, test the route, clear the program and debug any wrong turns. They finish by presenting one successful route and explaining how the places are connected.

Students choose a community helper connected to the unit topic and draw or photograph that person. In ChatterPix Kids, they add a mouth and record a short message explaining the person’s role and how they contribute to the local community. This directly supports the line of inquiry, “Contributing to the local community.” The simple mouth-drawing and voice-recording features produce a short talking-character video that students can share with the class.

Students create a simple ScratchJr scene showing people working together in a community place such as a school, shop or park. They program two characters to move in turn and use speech bubbles to show what each person does, connecting to the central idea, “Everyone has a role to play in the community.” Students test the sequence and change blocks if the actions happen in the wrong order. The character, background, movement-block and speech-bubble features help them make a short animated community scene to present.

Students use PicCollage to make a visual collection called “My Communities” using photos of drawings, classroom groups, family activities or familiar local places. They add short labels such as family, class, team and neighbourhood, linking directly to the line of inquiry, “My communities.” Each student arranges the images and presents the finished collage by explaining where they belong and one way they contribute. The built-in camera, text and simple layout features make the collage manageable for Prep students.

Elsternwick|Prep|How the World Works.d: In How the World Works, students act like scientists by testing how a Bee-Bot can reach a chosen square on a floor grid. They predict a sequence, enter it with the directional buttons, run the test and change the instructions if the Bee-Bot goes somewhere unexpected. This directly explores the scientific process because students predict, test, observe and draw a conclusion. Each pair presents its final working sequence by pressing the buttons and demonstrating the route to the class.

In How the World Works, students observe a plant or small animal in the school grounds and use Field Guide to Victoria to look for a possible match. They compare visible details such as colour, shape, body covering or number of legs with the photographs and information in the guide. This supports the line of inquiry Observing my world because students use careful observations rather than a quick guess. Each pair presents the matching entry and explains one piece of visible evidence that helped them decide.

In How the World Works, students make a simple digital science book about a class investigation such as finding out which objects roll down a ramp. On separate pages they record their question, prediction, test, observations and conclusion using the built-in camera, drawing tools and voice recording. This directly connects to the central idea that scientists follow a method to discover new things. The finished book becomes a shareable science report that students can read or play aloud to classmates.

In How the World Works, students use Stop Motion Studio to record a slow change that is difficult to notice all at once, such as an ice cube melting. They take a photo at regular points and use the playback feature to view the images as one short sequence. This supports Observing my world and Drawing conclusions because students look closely for what changed from the first frame to the last. Each group presents its finished stop-motion clip and records a simple spoken conclusion about what it noticed.

In How the World Works, students create a before-and-after observation page for a simple class test, such as placing one object in water and observing whether it floats or sinks. They use the built-in camera to take photos, place them in a layout and add short labels or teacher-scribed sentences. This connects to Drawing conclusions because students use the recorded result to say whether their prediction matched what happened. The finished collage is a clear, shareable record of the question, prediction, observation and conclusion.

Elsternwick|Year 1|How We Express Oursel.d: Students create one page about an emotion, using the drawing tools to show a face and body expressing it. They record their voice explaining how they recognised the emotion and one helpful way someone could respond. This directly explores recognising our own and others' emotions and responding to emotions. The class combines the pages into a shareable emotions book using Book Creator's page, drawing and audio recording features.

Students photograph a toy or classroom object and use it to speak as a character experiencing an emotion. They add the moving mouth, then record a short message such as, "I feel worried because I cannot find my friend, and I could ask a teacher for help." This explores different ways we express emotions and how we can respond to them. Students present their short talking-character recordings to the class using ChatterPix Kids' photo, mouth and voice recording features.

In pairs, students make a short puppet scene in which one character shows an emotion and another character works out how to respond. They choose characters and a background, move the puppets, and record simple dialogue as the scene plays. This supports responding to and interpreting our emotions by showing that words, facial expressions and actions all give clues. Each pair presents a recorded puppet scene using Puppet Pals' character movement and voice recording features.

Students code a character to express two different emotions during a simple story, such as feeling nervous before joining a game and happy after being welcomed. They choose a background, add short speech bubbles, and sequence blocks to make the character move between parts of the story. This connects to the central idea that emotions can be expressed in different ways. Students run and present their finished animated story using ScratchJr's characters, backgrounds and block-based coding.

Students make an emotions clue poster with three photos showing the same emotion through a face, body position and action. They arrange the photos, add the emotion word, and include a short response such as, "Ask if they need help." This develops recognising our own and others' emotions by asking students to notice visible clues. Students share their finished poster using PicCollage's photo layout, text and sticker features.

Elsternwick|Year 1|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students explore the Elsternwick area in Google Maps and look for local services such as the library, train station, medical centre and post office. This directly supports the line of inquiry into local services and why we need them in our community. In pairs, students use search, zoom and Street View to prepare a short on-screen tour showing one service, where it is and who might use it. Each pair presents its live map tour to the class without saving, editing or adding pins.

Students program a Beebot to travel across a teacher-prepared floor grid showing homes and local services. They choose a person’s need, such as borrowing a book or posting a letter, then code a route to the service that can help. This explores how services meet personal and community needs. Using the directional buttons, students enter, test and correct their sequence before presenting the successful journey to the class.

Students make a simple class book called Services That Help Our Community. Each child creates one page about a local service, showing what it provides, who needs it and how it helps. This connects directly to the central idea that services are established to help the needs of people in the community. Students use Book Creator’s drawing, text and voice-recording features to publish a page that classmates can read and listen to.

Students code a short ScratchJr scene about a person using a local service, such as visiting a library to find a book. They choose characters and a setting, then use movement and speech blocks to show the need and how the service responds. This supports the line of inquiry into how services meet personal and community needs. Students test and debug their sequence, then present the finished animation and explain the service shown.

In small groups, students record a short role-play showing a community service helping someone with an everyday need. One student acts as the community member and another acts as a service worker, such as a librarian, crossing supervisor or postal worker. This helps students explain why we need local services in our community. Students use the built-in camera, simple recording controls and titles to make a short video that can be played to the class.

Elsternwick|Prep|Who We Are.d: Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a simple floor grid showing people and places that help them feel healthy and safe. They press the directional buttons to plan a route from a child card to places such as the classroom, sick bay or a trusted adult, then test and debug the sequence. This directly explores the line of inquiry about keeping ourselves healthy and safe. Each pair presents its completed route and explains when the person or place could help.

Students work in pairs to record a short video showing how kind words and actions can support relationships and wellbeing. They act out one everyday Prep situation, such as inviting someone to play, taking turns or asking an adult for help. This connects directly to how those around us impact our behaviours and interactions. Using the app's simple video recording and text tools, each pair publishes a short clip to share with the class.

Students complete a teacher-made picture survey about actions that help them feel safe, included and cared for at school. They select choices such as sharing, listening, helping or getting an adult, then view the automatic class response charts together. This provides class data for discussing the line of inquiry about developing relationships. The class presents what the most common responses reveal about how relationships impact our wellbeing.

Students create a personal collage about relationships and wellbeing using teacher-provided photos or simple pictures of trusted people, healthy choices and safe places. They arrange the images and add short labels such as family, friend, teacher, rest or help. This links directly to the line of inquiry about keeping ourselves healthy and safe. The app's picture layout and text features allow each student to publish a clear wellbeing collage and explain it to a partner.

Students create a short puppet scene about developing relationships in the playground or classroom. They choose characters and a background, move the puppets, and record their voices as one character listens, shares, includes someone or solves a small disagreement. This shows how those around us can impact our behaviours and interactions. Each pair presents its recorded puppet story and names the action that helped the relationship.

Elsternwick|Prep|Sharing the Planet.d: In small, supervised groups, students use Seek by iNaturalist to look for and identify plants, insects and other living things around the school grounds. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the different living things around us. Students use the camera identification feature and save a small collection of observations to show the class. They then present one observation and explain where that living thing was found.

Students use Book Creator to make a class book called Living Things Share Our World. Each child creates a page about one animal or plant and explains the role it plays in nature, such as providing food, shelter or pollination. They add a drawing or photo and record a short spoken explanation, creating a book that can be read and listened to by families. The simple page tools, camera and voice recording feature make the task manageable for Prep students.

Students code a short ScratchJr animation showing how two living things help each other, such as a bee visiting a flower. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about the roles living things play in nature. They choose characters, create a simple background and use movement blocks to show what happens in the correct order. Each pair presents its finished animation and explains the important role shown.

As a class, students view Google Maps and use Street View to explore a park, a suburban street and a busy city area. They look for visible signs of how humans, plants and animals share space, linking directly to the line of inquiry about how humans and other living things share space. Small groups present a short guided Street View tour, pointing out trees, gardens, waterways, buildings and possible animal habitats. The teacher controls the search while students use the ordinary zoom, map view and Street View controls to examine each place.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short scene showing people sharing an outdoor space responsibly with plants and animals. This supports the central idea that living things share our world and have an important role in nature. Using simple classroom figures and paper scenery, students move one item at a time and capture each frame to show actions such as staying on a path, leaving a nest alone or planting flowers for insects. They play their finished stop-motion movie for the class and explain the helpful choices it shows.

Elsternwick|Year 1|How the World Works.d: Students code a Beebot to travel across a floor grid by repeating a movement pattern, such as forward, forward, turn. This explores how patterns can be created, interpreted and extended. Pairs test and debug their button sequence, then demonstrate the completed movement pattern to the class. The Beebot’s forward, backward and turn buttons make the repeating sequence easy for Year 1 students to enter and check.

Students use GarageBand to record a simple repeating sound pattern linked to patterns and cycles in our lives, such as wake, eat, learn and sleep. They arrange short recorded sounds or instrument notes into a sequence that repeats. Each pair plays its finished sound cycle and asks classmates to identify the part that repeats. GarageBand’s audio recorder and touch instruments allow students to make and replay the pattern easily.

Students use classroom objects to build a growing or repeating pattern, moving one piece at a time and taking a photo after each change in Stop Motion Studio. This directly explores how patterns can be created, interpreted and extended. They play back their finished stop-motion video and pause before the final frame so classmates can predict what comes next. The app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features turn each small change into a clear animation.

Students make a short digital book about patterns and cycles in their lives, with pages showing a morning routine, school day or weekly activity cycle. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about patterns and cycles in our lives. They draw or photograph each stage, add a short sentence and record themselves explaining how the cycle repeats. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and voice recording help students publish a simple book they can present to classmates.

Students draw a repeating pattern inspired by different patterns around us, such as stripes on clothing, tiles, leaves or animal markings. They choose two or three colours and repeat a simple set of shapes across the screen, then extend the pattern correctly. Each student presents the finished digital artwork and explains the repeating unit. Brushes Redux’s basic brushes, colours and undo control make it practical for Year 1 students to create and correct their pattern.

Elsternwick|Year 1|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Seek by iNaturalist to scan and identify plants growing around the school grounds. This directly explores the line of inquiry, plants all around us. In pairs, they record a small collection of plant observations in Seek and share one identification with the class. The camera identification feature helps Year 1 students match a real plant with its likely name.

Students use PicCollage to photograph everyday items made from plants, such as paper, fruit, wooden pencils and cotton clothing. This connects directly to the line of inquiry, products derived from plants. They arrange their photos into a labelled collage called “Plants Give Us…” and present it to a partner. The simple photo, text and layout features make the finished collage easy for Year 1 students to create and share.

Students use ScratchJr to code a short scene showing how a plant helps another living thing, such as a tree giving shade to a person or a flower providing food for a bee. This supports the line of inquiry, the interconnectedness of plants. They create characters, add simple speech and use movement blocks to show the connection in action. The picture-based coding blocks let students build, test and fix a short animation without needing to type.

Students use Google Maps to view Elsternwick streets and a large garden or park in Street View, looking for trees, lawns, gardens and other plants. This explores the line of inquiry, plants all around us. In pairs, they prepare a short on-screen walkthrough and present where plants can be seen in each place. Street View and the map’s zoom controls allow students to explore and compare real locations without creating or editing a map.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to animate paper pieces showing a flower, a bee and a piece of fruit. This connects to the line of inquiry, the interconnectedness of plants, by showing how a bee visits a flower and how fruit can later grow. They move the pieces a small amount, capture each frame and play back a short stop-motion explanation. The frame-by-frame camera and playback features turn their simple model into a shareable class movie.

Elsternwick|Year 1|Where We Are in Place.d: Students view homes in Melbourne and another part of the world using Google Maps and Street View. They look for roof shapes, building materials, gardens and nearby features, linking their observations to the line of inquiry about different types of homes. Pairs present a live comparison by showing two streets and explaining how culture or environment may have influenced the homes. The teacher uses the search box and Street View controls while students direct where to look and what to compare.

Students create a short digital book called “A Home That Suits Its Place” using Book Creator. On each page they draw or add a photo of a home, then record themselves explaining its important characteristics and how it suits the local culture or environment. Their finished book includes a cover, labelled pictures and a final page suggesting one sustainable feature such as shade, solar panels or a rainwater tank. The simple page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and voice recording make the task manageable for Year 1 students.

Students program Beebots to travel across a floor grid showing different homes and environmental features such as trees, water, roads and sunny spaces. They choose a home card, plan a route to a matching environment, then enter, test and debug the sequence using the directional buttons. This supports the line of inquiry about different types of homes by asking students to explain why a home suits a particular place. Each pair finishes by demonstrating its route and giving a short explanation of the match.

Students use ScratchJr to make a short animation showing how a home can become a more sustainable living space. They create a simple home scene and program a character to move between two or three features, such as closing curtains for shade, using a washing line or collecting water for plants. The animation directly supports the line of inquiry about the importance of sustainable living spaces. Students use the character, background and movement blocks to build, test and present their finished sequence.

Students complete a teacher-made Microsoft Forms survey about the characteristics of their homes, answering simple choice questions about features such as house type, outdoor space, windows and shared rooms. The class then views the automatic response charts and discusses which features are common and which are different. This provides class data for the line of inquiry about the characteristics of a home without asking students to share addresses or private details. Students finish by presenting one observation from the charts, using the form’s choice questions and response summary as their evidence.

Elsternwick|Year 1|Who We Are.d: Students program a Beebot to travel across a simple classroom floor map, stopping at places that help keep us safe, such as the bag area, doorway and meeting space. This explores safe environments and shows how careful actions influence our safety and wellbeing. Pairs use the directional buttons to enter, test and fix a sequence of steps, then present their safe route to the class. The finished result is a working route that classmates can watch and discuss.

Students make a short digital book about keeping their body and mind healthy, with one healthy action on each page. They draw or add a photo and record themselves explaining choices such as drinking water, resting, moving and asking for help. This directly supports the line of inquiry about keeping our body and mind healthy. Book Creator’s page, drawing and voice-recording features allow each child to publish a simple book to share with classmates.

Students photograph a familiar classroom object linked to safety, such as a chair, school bag or drink bottle, and add a moving mouth to make it speak. They record a short message explaining an action that keeps themselves and others safe around that object. This connects to how our actions affect ourselves and others. The photo, mouth line and voice-recording features create a short talking safety message that students can present to the class.

Students create a healthy choices collage for the Who We Are unit using photos of safe and healthy classroom actions. They arrange the photos and add short labels such as “wash hands,” “walk inside” and “take a calm breath.” This shows how the actions we take influence our safety and wellbeing. PicCollage’s photo layout, text and sticker features help students publish one clear poster for a classroom display.

Students code a short scene showing how one action can affect another person, such as walking safely past someone instead of pushing. They choose characters and backgrounds, then use simple movement and speech blocks to show the safe choice and its result. This directly explores how our actions affect ourselves and others. Each pair tests and fixes its sequence, then presents the finished animation and explains the wellbeing message.

Elsternwick|Year 2|How We Express Oursel.d: Students use Brushes Redux to create a digital artwork for How We Express Ourselves, choosing colours, lines and shapes that show an idea or feeling. This directly explores the line of inquiry, Forms of expression. They present their finished artwork to a partner and explain one artistic choice that might inspire someone else’s imagination. The simple brushes, colour palette and undo button make the task manageable for Year 2 students.

Students make a short digital art gallery about How We Express Ourselves using Book Creator. On each page, they add a photo of a class artwork, a sentence about what they notice and a voice recording explaining what they appreciate. This connects directly to Understanding and appreciating art and results in a shareable class gallery book. The built-in page layouts, camera, text and audio recording tools support the whole task in one place.

Students use ChatterPix Kids to make an artwork or classroom object speak about artistic expression in How We Express Ourselves. They take a photo, draw a mouth and record a short message explaining the colours, shapes or details that make it interesting. This supports the line of inquiry, Expressing thoughts and ideas, and produces a short talking-picture presentation. The camera, mouth-drawing line and voice recorder are simple enough for students to use with a partner.

Students use Puppet Pals to create a short scene in which two characters visit an art show and respond differently to the same artwork. They choose characters and a background, move the puppets while recording their voices, and include reasons for each character’s opinion. This explores Understanding and appreciating art by showing that people can notice and value different things. The character selection, backgrounds, puppet movement and voice recording turn the scene into a short performance the class can watch.

Students use ScratchJr to code a short animated artwork for How We Express Ourselves. They choose or draw characters and backgrounds, then join simple movement and appearance blocks so colours, shapes or characters move in a way that communicates an idea. This connects to the central idea that artistic expressions inspire imagination and creativity, and students finish with an animation they can present and explain. The block-based coding area, paint editor and start button let Year 2 students build, test and fix their sequence.

Elsternwick|Year 2|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students use Google Maps and Street View to explore Elsternwick shopping areas and compare them with a marketplace in another community. They look for shops, services and public spaces that show how marketplaces reflect the needs and wants of communities. Pairs present a short live walkthrough, pointing out three similarities or differences they noticed. The everyday map search, zoom and Street View features make the comparison easy to run without student logins.

Students use Book Creator to make a simple guide called Our Community Marketplace. Each page explains whether one local product or service meets a need or a want, linking directly to the needs and wants line of inquiry. Students publish a short book with drawings, labels and recorded explanations that can be shared with classmates. The page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and voice recording feature keep the task manageable for Year 2.

Students use ScratchJr to code a short marketplace scene in which a customer visits different stalls to find something they need and something they want. This helps them show how marketplaces reflect the needs and wants of communities. They create and present an animation with characters moving between stalls and speaking through simple text blocks. The picture-based movement, speech and start blocks allow students to build and debug a short sequence.

In small groups, students use Minecraft Education to build a model marketplace designed for the needs of their community. They follow the design process by planning stalls and paths, building them, testing whether people can move around easily, and improving the layout. Each group presents its finished marketplace and explains how two parts meet community needs or wants. The familiar block-building and sign features let students create a clear, walk-through model at a realistic scale.

Students use PicCollage to design a community market poster that sorts goods and services into needs and wants. This directly explores the needs and wants line of inquiry and prompts discussion about why different families may sort some items differently. Students create a shareable poster with pictures, headings and short reasons for their choices, then present it to a partner. The simple grid layouts, image tools, text boxes and stickers make the task quick and accessible for Year 2.

Elsternwick|Year 2|How the World Works.d: Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a floor grid showing a playground, using forward, backward and turn commands. They test how changing the sequence changes the robot’s motion, linking directly to the line of inquiry about forces around us. Pairs debug their commands until the Bee-Bot reaches a chosen location, then present the successful route to the class. The Bee-Bot’s directional buttons and clear button make the task manageable for Year 2 students.

Students use ScratchJr to show how a push can start motion or change an object’s speed and direction. They code a character or object with motion blocks, then adjust the number and direction of the blocks to compare what happens. This supports the central idea that forces and motion are all around us. Each student makes and shares a short animated demonstration, using ScratchJr’s characters, backgrounds and block-based coding.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short film showing a toy car being pushed, slowing down and changing direction. They move the car a small amount between each photo and play the sequence back to examine its motion. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about scientific laws of motion. The finished stop-motion film is a shareable explanation powered by the app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features.

Students test how far a toy car travels after gentle, medium and strong pushes, then enter the results into Microsoft Excel. They organise the numbers in a simple table and create a column chart to compare the distances. This investigation supports the line of inquiry about forces around us by showing how the size of a push can affect motion. The class presents its chart and discusses the pattern, using Excel’s cells and chart tool.

Students use Seesaw to record examples of pushes, pulls and motion around the classroom or playground. They capture a short video of one safe example and add a spoken explanation describing the force and what moved. This provides clear evidence for the central idea that forces and motion are all around us. Each student publishes a narrated learning post using Seesaw’s built-in video and voice recording features.

Elsternwick|Year 2|Sharing the Planet.d: Students explore the school grounds and use Seek by iNaturalist to identify plants, insects and other living things that share our environment. This connects to the line of inquiry about Earth's resources and helps students notice that habitats provide food and shelter. Pairs use the live camera identification feature and save a small collection of observations to share with the class. They present one living thing they found and suggest one choice people can make to protect it.

Students use Book Creator to make a short class book about everyday choices that help care for our Earth. Each pair creates a page linked to the line of inquiry about ways we can care for our planet, such as saving water, reusing paper or sorting waste. They add a drawing or photo, write one clear action and record themselves reading it aloud. The simple page tools and built-in voice recording produce a shareable book for another Year 2 class or families.

Students program Beebots to travel across a floor grid showing items such as a drink can, food scraps, paper and a reusable bottle. They plan and enter directional steps to move each item towards the matching reuse, recycling or compost area, then test and debug the route. This directly explores how our actions affect the environment and shows that caring for Earth starts with the choices we make. Each group presents one completed route and explains the environmental choice represented by its sequence.

Students use a simple Microsoft Forms survey to collect class data about choices such as using reusable drink bottles, switching off lights and using both sides of paper. This supports the central idea that taking care of our Earth starts with the choices we make. Students ask classmates the questions, enter the responses and view the automatic response charts. Small groups present one chart and name one realistic action the class could improve next week.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short film showing what happens when someone makes a more Earth-friendly choice. They might animate a piece of paper moving from the rubbish bin to the recycling bin or a tap being turned off while hands are soaped. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about how our actions affect the environment. Using the frame-by-frame camera and playback controls, pairs record and present a simple film with a clear before-and-after message.

Elsternwick|Year 2|Who We Are.d: Students make a short class book about how relationships with family, friends and classmates impact our lives. Each pair creates one page showing an everyday example of developing and maintaining a healthy relationship, such as listening, including others or solving a disagreement calmly. They add a drawing or photo, write a simple explanation and record themselves reading it aloud. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and voice recording make the finished book easy to share with the class.

Students draw a character who gives one useful tip for maintaining healthy relationships. They photograph the drawing in ChatterPix Kids, add a mouth and record the character explaining an action such as taking turns, apologising or asking someone to play. This directly explores developing and maintaining healthy relationships. The class watches the short talking-character clips and discusses which tips could help in the playground or classroom.

Students complete a short picture-supported class survey about actions that help relationships and wellbeing, such as being listened to, receiving help or being invited to join a game. This explores the impact of relationships on wellbeing by collecting real class responses without asking students to name particular people. The teacher displays the automatic response charts, and students identify the most common answers and share what they notice. Microsoft Forms’ simple questions and built-in response charts power the activity and create a clear class data summary.

In pairs, students code a short animated scene about two characters developing and maintaining a healthy relationship. They choose characters and backgrounds, then use movement, speech and sequencing blocks to show a small problem and a helpful response, such as sharing, listening or including someone. Students test and debug the sequence so the conversation happens in the correct order. They present the finished animation and explain how the characters’ relationship affects their wellbeing.

Students create a personal relationship web showing people and groups who support them, using first names, roles or drawings rather than private photographs if preferred. They arrange these around a central picture of themselves and add short captions explaining why each relationship is important. This directly explores the importance of relationships and the central idea that our relationships with others impact our lives. PicCollage’s layout, text, sticker and drawing features help students produce a clear visual poster to present to a partner or small group.

Elsternwick|Year 2|Where We Are in Place.d: Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a teacher-prepared floor map showing local landmarks and places of significance around Elsternwick. This directly explores the connection between landmarks and identity as students explain why each stop matters to the community. Pairs enter and test a sequence using the forward, backward and turn buttons, then debug the route if the Bee-Bot reaches the wrong place. Each pair presents a working landmark tour and gives a short spoken explanation at each stop.

Students choose a photograph of a local landmark and use ChatterPix Kids to make the landmark tell a short story about its history. This supports the central idea that landmarks and places of significance tell stories about our history. Students draw a mouth on the photograph, record a simple first-person message and add a title or decoration. They publish a short talking-landmark video to share with the class.

In pairs, students use Minecraft Education blocks to build a simple model of a landmark connected to their family, culture or the local area. This explores the significance of places to different people and cultures. Students add signs with a few key words explaining who values the place and why, then guide classmates through the model. Their finished build becomes a small virtual landmark exhibition that they can present from the screen.

Students create a collage comparing two landmarks from different times or cultures using teacher-provided photographs. This connects with the line of inquiry about how landmarks and symbols represent our history. Students arrange the images with the collage layout tools and add short labels for visible symbols, materials and clues about the past. They publish a one-page comparison poster and explain one important similarity or difference to a partner.

Students use ScratchJr to make a short animated visit to a landmark linked to the history of Melbourne or their own culture. This explores the connection between landmarks and identity by showing who visits the place and why it matters. Students create two or three scenes, move a character with coding blocks and add simple recorded narration or speech. They test and debug the sequence, then present the finished animated landmark story to the class.

Elsternwick|Year 3|How We Express Oursel.d: Students create a class digital book about the ways personal and cultural events are celebrated. Each pair makes a page about one celebration, adding a drawing or photo, a short explanation and a recorded voice description. The finished book connects to the line of inquiry about appreciating the diversity of cultures and can be read together or shared with families. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and voice recording make the task manageable for Year 3 students.

Students explore how music helps people express joy, belonging and identity during celebrations and traditions. In small groups, they use GarageBand’s ready-made loops and virtual instruments to create a short piece of welcoming music for a class community celebration. Each group records a spoken introduction explaining how its choices connect to the central idea that celebrations and traditions shape community culture. The class listens to the finished recordings and discusses how different sounds can create different celebration moods.

Students build a shared class display showing the different ways families and communities celebrate important events. Each student publishes one post with a title, a short description and a drawing, photo or voice recording, using information they are comfortable sharing. They then read classmates’ posts and add respectful comments about similarities and differences, supporting the line of inquiry about appreciating the diversity of cultures. Padlet’s simple post and comment features create a shareable celebration wall that can be revisited throughout the unit.

Students make a visual comparison of two celebrations connected to the unit How We Express Ourselves. They arrange pictures, labels and short captions to show features such as food, clothing, music, symbols and community activities. Their finished collage explains both shared features and important differences, connecting directly to the line of inquiry about the ways personal and cultural events are celebrated. PicCollage’s grids, text boxes, stickers and image tools help Year 3 students organise the comparison clearly on one page.

Students use classroom objects or paper figures to create a short stop-motion scene showing how a celebration brings a community together. They plan and photograph a simple sequence such as preparing a shared space, welcoming people, taking part in a tradition and celebrating together. The finished animation includes a title and presents an example of the line of inquiry about how celebrations shape community identity. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback tools let students test their movement, fix unclear sections and present the final animation to the class.

Elsternwick|Year 3|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students create a short digital handbook about the rights and responsibilities of citizens in their school community. Each page explains one right, the matching responsibility and a possible consequence when it is not respected, directly exploring the line of inquiry about rights and responsibilities of citizens. Students publish a shareable class book with written examples, drawings and recorded explanations. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and audio recording make the handbook manageable for Year 3 students.

Students create a class quiz using everyday situations about rules and laws, such as playground expectations, road rules and wearing a seatbelt. They ask classmates to decide whether each example is a rule or a law and explain who is responsible for enforcing it, linking directly to the differences between rules and laws. Students collect responses and present the automatic results charts, discussing any questions where the class disagreed. Microsoft Forms’ question choices and response charts provide a simple way to collect and compare the class data.

In small groups, students build a simple community that shows how rules and laws help people organise themselves. They add places such as a school, road, park and council office, then use signs to label a relevant rule or law, who enforces it and what may happen if it is not followed. Each group presents a walkthrough of its finished community, connecting the build to the central idea that citizens’ rights and responsibilities are determined by community rules and laws. Minecraft Education’s blocks and writable signs are the main features students use to build and explain their ideas.

Students design a one-page citizen guide called “What Should I Do?” about the consequences when rules, laws and rights are not met. They choose a realistic situation, such as unsafe road crossing or damage to a shared playground, and show the rule or law, the people affected, the responsible authority and a fair next step. Students present or publish their finished guide for classmates to read and discuss. Canva’s ready-made page layouts, text boxes and icon library help Year 3 students organise the information clearly.

Students use Padlet to investigate the people responsible for enforcing rules and laws in a community. Each pair adds a post about one person, such as a teacher, police officer, local councillor or crossing supervisor, and records what that person is responsible for and one limit on their authority. Classmates comment with a question or an additional example, creating a shared wall that can be presented and revisited during the unit. Padlet’s post, image and comment features make it easy to collect and compare everyone’s contributions in one place.

Elsternwick|Year 3|Who We Are.d: Students create a “Who We Are” page showing three things that shape their identity, such as family traditions, interests and personal values. This connects to the central idea’s focus on the nature of the self, beliefs and values. They use Seesaw’s drawing, text and voice-recording tools to make and explain their page. Each student publishes a finished reflection that can be shared with classmates and families.

Students create a short class survey about everyday habits that support physical, mental and social health in the Who We Are unit. This directly explores the central idea’s focus on personal health and wellbeing. In small groups, they write simple multiple-choice questions, collect classmates’ responses and examine the automatic response charts. Each group presents one pattern they noticed and one realistic wellbeing suggestion based on the class data.

Students build a small community space that helps people feel healthy, safe and connected as part of the Who We Are unit. This links to the central idea’s focus on personal, physical, mental, social and spiritual health and human relationships. Using Minecraft Education’s blocks and signs, they might create a garden, quiet area, play space or welcoming meeting place and label how each part helps people. Pairs present a short in-game walkthrough of their completed space and explain their design choices.

Students explore Dollar Street photographs to see how families in different places live, spend time together and meet everyday needs in the Who We Are unit. This connects to the central idea’s focus on beliefs, values and human relationships. They use the location, income and topic filters to compare photographs of homes, meals, play or family life without ranking one way of living as better than another. Pairs present two photographs directly from Dollar Street and share respectful observations about similarities, differences and what may matter to each family.

Students make a one-page “My Wellbeing Toolkit” for the Who We Are unit, choosing practical actions that support their body, mind and relationships. This directly connects to the central idea’s focus on personal, physical, mental and social health. They use a simple Canva poster template with text boxes, shapes and approved images to organise ideas such as movement, rest, calming strategies and asking for help. Each student publishes and presents a clear poster they could genuinely use during an ordinary school week.

Elsternwick|Year 3|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Seek by iNaturalist to photograph and identify plants, insects and other living things around the school grounds. They record several photo observations to explore the roles of living things in an ecosystem. Each group presents its observations and explains how one identified living thing may depend on others for food, shelter or pollination. The tool’s camera-based identification feature makes the investigation manageable for Year 3 students.

Students use Google Maps and Street View to explore two environments, such as a Melbourne wetland and a dry inland area. They compare visible vegetation, water, shelter and signs of human activity while investigating how changing environments affect the survival of living things. Pairs present a short guided Street View walkthrough, pointing out features that may benefit or harm each ecosystem. The familiar search, zoom and Street View controls allow students to examine real places without creating or saving a map.

Students build a small Minecraft Education ecosystem containing suitable plants, animals, water, food and shelter. They use the model to show the roles of living things in an ecosystem and then change one part, such as removing trees or adding too much development, to show how survival may be affected. Each group creates signs explaining key relationships and presents a guided walkthrough of its completed world. The tool’s block building, animals, plants and in-world signs make the ecosystem visible and easy to discuss.

Students create a one-page Canva action guide about protecting a local ecosystem, such as a beach, wetland or school garden. They explain one action that benefits the ecosystem and one action that harms it, directly addressing the line of inquiry about human actions. The finished guide includes a clear heading, short explanations and labelled images, and can be presented to classmates or shared with families. Canva’s simple page templates, text boxes and built-in image library keep the task realistic for Year 3.

Students code Sphero BOLT to travel across a teacher-prepared floor map as if it were carrying seeds from one habitat patch to another. They plan and debug a route that avoids marked roads, buildings and damaged areas, linking the task to actions that benefit or harm ecosystems. Each group presents its final code and runs the robot route, then explains how connected habitats can help living things survive in changing environments. Sphero BOLT’s block coding, movement controls and programmable LED matrix provide clear feedback as students test and improve the route.

Elsternwick|Year 3|Where We Are in Place.d: Students use Google Maps to retrace part of an explorer’s journey, viewing key locations, landmarks and distances along the route. They connect their observations to the line of inquiry about the factors that motivate exploration by discussing how distance, landscape and access to water may have affected decisions. Each group presents a short guided walkthrough of the journey to the class, pointing out three important places and one challenge. The everyday map, distance and Street View features make the route visible and understandable for Year 3 students.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital book about a past exploration and the discovery or new understanding that followed. They link their work to the central idea that exploration leads to new discoveries that can shape and change society. Each book includes a title page, a simple route or sequence, key facts, a reflection on the change created, and a recorded student narration. The easy page templates, text boxes, drawing tools and voice recording feature allow students to publish and share a clear explanation.

Students code Sphero BOLT to travel across a teacher-prepared floor map representing an exploration route with several stopping points. They test and debug the speed, time and compass headings needed to reach each location, connecting the task to how navigation supports exploration and new discoveries. Each group presents its completed route and explains one change it made after testing. The block coding controls for movement, heading and the programmable light display make the navigation challenge practical and visible.

Students use Padlet to build a class evidence wall showing how discoveries from past exploration led to changes for people, places or society. Each pair posts one example with a short explanation, an image supplied by the teacher and a reflection on whether the change had positive, negative or mixed effects. This directly addresses the line of inquiry about how people reflect on discoveries from the past to inform change. Padlet’s simple post, image and comment features let the class publish, compare and respond to examples in one shared space.

Students use Canva to create a one-page timeline showing the motivation, journey, discovery and lasting change connected with one exploration. They link each stage to the line of inquiry about how exploration brings about change and new understandings for people, places and society. Students present the finished timeline to a partner, using arrows and short captions to explain cause and effect. Canva’s ready-made timeline layouts, text boxes, shapes and image library help Year 3 students produce a clear, shareable visual summary.

Elsternwick|Year 3|How the World Works.d: Students explore How the World Works by using block coding to make Sphero BOLT’s LED matrix change when its ambient light sensor detects light or darkness. They test the program in several classroom locations, record what happens and debug any instructions that do not work as expected. This connects directly to the process of learning and shows how people use a scientific understanding of light to create an automated response. Each group presents a working light-responsive program and explains the evidence that helped them improve it.

Students explore How the World Works by creating a short digital book about a scientist and the understanding that scientist helped change. They use pages, text, drawings, images and voice recording to explain the scientist’s question, process, evidence and impact. This directly supports the lines of inquiry into the work of scientists and how science brings about new understandings and changes. Each student publishes a clear, shareable scientist profile for classmates to read or listen to.

Students explore How the World Works by making a stop-motion explanation of a simple scientific investigation completed in class. They arrange and move classroom objects frame by frame to show the question, prediction, fair test, observations and conclusion. This connects directly to the process of learning by showing that scientific understanding develops through careful testing and evidence. Students add titles and narration in Stop Motion Studio, then present their finished science-process film to the class.

Students explore How the World Works by entering predictions and results from a class investigation into a shared Microsoft Form. They answer simple multiple-choice and number questions, then examine the automatic charts to find patterns in the class data. This supports the process of learning by showing how scientists collect evidence before making a conclusion. The class presents the completed response charts and agrees on an evidence-based statement about what the investigation showed.

Students explore How the World Works by creating a one-page explanation of a scientific principle people use to take action, such as using shade to reduce heating or reflective clothing to improve visibility. They combine a heading, short text, labelled images and a practical action people can take. This links directly to the central idea that humans use their understanding of scientific principles to take action. Using Adobe Express templates and simple page-design tools, students publish a clear science action poster for a class display.

Elsternwick|Year 4|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to investigate how transport systems connect people and services in a community. They add routes, labels and symbols to show links between homes, schools, shops, hospitals and public transport. This directly explores the line of inquiry about interconnections within and across systems. Each group presents its annotated map and explains what could happen if one important connection stopped working. The everyday map layers and drawing tools make the connections clear and manageable for Year 4 students.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital book about a familiar human system, such as rubbish collection, food delivery or public transport. On each page, they explain one part of the system and show how it connects with the next part. This supports the central idea that systems connect us. Students combine text, drawings, photos and recorded narration, then share their finished books with classmates. Book Creator's simple page templates and audio recording button help students explain their thinking clearly.

Students use Microsoft Forms to collect class data about how people use community systems such as transport, libraries, recycling and local shops. In small groups, they write a short set of multiple-choice questions, share the form with classmates and examine the response charts. This investigates the influence of systems on communities by showing which services people rely on and why. Each group presents two findings and one question raised by the data. The built-in question choices and automatic charts keep the task practical and easy to read.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small community containing connected systems such as roads, public transport, water supply, food distribution and waste collection. Teams construct one system and use signs to explain how it connects with the work of other teams. This directly explores the interconnections that exist within and across systems. The class then walks through the shared world while each team presents what it built and explains how a breakdown would affect the community. Minecraft's building blocks, signs and shared world provide a clear way to create and test the layout together.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show how an item moves through a human system, such as a library book being borrowed and returned or a parcel travelling from sender to receiver. They arrange simple classroom objects, capture one frame at a time and add short titles for each stage. This connects to the line of inquiry about human systems and shows that each step depends on other people and processes. Pairs publish a short stop-motion film and present where the system could be delayed or improved. The frame-by-frame camera and title tools are the main features used for the task.

Elsternwick|Year 4|How We Express Oursel.d: Students use Book Creator to make a short digital book showing how technology transforms how we create and share ideas. Each page compares an older communication tool, such as a handwritten letter, with a newer tool, such as a video message, directly exploring the evolution of communication tools. Students combine their own writing, drawings, voice recordings and page layouts, then present the finished book to classmates. The simple add-text, drawing and audio recording features make this manageable for Year 4 students.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short animation about how technology expands creative possibilities. In small groups, they move paper shapes or classroom objects a little at a time, photograph each change and test the sequence before fixing any unclear sections. They finish with a shareable stop-motion film that communicates an idea which would be difficult to show in one still picture. The frame-by-frame camera, playback and simple editing controls are the key features used.

Students use Brushes Redux to explore the impact of technology on expression by creating a digital artwork about a place, memory or issue that matters to them. They test different brushes, colours, line widths and layers, then use undo to revise choices without starting again. Each student presents a finished digital artwork and explains one creative choice that the technology made possible. The everyday brush, colour, layer and undo tools are central to the task.

Students use Podcasting using Canva to record a short class podcast episode about how technology transforms how we create and share ideas. Pairs plan and record an interview in which one student describes an older communication tool and the other explains how a newer tool changed expression. They replay their recording, improve unclear sections and publish a short episode for the class to hear. Canva’s audio recording, trimming and page-based presentation features support the whole task.

Students use Padlet to build a class display about the evolution of communication tools. Each student adds a post describing one tool, such as a printing press, telephone, email or video call, and explains what it allowed people to share. Classmates read the posts and add a thoughtful comment about how that technology affected expression. Padlet’s shared board, post and comment features create a concrete class collection that can be presented and revisited.

Elsternwick|Year 4|How the World Works.d: Students code Sphero BOLT to travel the same distance at different speeds, then test how its movement changes on smooth and rough classroom surfaces. This directly explores interactions between objects and materials within a moving system. They compare the movement data from each trial, debug their code and present which surface had the greatest effect. The block coding controls and motor movement data make the investigation practical and repeatable.

Students investigate how quickly ice melts in different classroom locations and enter the time and conditions for each trial into Microsoft Forms. This supports the line of inquiry into gathering and analysing evidence about interactions between materials and their surroundings. The class uses the automatic response charts to compare results, identify patterns and discuss whether the evidence supports their predictions. Their final product is a shared set of results and a class conclusion based on the charts.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to explore how water, land and living things interact within a chosen environment. This connects to the line of inquiry about interactions between objects, materials and living things within systems. They turn map layers on and off, examine patterns, and add drawings and labels to show where particular interactions may occur. Each group presents an annotated digital map explaining one clear relationship, such as how a river supports nearby plants, animals and people.

Students use Explain Everything to create a short scientific explanation based on evidence from a class investigation into dissolving, melting or another change in materials. This directly supports gathering and analysing evidence and the central idea that scientific investigations help us understand interactions within systems. They place their observations on the canvas, draw arrows or simple diagrams to show cause and effect, and record a spoken conclusion. The everyday whiteboard, drawing and voice-recording features produce a clear presentation that can be replayed and discussed.

Students use Padlet to build a class timeline showing how scientific knowledge about a familiar topic, such as the water cycle or animal habitats, has changed as new evidence was gathered. This addresses the line of inquiry into how scientific knowledge develops. Working from teacher-provided information, students publish short posts that name an earlier idea, the new evidence and the revised explanation, then comment with questions about the evidence. Padlet’s posts, columns and commenting tools create a shareable timeline that shows science developing through testing and discussion.

Elsternwick|Year 4|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Google Maps to explore several First Nations communities and Countries identified in teacher-provided, trusted sources, including local Bunurong Country. They switch between the map, satellite view and Street View where available to compare location, distance, waterways and nearby landmarks. This directly supports the line of inquiry into the diversity of First Nations people and avoids treating all communities as the same. Pairs present a short guided comparison to the class by moving around the map and explaining three observations.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital book about why Country is important to First Nations people. Using teacher-provided information from First Nations organisations, they create pages about land, waterways, language, community and caring for Country. This directly addresses the line of inquiry about the importance of Country to First Nations people. Each finished book combines typed explanations, images and the student's recorded narration, then is shared with classmates.

Students use Padlet to build a class collection showing the diversity of First Nations people across Australia. Each pair adds a post about one teacher-selected Nation or community, including its correct name, location, language information and one fact from a trusted First Nations source. This supports the line of inquiry into the diversity of First Nations people and helps students notice both shared connections and important differences. Padlet's simple post, image and comment features allow the class to publish the collection and leave respectful questions for other pairs.

Students use Explain Everything to create a visual explanation of how family, kinship and community can connect people, based only on teacher-provided First Nations sources. They arrange key words and simple symbols on the canvas, draw connecting lines, and record themselves explaining what each connection means without copying sacred designs or personal family structures. This directly supports the line of inquiry about the importance of community, family and kinship. The finished narrated canvas becomes a short presentation that students can play for a partner or the class.

Students use the Podcast Equipment to record a short class podcast responding to the central idea that Country, language and community are significant to the lives of First Nations people. Small groups prepare questions and answers from teacher-provided First Nations voices and sources, with roles such as host, fact-checker and speaker. They record a clear introduction, three key ideas and a respectful closing using the microphones and recorder. The completed audio episode is played to the class as a shared summary of the unit learning.

Elsternwick|Year 4|Who We Are.d: Students survey classmates about which qualities make an effective leader, such as fairness, courage, listening and honesty, and enter the responses into Excel. They use the results to explore the line of inquiry about qualities of influential leaders. Using simple tables and chart tools, each group makes a labelled column chart showing the class’s most valued leadership qualities. Groups present their chart and explain what the data suggests about how leaders shape communities.

Students use iMovie to record a short mock news report about a community leader responding to a realistic issue, such as improving a playground or making a school event fairer. The report explores the purpose of leadership in communities by showing the leader listening, making a decision and explaining it. Students edit their clips, add a title and record clear narration using iMovie’s everyday video and audio tools. Each group publishes and screens a one- to two-minute news report for the class.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to locate places where leadership happens in the local community, such as schools, council buildings, sporting clubs and community centres. They add map markers and short notes explaining who leads in each place and what responsibilities that person or group has. This directly supports the line of inquiry about the roles and responsibilities of effective leadership. Students present their annotated map and explain how the different leaders help the community function.

In small groups, students use Minecraft Education blocks to build a compact community containing places such as a school, council office, park and emergency service. They add signs naming the leaders connected with each place and describing one important responsibility. Groups then respond to a teacher-set community problem by changing their build or signs to show how leaders could listen, decide and act, linking to the central idea that leaders shape communities. Students give the class a live guided tour of their finished Minecraft community and explain their choices.

Students use Explain Everything to create a narrated leadership web with an influential leader in the centre and examples of their actions, responsibilities and qualities around the outside. They use the canvas, drawing tools, text boxes and voice recording to explain how each action affected a community. This brings together the lines of inquiry about effective leadership and the qualities of influential leaders. Each student finishes with a short, shareable presentation that can be played for a partner or the class.

Elsternwick|Year 4|Where We Are in Place.d: Students create a short digital book about one real example of human migration, such as a family moving to Australia after war or in search of work. Their pages explain the reasons people migrate and show the challenges and opportunities faced before, during and after the move. Each student publishes a book with a simple route map drawn on the page, short factual captions and a recorded first-person reflection based on their research. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tool and voice-recording button make the task manageable for Year 4 students.

Students enter a small teacher-provided set of migration data, such as the birth countries represented in a community across several decades. They use the data to investigate migration throughout history and notice which groups grew, changed or stayed similar over time. Each pair produces a clearly labelled table and a column chart, then presents two observations supported by the numbers. Excel’s cells, simple formulas and chart button are the everyday features that power the activity.

Small groups add posts about different migrant groups that have helped shape Melbourne, including when they arrived, why they migrated and one contribution they made. The class uses the shared board to explore the effects of migration on communities, cultures and individuals. Students publish a concise case-study post with a heading, image, factual paragraph and source link, then respond to another group with a thoughtful comparison. Padlet’s shared posting board and comment feature allow the whole class to build and discuss one collection.

Students make a short stop-motion sequence showing a real migration journey from one historical period studied in the unit. Using paper people, labels and a simple background map, they show the challenge that prompted the move, the journey and an opportunity or change at the destination. The finished film presents migration as a response to challenges and opportunities rather than as movement without a reason. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback controls let students capture, check and improve the sequence as they work.

Students design a one-page comparison of a community before and after a significant period of migration. They include evidence of changes to food, language, work, celebrations or local places, directly addressing the effects of migration on communities, cultures and individuals. Each student presents a finished visual comparison with two clear sections, brief captions and a concluding statement about both benefits and challenges. Canva’s ready-made page layouts, text boxes and image library help Year 4 students organise the information clearly.

Elsternwick|Year 5|How We Express Oursel.d: Students use Canva to create two advertisements for the same imaginary product, with each version targeting a different audience such as younger children and parents. They change the colours, images, wording and layout to explore the devices used to target audiences. Each student presents the two finished advertisements and explains why particular choices may influence each audience. Canva’s ready-made layouts, image library and text tools make the task manageable in two lessons.

Students use Book Creator to make a short guide called “How Messages Influence Us” about the critical evaluation of messages. On each page, they add an example message and identify devices such as emotional words, celebrity support, selective facts or eye-catching images. They record a brief audio explanation of how a reader could check the message before believing or sharing it. Book Creator’s page templates, text, drawing and audio recording tools allow students to publish a clear digital guide for classmates.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to make a 20-second advertisement for a simple classroom object, targeting a chosen audience. They move paper shapes, labels or the object a small amount between photos, then test whether music, pace and repeated slogans make the message more persuasive. This directly explores how people can create or manipulate messages to target specific audiences. The frame-by-frame camera and playback controls let students film, review and improve a short advertisement within a lesson or two.

Students use Padlet to collect and critically evaluate messages found in teacher-provided advertisements, posters and product packaging. Each student publishes a post naming the intended audience, the persuasive devices used and one sign that the message may be manipulating the viewer. Classmates add comments explaining whether they felt influenced and what caused that response. Padlet’s post, image and comment features create a shared evidence wall that the class can present and discuss.

Students use Podcasting using Canva to record a short interview-style episode about how we know we have been influenced by a message. One student plays an advertiser and explains choices such as repetition, humour or emotional language, while another plays a careful audience member who questions those choices. Pairs produce a two-minute episode that ends with practical tips for checking persuasive messages. Canva’s audio recording, editing and presentation tools allow students to record and publish the episode in one place.

Elsternwick|Year 5|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to survey classmates about what they value in sustainable products, such as reusable packaging, local materials or donations to a community group. This explores sustainable business practices and helps students see how entrepreneurs can research customer needs responsibly. They create questions, collect responses and study the automatic charts to identify patterns. Each group presents one product decision supported by its survey data.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to investigate how the environment may be affected when materials and products travel between different places. They mark and label a possible supply chain for a familiar product, such as a cotton T-shirt, and compare a long-distance option with a more local option. This directly explores how our environment is impacted by the products we create. Students present an annotated map showing locations, routes and a practical change an entrepreneur could make to reduce impact.

Students use Adobe Express to create a simple marketing page for a sustainable product or service they have planned. Their page explains the product, its environmental benefits, its price and how part of the profit or service will give back to others. This connects the central idea that entrepreneurs have a responsibility to develop, market and sell sustainable products and services. Students use ready-made templates, text boxes and images to publish a clear advertisement for a class showcase.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small model of a sustainable business, such as a repair shop, refill store or food-waste collection service. They include clear areas for customers, materials, waste reduction and a way the business gives back to the community. This brings together sustainable business practices and the power of giving back. Using blocks, signs and in-game books, each group creates a walk-through model and leads classmates on a short guided tour.

Students use Podcasting using Canva to record a short entrepreneur pitch for a sustainable product or service. The recording explains the customer need, environmental impact, marketing plan and how the business will give back. This directly addresses the responsibility entrepreneurs have when developing, marketing and selling sustainable products and services. Students use Canva’s audio recording and timeline editing tools to produce and present a two-minute class podcast episode.

Elsternwick|Year 5|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to collect anonymous class views about common types of conflict, such as disagreements over games, group work or shared spaces. This directly explores the lines of inquiry into types of conflict and their causes and impacts. In pairs, students write clear multiple-choice questions, share the form with classmates and examine the automatic response charts. They present two patterns they noticed and suggest one peaceful response supported by the collected data.

Elsternwick|Year 5|Sharing the Planet.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
Elsternwick|Year 5|Sharing the Planet.d: Students create a short animated conversation showing two characters resolving a conflict peacefully. This connects directly to the central idea that finding peaceful solutions to conflict can make a difference. Students choose a character and background, then record their own dialogue so the character moves with their voice. They publish a one-minute scene that clearly shows the conflict, a listening or compromise strategy, and the outcome.

Small groups build a shared Minecraft Education space where two communities initially disagree about how limited land or resources should be used. This practical challenge explores causes and impacts of conflict as well as conflict resolution. Students build the two viewpoints, negotiate a fair solution, and change the world to show their agreed plan using ordinary building blocks and in-world signs. Each group gives classmates a guided walk-through explaining what caused the conflict and how its final design supports a peaceful solution.
