Students use Padlet to create a class collection of realistic conflict scenarios connected to school, communities and the wider world. This helps the class compare types of conflict and identify their possible causes and impacts. Each pair publishes a short scenario card, then uses comments to suggest a peaceful response to another pair’s situation. The finished Padlet becomes a shareable conflict-resolution wall containing scenarios, solutions and reasons those solutions may work.

Students use Explain Everything to make a narrated conflict-resolution flowchart for a familiar Year 5 disagreement. This directly addresses the line of inquiry into conflict resolution and the central idea about peaceful solutions making a difference. They draw each step on the canvas, move simple shapes or characters through the choices, and record a voice explanation using the built-in drawing and recording tools. Their finished presentation shows the conflict, two possible responses, the likely impact of each response and the most peaceful outcome.

Elsternwick|Year 5|Who We Are.d: Students collect anonymous class responses to everyday choice scenarios linked to beliefs and values, such as including someone, reducing waste or speaking up when something is unfair. They enter the results into Microsoft Excel and examine how values and beliefs impact choices. Using a simple table and chart feature, each group creates a graph showing the class patterns and adds a short written conclusion. Groups present their chart and explain how the same situation can lead people to make different choices.

Students create a short digital case study about a fictional Year 5 student whose beliefs and values influence a difficult choice. Each page shows the choice, the reasons behind it and the impact on other people, directly exploring how people's choices and actions impact others. Students use Book Creator's page templates, text, drawing and voice-recording features to make an illustrated book with a spoken reflection. They publish and share the finished book with classmates, who identify whether the decision was responsible and suggest another possible action.

Students design a one-page campaign about responsible decision-making in a familiar setting such as the classroom, playground, sports field or online group. They connect the campaign to the central idea by showing how one person's choices, guided by beliefs and values, can affect others. Using Adobe Express templates, text boxes, images and simple design tools, students create a clear poster with a practical call to action. The posters are presented to the class and published for a suitable school audience.

In small groups, students plan and record a short stop-motion scene in which a character faces a choice involving fairness, honesty, inclusion or responsibility. The scene shows what the character values, the choice they make and the resulting impact on others, addressing responsible decision-making. Students use Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame camera and playback features to move simple classroom objects or paper characters and check whether the sequence is clear. Each group presents its finished animation and explains how a different belief or value might have changed the ending.

Students work in small groups to build two versions of a shared community space in Minecraft Education, such as a park or school courtyard. One version shows choices based mainly on individual wants, while the other shows responsible choices that consider access, safety, inclusion and care for others. Using the building blocks, signs and in-world camera, students create and record a guided comparison that explores how people's choices and actions impact others. Groups lead classmates through their builds and justify which beliefs and values shaped each design decision.

Elsternwick|Year 5|Where We Are in Place.d: Students explore places connected to British colonisation in Australia, such as the Melbourne area, Sydney Cove and selected First Nations cultural sites. They use the map, satellite view, Street View and distance tool to examine location, landscape, travel distances and how places have changed, linking to the impact of colonisation. In pairs, students prepare and present a live map walkthrough that explains three significant locations and what happened there. The teacher can provide a short list of reliable place names so students spend their time observing and discussing rather than searching widely.

Students create a short digital book about how colonisation has shaped Australian society. Each pair builds pages that include a colonist account, a First Nations account, and a present-day reflection, connecting directly to the line of inquiry about colonisation stories. They combine written summaries, sourced images, captions and their own audio narration to make a book that can be shared with classmates. Book Creator's simple page layout and built-in audio recording make the task manageable for Year 5 students.

Students build an annotated timeline showing selected effects of colonisation in Australia across the past, present and possible future. They place dates, short explanations and images on the whiteboard canvas, then draw arrows to show links between events and continuing effects. Each group records a brief presentation that explains its timeline and identifies one effect that is still visible today. Explain Everything's movable canvas, drawing tools and voice recording are the main features used for the task.

Students create a class collection of colonisation stories based on teacher-approved sources. Each pair publishes one post containing a short summary, an image or quotation, the perspective represented, and a note about what may be missing from the account. They then read and comment on two other posts to compare how the same period can be told differently, linking to the line of inquiry about colonisation stories. Padlet's shared board, posts and comments allow the class to publish and discuss the collection in one place.

Students record a three-minute podcast episode answering the question, “How has colonisation shaped society in Australia?” Working in small groups, they plan a host introduction, two evidence-based points about past and present effects, and a respectful concluding reflection about the future. They record their voices, arrange the audio and add a simple title screen to produce an episode for a class listening session. Canva's audio recording and timeline editing tools support the whole task without requiring specialist sound skills.

Elsternwick|Year 5|How the World Works.d: Students code Sphero BOLT to travel through a model emergency route after a natural hazard, avoiding blocked roads and stopping at a marked supply point. This connects to how design processes are used to generate and test solutions. They test the route, adjust distances and turns, debug their code, and finish with a working program and live demonstration. The key feature is Sphero BOLT’s simple block coding for movement, direction and lights.

Students build a small community designed to cope with a chosen natural hazard such as flooding, bushfire or earthquake. This explores how design processes enable people to respond creatively to challenges in the natural world. Their finished world includes homes, safe routes and protective features, with signs explaining the purpose of each design choice. The everyday Minecraft features of placing blocks, adding signs and walking through the world let students build and present their solution.

Students enter a supplied set of data about natural hazards, such as rainfall, earthquake strength, damage costs or numbers of people affected. This supports the line of inquiry into the nature and impact of natural hazards by helping students look for patterns and compare events. They create a clear table and chart, then add a short written conclusion explaining what the data shows. Excel’s cells, sorting tools and chart button are the main features used.

Students create a short digital design proposal for helping a community prepare for a natural hazard. This connects to how design processes are used to generate and test solutions, as students explain the problem, sketch two possible ideas and justify their final choice. They publish a shareable book containing labelled drawings, written explanations and a brief recorded pitch. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tool, text boxes and audio recording make the task manageable for Year 5.

Students create a short class survey about the ethical and practical choices involved in responding to a natural hazard, such as whether limited funds should go towards shelters, warning systems or rebuilding. This directly explores the line of inquiry into responsibility in human responses to natural challenges. Classmates complete the survey, and students use the response summary to present the class priorities and explain any difficult trade-offs. Microsoft Forms’ question types, response collection and automatic charts power the activity.

Elsternwick|Year 6|How the World Works.d: Students build and code a small motorised lifting machine to explore how electrical energy is converted into movement and used to support human progress. They test how reliably the machine lifts the same load and adjust the code, gearing or structure when it struggles. This directly addresses different forms of energy and how they are used. Each group presents its working model and explains the energy changes, using the motor, building pieces and block coding as the key features.

Students use Microsoft Excel to compare supplied data about the energy produced, cost and greenhouse gas emissions of sources such as coal, gas, solar, wind and hydroelectricity. They enter or organise the figures, calculate simple totals or averages, and create charts that make the differences easy to see. This supports the line of inquiry into the impact of different energy sources on the planet. Each pair presents a chart and a short evidence-based recommendation, using spreadsheet cells, formulas and chart tools.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to investigate where solar, wind, hydroelectric and fossil-fuel energy are produced and what geographical conditions support each source. They add selected locations and brief annotations showing features such as strong winds, major rivers, sunny climates or nearby settlements. This connects directly to different forms of energy and sustainable energy practices. Students publish or present an annotated energy map, using MapMaker’s map layers, drawing and annotation tools.

Students create a one-page public information graphic explaining practical sustainable energy practices for homes, schools or local communities. They include examples such as reducing unnecessary electricity use, choosing renewable power and improving heating or cooling habits, with a brief explanation of the energy saved or transformed. This addresses sustainable energy practices and how energy use can support human progress with less impact on the planet. Students share a polished digital poster made with Adobe Express templates, text boxes, icons and images.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to make a short animation showing a chain of energy transformations, such as sunlight becoming electrical energy in a solar panel and then light from a lamp. They move simple classroom objects or paper pieces a small amount between each photo and add labels so each energy change is clear. This directly explores the central idea that energy may be converted and transformed. Each group presents a finished stop-motion explanation, using the app’s frame-by-frame camera, timeline and title tools.

Elsternwick|Year 6|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students plan their student-led exhibition (PYPEX) inquiry on a Freeform board, adding their chosen issue, questions, possible sources and next steps. This directly supports the line of inquiry into approaches to learning by helping them organise their time, thinking and responsibilities. They finish with a clear inquiry plan they can show to their teacher and mentor. Freeform’s sticky notes, text boxes, shapes and connecting lines make it easy to move ideas around as the inquiry develops.

Students use Padlet to collect and sort research for their student-led exhibition (PYPEX) topic. This supports the line of inquiry into research skills as they post short notes, source links, images and summaries under useful headings such as causes, viewpoints and possible action. Each group creates a shareable research wall and uses comments to give another group specific feedback about missing evidence or unclear claims. Padlet’s columns, posts and comment feature keep the task simple and visible.

Students create a digital process journal showing how their student-led exhibition (PYPEX) inquiry changes from the first question to the final conclusion. This connects to the central idea that students develop and present their own units of inquiry, while making their choices and learning visible. Their finished book includes research notes, source checks, reflections, images and short audio explanations, and can be shared with teachers, families or exhibition visitors. Book Creator’s page templates, text, drawing, image and audio tools allow students to keep everything together in one place.

Students design a short visual presentation for their student-led exhibition (PYPEX) topic, explaining the issue, key evidence, different viewpoints and the action they recommend. This directly develops the unit’s line of inquiry into presentation skills because students must turn a large amount of research into a clear message for an audience. They produce a polished set of presentation pages that can be shown during the exhibition or shared as a link. Adobe Express’s templates, text tools, image placement and simple page layouts help Year 6 students create a consistent design without needing advanced editing skills.

Students create a short Kahoot quiz to check what visitors understand after hearing their student-led exhibition (PYPEX) presentation. This supports the line of inquiry into presentation skills by asking students to identify the most important ideas and write clear, fair questions about them. Each group publishes and hosts a five-question quiz, then reviews the class results to see which parts of its explanation may need improving. Kahoot’s multiple-choice questions, timed responses and automatic results provide quick audience feedback.

Elsternwick|Year 6|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to survey classmates about how the local community should care for parks, beaches and wildlife. This directly explores how community values shape the management of the natural environment. They write clear multiple-choice and short-answer questions, collect responses and examine the automatic response charts. Each group presents one finding and explains how it could influence an environmental decision. The everyday features doing the work are the question builder, response link and automatic charts.

Students use Microsoft Excel to record data from a one-week classroom waste audit linked to Sharing the Planet. This investigates the need for sustainable practices by showing how much paper, food packaging and other waste the class produces. They enter daily totals, use simple formulas to calculate category totals and create a column chart. Each group shares its chart and proposes one realistic change the class can test the following week. The key features are the spreadsheet cells, simple formulas and chart tool.

Students use Google Maps and Street View to compare how two communities interact with a river, coastline, park or other natural environment. This connects directly to the central idea that communities interact with the environment in different ways. They view each location, note visible features such as paths, vegetation, buildings, bins and access points, and measure useful distances using the map scale or distance tool. Pairs then present a live map and Street View walkthrough, explaining which choices appear to support environmental care and which may place pressure on the area. The everyday features are map search, satellite view, Street View and distance measurement.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small community that balances housing, transport, food production and protected natural areas. This addresses the need for sustainable practices and shows how community decisions affect the environment. Teams construct a manageable section of the community and add signs explaining choices such as shared green space, renewable energy, water protection and reduced car use. They guide classmates through the finished world and explain the environmental trade-offs they considered. The core features are the block-building tools, signs and shared world.

Students use Podcast Equipment to record a short Sharing the Planet interview about taking action for environmental stewardship. In pairs, one student acts as a local resident, ranger, Traditional Owner, council representative or business owner while the other asks how community values influence environmental choices. They plan focused questions, record a three-minute interview and listen back to check that the voices are clear and the ideas are supported with examples. The finished audio episode is played to the class, followed by one practical action listeners could take. The central features are the microphone, headphones and recorder controls.

Elsternwick|Year 6|How We Express Oursel.d: In How We Express Ourselves, students create a digital process journal showing how thinking beyond themselves led to a small action at school or in the community. This directly explores how we evidence our process and how taking action helps us grow our understandings. Each student publishes a short book containing planning pages, photographs, captions and recorded reflections from before, during and after the action. Book Creator’s page templates, camera, audio recording and publishing tools keep the whole journal in one place.

In How We Express Ourselves, students design a short survey to find out which local issue their classmates believe needs meaningful change. They collect responses before and after presenting an action idea, linking directly to how we provoke others to make meaningful change. Students present the automatically generated charts and explain whether opinions shifted and what the evidence suggests. Microsoft Forms’ question types, response collection and automatic charts make the task manageable in a few lessons.

In How We Express Ourselves, pairs record a three-minute podcast episode about a person or group whose thinking beyond themselves led to action. This connects to the central idea that thinking beyond ourselves empowers us to act. Students publish an episode with a clear introduction, key evidence, a short reflection and a practical call to action for listeners. Canva’s audio recording, simple editing timeline and ready-made podcast layouts support the recording and presentation.

In How We Express Ourselves, students map places where a local or global issue is visible and where people are taking meaningful action. This helps them examine how action can grow our understanding by showing patterns across different locations. Students create and present an annotated map with selected map layers, marked locations and brief explanations of the change happening in each place. National Geographic MapMaker’s map layers, location search and drawing and annotation tools make the spatial evidence clear and shareable.

In How We Express Ourselves, students create a digital campaign poster that encourages the school community to take one realistic action for a chosen issue. This directly addresses how we provoke others to make meaningful change. Students publish a poster with a strong headline, one piece of evidence, an original visual and a clear call to action, then present the design choices they used to influence an audience. Adobe Express’ poster templates, text controls, image tools and shareable publishing option allow students to produce a polished message without specialist design skills.

Elsternwick|Year 6|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital book called “My Evolving Self” about personal changes and influences that have shaped them. This directly explores the central idea that personal changes and influences contribute to our evolving sense of self. Each page can include writing, drawings, photos or an audio reflection, with students choosing only details they feel comfortable sharing. They publish a finished book to share with a partner, their teacher or the class using Book Creator’s simple page templates and multimedia tools.

Students design a short, anonymous class survey about influences that shape identity, such as family, friends, culture, interests and experiences. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about influences that shape our identity. Classmates complete the survey, then students examine the automatically generated charts and record three patterns they notice in the response summary. Each group presents its survey findings using Microsoft Forms’ question types, response collection and built-in charts.

Students make a one-minute stop-motion sequence showing one character at different life stages and the physical, social, emotional and intellectual changes they may experience. This directly addresses the line of inquiry about changes that occur throughout life. They move paper figures or classroom objects a small amount between each captured frame, then add short titles to explain the changes shown. The finished animation is screened for the class using Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback tools.

Students create an “Identity Iceberg” infographic about the parts of a person that others may notice and the less visible influences, values and experiences underneath. This supports the lines of inquiry about influences that shape identity and developing a sense of self. Students use respectful fictional examples or personal examples they are comfortable sharing, then organise them with labels, icons, colour and short explanations. They publish and present a one-page infographic using Canva’s templates, text boxes, shapes and image library.

Students produce a short audio piece called “Sounds That Shaped Me” to explore how interests, relationships, places and experiences can influence identity. This connects directly to the central idea that personal changes and influences contribute to our evolving sense of self. They combine a brief spoken reflection with selected GarageBand loops, adjusting the order and volume so each sound has a clear purpose. Students play their finished audio piece for a small group and explain one creative choice using GarageBand’s voice recording, loop browser and track controls.

Elsternwick|Year 6|Where We Are in Place.d: Students investigate how a significant event, such as the Victorian gold rush, shaped Melbourne and nearby places. They use the standard map, satellite view and Street View to examine transport routes, civic buildings, old mining areas and other visible evidence of change. This directly explores the central idea that significant events shape a place and the line of inquiry about their impact. Each group presents a live Google Maps walkthrough, explaining what they noticed and how the locations connect to the event.

Students enter a small teacher-provided set of historical data linked to a significant event, such as population figures before, during and after the Victorian gold rush. They organise the figures in a table and use Excel’s chart tool to create a clear column or line graph. This helps them investigate the impact of significant events by identifying changes, patterns and turning points. Students finish with a labelled chart and a short written conclusion in the spreadsheet explaining what the data shows about how the place changed.

Students create a visual explanation of why a chosen significant event occurred and how it shaped a place. On separate whiteboard pages, they arrange short notes, arrows, dates and images to show causes, the event itself and its effects. They then use Explain Everything’s drawing tools and voice recording to talk through their reasoning. The finished product is a short recorded explanation that directly addresses the lines of inquiry about why events occurred and their impact.

Students make a short stop-motion sequence showing a local or Australian place before, during and after a significant event. They build simple paper scenes and move labelled people, buildings, transport routes or boundaries a little at a time, photographing each change with Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera. This demonstrates the central idea that significant events shape a place by making the changes visible in sequence. The final animation is shared with the class, with students explaining which changes are supported by historical evidence.

Students design a one-page historical feature about an event that significantly shaped Melbourne, Victoria or Australia. They use Canva’s timeline templates, text boxes, image placement and simple charts to explain what happened, why it occurred and how the place changed. This brings together all three lines of inquiry while requiring students to decide which evidence makes the event significant. Students publish or present a finished page containing a timeline, a cause-and-effect section and a clear statement about the event’s lasting impact.

Glen Waverley|Prep|How We Express Oursel.d: Students photograph a simple face drawing, add a moving mouth and record the character explaining an emotion such as happy, worried or angry. They describe what happened, how the feeling affected them and one helpful response, linking to how our feelings and emotions affect us. Each student makes a short talking-face recording to share with the class. The activity uses ChatterPix Kids’ everyday photo, mouth-drawing and voice-recording features.

In pairs, students choose puppets and act out a familiar situation where one character’s behaviour affects another character’s feelings. They connect their scene to how our emotions and behaviour affect relationships by showing a problem and a caring way to respond. Students move the puppets while recording their voices, then present the finished puppet scene to the class. The activity uses the tool’s ready-made puppets, backgrounds and record button.

Students make a short class book about emotions and wellbeing, with each child creating one page for a different feeling. They draw a face or situation, add a simple sentence and record themselves explaining what the feeling might do to the body or behaviour. The finished shared book connects directly to the central idea that emotions influence our wellbeing. The activity uses Book Creator’s page templates, drawing pen, text and audio recording.

Students arrange teacher-provided pictures of faces and everyday situations into an emotions poster. They match each picture with a feeling word and add a short caption about the clues they noticed, such as tears, a smile or crossed arms. Their finished collage explores how feelings and emotions are interpreted and can be presented during a class discussion. The activity uses PicCollage’s simple layouts, picture arranging and text labels.

Students record a short video showing one emotion with their face, voice and body, then explain the clues that help others recognise it. They also name one safe action that could support their wellbeing, such as asking for help, resting or taking slow breaths. Each child publishes a brief video response for the teacher and classmates to view, linking to how feelings and emotions are interpreted. The activity uses Seesaw’s built-in video recording and simple posting tools.

Glen Waverley|Prep|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students make a simple digital book showing where a familiar food, such as bread or milk, comes from. This directly explores the line of inquiry, “Where food comes from.” On each page, they add a photo or drawing, place the stages in order and record a short spoken explanation. The finished books can be read aloud to classmates using Book Creator’s pages, drawing tools and voice-recording feature.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show how food can change, such as a whole banana becoming mashed banana or separate ingredients becoming a sandwich. This connects directly to the central idea that the products people use go through a process of change. In small groups, they move the food or picture pieces a little at a time and capture each step with the frame-by-frame camera. They play back and share a short stop-motion movie that clearly shows the food before, during and after the change.

Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a teacher-made floor mat from a food source to the place where it is changed, sold and eaten. This supports the line of inquiry, “Where food comes from,” using examples such as wheat, bakery, shop and home. Students press the forward, backward and turn buttons to create a sequence, test the route and fix it if the Bee-Bot reaches the wrong picture. Each pair presents its completed route and explains the food’s journey to the class.

Students photograph a familiar food and use ChatterPix Kids to make it explain where it came from and how it was changed. This addresses both “Where food comes from” and “How food can be changed for different purposes.” They draw a mouth on the photo and record one or two simple sentences, such as a strawberry explaining that it grew on a farm and was made into jam. The class finishes with a collection of short talking-food recordings made with the app’s camera, mouth-drawing and voice-recording features.

Students create a short food appreciation video about a food that is important in their family or that they enjoy sharing with others. This connects directly to the line of inquiry, “An appreciation of food.” They record a few brief clips showing the food or a picture of it, explain where it comes from and say why they value it. Using Apple Clips’ simple video camera and text labels, they produce a short video to present to the class.

Glen Waverley|Prep|Where We Are in Place.d: Students use Seesaw’s drawing tool to create a picture showing the people they consider family. They add a voice recording to introduce each person and explain something they enjoy doing together. This directly explores the line of inquiry, “The people in your family,” while recognising that families can look different. Each student publishes a narrated family picture to their class journal to share with the teacher and family.

Students make a collage about what is important to their family, such as celebrations, food, pets, places or time together. They use PicCollage’s camera, picture layout and simple text labels to arrange their ideas on one page. This connects directly to the line of inquiry, “What is important to your family,” and shows how family values help shape who we are. Students present their finished family values collage to a partner or small group.

Students use Google Maps with an adult to view a town, suburb or country that is part of their family history. They explore the map and Street View, noticing landmarks, homes, streets or natural features that help them understand the place. This supports the line of inquiry, “Your family history,” by connecting family stories with real locations. Each student presents a short on-screen walkthrough and explains why that place matters to their family.

Students create a short ScratchJr scene showing family members taking part in a familiar tradition or everyday routine. They choose characters and a background, then code simple movement and speech sequences using the block buttons. This explores the central idea that family histories shape who we are and what we value. Students play their finished animated family scene for classmates and explain the tradition or routine they represented.

Students record a short show-and-tell video about a family object, photograph or tradition connected to their history. They make two or three brief clips explaining what it is, who it connects to and why it is important. This directly supports the lines of inquiry, “Your family history” and “What is important to your family.” Using Apple Clips’ simple video recording and title features, students create a short family history story to present to the class.

Glen Waverley|Prep|Who We Are.d: Students use Sphero Indi’s coloured tiles to build and test a simple route showing a safe school arrival routine, such as moving forward, turning and stopping at the classroom. This connects to routines that allow developing independence and how the school is organised to help students learn and work together. In small groups, students arrange the tiles, run Indi, notice mistakes and change the sequence until the robot completes the route. Each group presents its working route and explains the safe choices represented by the coloured tiles.

Students create a short ScratchJr animation about a classroom routine, such as unpacking a bag, placing a drink bottle away and joining the group. This directly explores routines that allow developing independence in the Junior School. Students choose characters and backgrounds, then use simple movement and speech blocks to place the routine in the correct order. They publish and present an animated routine that another Prep student could follow.

Students use Puppet Pals to record a short scene about people in the Junior School and how they help students learn and work together. This connects directly to the organisation of the Junior School and the unit’s central idea. Pairs choose characters and a background, move the characters on screen and record their own voices explaining roles such as teacher, student or office staff member. They present a short puppet show showing who can help in an everyday school situation.

Students make a Seesaw post showing one way to keep the classroom or playground healthy and safe. This addresses how to make the classroom and playground healthy and safe. Each student uses Seesaw’s drawing tools to illustrate a safe action, then records a short voice explanation of what to do and why. The finished picture-and-voice safety messages can be shared with classmates as a simple Prep safety guide.

Students complete a teacher-made Microsoft Forms class survey about which school routines they can do independently, such as packing away, washing hands or lining up safely. This explores routines that allow developing independence. Students select from clear picture-supported choices, and Forms collects the responses and displays a class summary chart. The class views the chart together and presents one routine they already manage well and one they will practise next.

Glen Waverley|Prep|How the World Works.d: Students build simple routes with Indi’s coloured tiles and test how the robot moves, turns and stops. They change one tile at a time and observe how this affects the line of inquiry, how objects move. Each group presents a completed route and explains what they changed when the robot did not travel as planned. The colour-sensing robot and reusable tiles make the testing and fixing manageable for Prep students.

Students use Apple Clips to record short videos of classroom objects rolling, sliding or staying still on surfaces such as carpet, cardboard and smooth flooring. They describe what they notice about how the properties of materials influence movement, linking directly to the central idea. Each pair produces a short narrated collection of movement tests to show the class. The large record button, simple trimming and spoken narration are the main features used.

Students photograph everyday objects made from materials such as wood, metal, fabric, plastic and paper, then place one object on each page in Book Creator. They record a short explanation of the material’s properties and how those properties suit the object’s use, connecting with the line of inquiry, how we use materials. Each pair creates a small digital materials book that can be read and listened to by classmates. Book Creator’s page templates, photo tool and voice-recording button support the whole task.

Students choose or draw two simple objects in ScratchJr and code them to roll, slide, bounce or stop across the screen. They use the animation to explain the line of inquiry, how objects move, and discuss which material property might help each movement. Each student makes a short coded scene and presents the sequence to a partner. ScratchJr’s movement blocks, start blocks and drawing tool provide the actions they need.

Students photograph classroom objects and arrange the pictures into groups such as hard, soft, bendy, stiff, rough or smooth in PicCollage. They talk with a partner about the line of inquiry, properties of materials, and decide where each object belongs. Each pair makes a labelled sorting poster to display and explain to the class. PicCollage’s photo, text and drag-and-resize features make it easy for Prep students to build the poster.

Glen Waverley|Prep|Sharing the Planet.d: In a supervised walk around the school grounds, pairs use Seek by iNaturalist to photograph and identify common plants, insects and other small living things for Sharing the Planet. They discuss our responsibility to protect the living things that share the school’s limited space and resources. Each pair records several identified species in the app and presents one discovery and a simple way people can care for it. The camera identification feature is the main tool students use.

Students use Google Maps to view two contrasting places, such as central Melbourne and a nearby forest or wetland, as part of Sharing the Planet. They look for signs of how people and other living things share finite resources such as land, water and green space, directly linking to the central idea. Pairs use the screen to present one place where sharing appears to work well and one place where living things may need more care. Satellite view and Street View let students explore and compare the places without creating or editing a map.

Students program Beebots to travel across a teacher-prepared habitat mat and reach pictures of water, food and shelter during Sharing the Planet. They plan routes that allow several animals to reach the finite resources, connecting directly to the central idea about sharing with other living things. Students enter the steps, test the route, clear the code and debug it when the Bee-Bot reaches the wrong square. Each pair presents one successful route and explains how it helped the habitat’s living things share fairly.

Students create a simple class book called Our Sharing the Planet Responsibilities. Each child makes one page showing a living thing, a finite resource it needs and one responsibility people have when sharing that resource. Students add a drawing or photo, dictate or type a short sentence, and record themselves reading it aloud. Book Creator’s page-making and voice-recording features produce a shareable book for classmates and families.

Students use ScratchJr to code a short Sharing the Planet scene in which two characters need to share a limited resource such as water, food or space. They choose a background and characters, then join simple movement and speech blocks to show a fair choice and its result. This directly explores the central idea about rights and responsibilities when people and living things share finite resources. Each pair tests and debugs its animation, then plays it for the class and explains the responsibility shown.

Glen Waverley|Year 1|How We Express Ours.d: Students choose characters and a background, then create a short puppet performance about a familiar story or an idea from their imagination. This directly explores the features and purposes of puppet performances. They move the characters while recording their voices to make a digital puppet show for the class. The simple character movement and voice-recording features make the task manageable for Year 1 partners.

Students photograph a puppet they have made from classroom materials and draw a mouth on the image. They record the puppet explaining what it is made from and why those materials were chosen, linking directly to different materials used to make puppets. Each student produces a short talking-puppet video that can be presented to the class. The everyday photo, drawn-mouth and voice-recording features power the activity.

Students code two puppet characters to move across a stage and take turns telling a simple story. This supports the central idea that people use imagination to express stories through performance. They make a short digital performance with a beginning, a problem and an ending, then present it to a partner. The block commands for movement, speech and starting actions let Year 1 students build and debug a simple sequence.

Students photograph a small collection of puppet-making materials such as paper, fabric, wool, cardboard and craft sticks. They arrange the photos in a collage and add short labels showing how each material could become part of a puppet, linking to the line of inquiry about different materials used to make puppets. The finished material-planning collage can be shared before students begin building. PicCollage’s camera, picture layout and text-label features keep the task simple and visual.

Small groups record a one-minute performance with their handmade puppets to show how puppets can entertain, teach or share a cultural story. This directly explores the types, uses, features and purposes of puppet performances. Students record a few short scenes, add a clear title and present the finished video to the class. Apple Clips’ large record button, simple trimming and title tools make filming and tidying the performance realistic for Year 1.

Glen Waverley|Year 1|How We Organise Our.d: Students create a class book about How We Organise Ourselves, with each pair making a page about a person who helps the school community. They add a drawing or photo, a short sentence about the person’s role, and an audio recording explaining the need that person helps meet. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about the roles people play in a community. Book Creator’s simple page, drawing, photo and voice-recording tools let the class publish one shared book to read together.

Students use ScratchJr to show a familiar classroom routine from How We Organise Ourselves, such as arriving, borrowing a book or packing up. They choose characters and backgrounds, then connect movement and speech blocks in the correct order to animate each step. This supports the line of inquiry about systems and routines that help us stay organised. Each pair presents its working animation and explains why the steps need to happen in that order.

Students build and test a colour-tile route that helps Sphero Indi carry out a classroom job, such as travelling from the supply area to a group table. They arrange the tiles to control the robot’s movement, run the route, and change the sequence when it does not reach the correct place. This practical task explores how communities work together to meet needs through organised systems. Each group presents its successful route and explains the job it represents and how the colour tiles control Indi.

Students view the Glen Waverley area in Google Maps and use Street View to look for places that help a community work, such as schools, shops, parks, libraries or emergency services. They follow a teacher-selected route and discuss the role each place plays in meeting people’s needs. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about how communities work together to meet needs. Using the ordinary map view, zoom controls and Street View, pairs give a short live walkthrough and point out two helpful community places.

Students use Puppet Pals to create a short conversation between two people who help a community, such as a teacher and librarian organising how children borrow books. They choose characters and a setting, move the characters on screen, and record their own voices to explain each person’s role. This develops the line of inquiry about the roles people play in a community and shows how those roles work together. Each pair shares a recorded puppet scene that includes a community need, the people involved and the system they use.

Glen Waverley|Year 1|How the World Works.d: Students use the arrow buttons to code a Bee-Bot to move across a floor grid, testing different sequences of forward moves and turns. This explores ways objects move and shows that the robot’s movement depends on the instructions entered. Pairs debug their sequence until the Bee-Bot reaches a chosen picture, then demonstrate the successful route to the class. The clear, forward, backward and turn buttons make the task manageable for Year 1 students.

Students arrange Indi’s coloured tiles to create a simple track, then watch how the robot moves across each tile. This connects to how designs can be adapted and improved because students change the order and position of tiles when the route does not work as planned. Each group builds and presents a finished route that makes Indi travel, turn and stop at a chosen place. Indi’s colour-sensing drive system lets students change the robot’s movement by rearranging the physical tiles.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show different ways objects move, such as rolling, sliding, spinning and bouncing. They move a classroom object a small amount between each photo and discuss the push or pull causing its movement. Each pair produces a short stop-motion film with simple spoken or written labels naming the movements shown. The frame-by-frame camera is the key feature, allowing students to make small changes in position visible as a moving sequence.

Students test a small toy car on different surfaces, such as carpet, cardboard and fabric, to explore the influence different materials have on movement. In Book Creator, they make one page for each surface using a photo, a short sentence and a voice recording explaining whether the car travelled easily or slowed down. Their finished digital book presents the test results and identifies which material had the greatest effect on movement. Book Creator’s page templates, camera and voice-recording tools keep the report simple enough for Year 1 students.

Students investigate ways objects move by photographing classroom examples of rolling, sliding, spinning and bouncing. They arrange the photos in PicCollage under matching movement headings and add short labels such as “the ball rolls” or “the block slides.” The completed collage becomes a shareable class poster showing that different objects move in different ways when a force is applied. PicCollage’s photo, text and drag-and-drop layout features make it easy for students to organise their evidence visually.

Glen Waverley|Year 1|Sharing the Planet.d: Students create a simple class book about invertebrates such as worms, snails, spiders and butterflies. Each pair makes one page showing the animal’s body features, habitat and importance to other living things, linking to the characteristics of invertebrates and the central idea. They add a drawing or photo, a short sentence and a recorded explanation, then share the finished book with the class. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and audio recording make this manageable for Year 1 students.

Students use ScratchJr to show the life cycle of an invertebrate such as a butterfly. They draw or choose characters for each stage, then code simple movements and page changes to put the stages in order, directly exploring life cycles of invertebrates. Students test and debug their sequence before presenting the finished animation to a partner. ScratchJr’s picture-based coding blocks and drawing editor let students build the animation without needing to type much.

Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a teacher-prepared floor mat showing places in a garden, such as soil, leaf litter, flowers and a pond. They choose a suitable route for an invertebrate and explain how each stop provides food, shelter or water, linking to the interdependence of invertebrates and their environment. Students enter the steps, test the route and fix their sequence if the Bee-Bot reaches the wrong place. The Bee-Bot’s forward, backward, left and right buttons make the planned journey clear and achievable for Year 1.

Students use Seesaw to make a labelled observation page about one invertebrate from the unit. They draw the animal, label visible characteristics such as legs, wings, segments or shell, and record a short voice explanation about where it lives. The finished post provides a shareable record of learning about the characteristics of invertebrates. Seesaw’s drawing, text label and voice recording features allow students to explain their ideas with limited writing.

Students record a short nature-reporter video explaining why one invertebrate is essential to living things and the environment. They might describe how bees pollinate flowers, worms improve soil or spiders help control insect numbers, directly addressing the central idea. Each student records one or two clear sentences and adds a simple title before presenting the clip to the class. Apple Clips’ built-in video recording and title tools support a short, polished result without complicated editing.

Glen Waverley|Year 1|Where We Are in Pla.d: Students use Book Creator to make a short class book about how children’s lives have changed over time. Each pair creates a then-and-now page about one area such as toys, school, clothing or communication, connecting directly to the line of inquiry about ways children’s lives have changed. They add drawings, simple labels and a recorded sentence explaining one reason for the change. The finished book can be read aloud and shared with families using Book Creator’s page-making and audio recording features.

Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a floor timeline showing stages in children’s lives from the past to today. They press the directional buttons to plan the route, test it and debug any steps that take the robot to the wrong picture. This supports the central idea that understanding history helps us see how the past shapes the future. Each group presents its completed robot journey and explains one change shown along the route.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short then-and-now film about children’s toys, games or school life. They move simple classroom figures and objects a little at a time, taking a photo after each movement with the app’s frame-by-frame camera. The film shows a change over time and includes a simple reason for that change, linking to both lines of inquiry. Groups play their finished animation to the class and explain what is different between the past and today.

Students use PicCollage to make a visual comparison called “Children Then and Now” for the unit Where We Are in Place and Time. They arrange teacher-provided pictures of past and present clothing, toys, classrooms or transport into two clearly labelled sections. They add short captions explaining how children’s lives changed and one possible reason, such as new inventions or safer materials. The finished comparison poster is shared in a class gallery, using PicCollage’s picture layout, text and background features.

Students use Seesaw to record a simple history explanation about an old and a modern object connected to children’s lives, such as a toy, lunchbox or telephone. They photograph the objects, then use the voice recording feature to describe what changed and why they think the change happened. This directly explores the line of inquiry about reasons for changes to children’s lives over time. Each student publishes a photo-and-voice post that classmates and families can view and discuss.

Glen Waverley|Year 1|Who We Are.d: Students photograph a simple face they have drawn showing a pleasant or unpleasant emotion, then use ChatterPix Kids to make the face speak. They record the character naming the feeling, explaining a situation that might cause it, and suggesting one helpful response. This directly explores situations that cause pleasant and unpleasant feelings. The app’s mouth line and short voice-recording feature turn each drawing into a shareable talking emotion character.

Students code a short ScratchJr scene about two characters trying to play or work together. They use movement and speech blocks to show a problem, the feelings it causes, and an action such as listening, sharing or asking for help. This connects to the central idea that emotions, values and relationships guide how we connect and collaborate. Students present their finished animated story to a partner and explain the sequence they coded.

Students complete a simple class check-in about actions that support wellbeing, such as resting, moving, talking to someone or taking calm breaths. The teacher reads each question aloud, and students select the picture or choice that best matches what helps them. This supports the line of inquiry into actions that support wellbeing. Microsoft Forms collects the responses and produces class charts that students can view and discuss together.

In pairs, students create and record a short puppet scene showing a friendship disagreement and a kind way to solve it. They move the characters, speak the dialogue and show how each character’s feelings change after someone listens, apologises or includes others. This explores how emotions, values and relationships guide collaboration. The tool’s movable characters, backgrounds and built-in recording create a puppet show the class can watch and discuss.

Students use a teacher-provided brain picture in Seesaw and add simple labels for parts linked with thinking, memory and strong feelings. They draw arrows or circle each part, then record a short voice explanation of one job it does. This directly explores the function of different parts of the brain at a Year 1 level. Seesaw’s drawing, text and voice-recording tools create a labelled explanation that can be shared with classmates and families.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|How We Express Ours.d: Students create a short digital picture book for How We Express Ourselves, combining a simple story with drawings, text and recorded narration. They choose where an illustration can show an important detail that is not stated in the words, exploring the connection between story and illustrations. Each pair publishes a shareable book with a cover and three or four story pages. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and audio recording make the task manageable for Year 2 students.

Students retell a familiar story for How We Express Ourselves by choosing characters and backgrounds, then moving the characters while speaking their dialogue. They experiment with voice, movement and setting to explore the mediums and techniques storytellers use. Each group records and presents a short puppet performance with a clear beginning, problem and ending. Puppet Pals’ movable characters, scene backgrounds and built-in voice recording are the main features used.

Students use GarageBand to create a short sound story for How We Express Ourselves, such as walking through a storm and finally reaching home. They arrange sounds, simple music and their own recorded voice to explore how ideas and information are communicated without relying mainly on pictures. Each pair produces a one-minute audio story and plays it to classmates, who explain what they thought was happening. GarageBand’s audio recorder and ready-made loops allow students to build and rearrange the soundtrack easily.

Students code a short animated story for How We Express Ourselves using two characters, a setting and a simple problem. They sequence movement, speech and scene changes to investigate how storytellers use different methods to convey meaning. Each pair tests and debugs its code, then presents an animation with a beginning, middle and end. ScratchJr’s picture-based coding blocks, characters and backgrounds keep the coding suitable for Year 2.

Students photograph a classroom object and turn it into a talking character for How We Express Ourselves. They write and record a short first-person message that uses expression to communicate the character’s idea or point of view. Each student makes a brief talking-picture clip and shares it with the class as part of a character gallery. ChatterPix Kids’ simple mouth line, voice recording and decorations provide the storytelling technique.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|How We Organise Our.d: Students use Book Creator to make a short book about how the school library borrowing system works as part of How We Organise Ourselves. Each page shows one step in order, such as choosing a book, borrowing it, taking care of it and returning it. This directly explores the central idea that a sequence of processes enables a system to function. Students use the simple page, drawing, text and voice-recording features to publish a book that can be shared with another Year 2 class.

Students use ScratchJr to code a character moving through the steps of a familiar system, such as ordering and collecting lunch from the canteen. They arrange movement, speech and wait blocks in the correct order, run the program and debug any steps that happen too early or are missing. This explores the line of inquiry about the purpose of various systems and shows why sequence matters in How We Organise Ourselves. Each pair presents a working animation and explains how its coded sequence helps the system function.

Students use Sphero Indi to model a classroom delivery system in which an item must travel from a collection point to the correct table. They arrange the coloured tiles to create a route, test the robot and change the tile sequence when it does not reach the intended place. This connects to the line of inquiry about how systems are made of many interdependent parts because the route, tiles, robot and delivery points must all work together. Each group presents a tested delivery route and explains the purpose of each part in the system.

Students use PicCollage to create a visual guide to one system in their lives, such as getting ready for school, sorting classroom rubbish or packing up after a lesson. They place photos or pictures in sequence and add short labels and arrows to show what happens first, next and last. This directly supports the line of inquiry about the systems in our lives and the central idea that a sequence of processes enables a system to function. The finished collage is a clear, shareable process poster made with the tool’s picture, text and layout features.

Students use Puppet Pals to record a short role-play showing how a classroom system works, such as borrowing equipment or handing in completed work. They choose characters and a background, move the characters while recording their voices, and include each part of the process in the correct order. This explores the line of inquiry about the purpose of various systems by showing how agreed steps help people work together in How We Organise Ourselves. Each group produces and presents a short recorded puppet scene that classmates can check for missing or unclear steps.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|How the World Works.d: Students use Stop Motion Studio to show how a clean cardboard box can be physically changed into something useful, such as a desk organiser. They photograph each step as they cut, fold and join the cardboard, linking directly to reuse and recycling through physical change. Using frame-by-frame capture and playback, they make a short stop-motion film showing the material’s transformation. The class watches the films and discusses how changes to materials affect how we reuse them in daily life.

Students use a simple Microsoft Forms survey to record what happens when they test everyday materials for properties such as flexibility, absorbency and strength. They select results from picture-supported multiple-choice questions, connecting directly to understanding material properties. The response charts provide a class record that students can view and discuss together. Students then present one conclusion about which material would be suitable for an everyday object and explain why.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital book about sustainably managing materials at school. Each page shows one common item, what material it is made from, and whether it could be reused, recycled or placed in rubbish. They use the page templates, drawing tools, photos, text and voice recording to explain their choices. The finished books are shared with classmates as practical guides to reducing material waste.

Students use PicCollage to create a visual materials sorting poster using photos of classroom objects. They group the objects by material, such as paper, plastic, metal, fabric or wood, and add short labels describing useful properties. This connects directly to understanding material properties and how those properties affect an object’s use. The photo, layout and text features help students produce a clear poster to present during a class gallery walk.

Students use ScratchJr to code a short animated explanation of an object being reused instead of thrown away. They choose or draw characters and objects, then use movement, speech and sequencing blocks to show the material changing into a new useful item. This links to the central idea that changes to materials affect how we use and reuse them in daily life. Students debug their sequence and present the finished animation, explaining the reuse choice shown in their project.

Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a floor mat showing the Sun and planets in their correct order. They plan and test the button sequence, then debug it if the Bee-Bot reaches the wrong planet. This supports the line of inquiry into Earth’s place in the solar system through simple movement and spatial thinking. Each group presents a successful route and explains when the Bee-Bot reaches Earth, using the robot’s forward, backward and turn buttons.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show how Earth rotates, using a simple Earth model and a fixed light source representing the Sun. They move the model a small amount between each photo and play the frames back as an animation. This connects to observable patterns in the sky by helping students explain why we experience day and night. Each pair publishes a short stop-motion sequence with a clear daytime side and nighttime side, powered by the app’s frame-by-frame camera capture.

Students create a Seesaw page showing an observable sky pattern, such as the Moon appearing different across several nights or the Sun appearing in different parts of the sky during the day. They draw the sequence, add simple labels and record a spoken explanation of the pattern. This directly explores how patterns in the sky help us understand our place in the universe. The finished page can be shared with classmates and families using Seesaw’s drawing, text and voice-recording tools.

Students work in pairs to build a simple solar system display in Minecraft Education, placing the Sun, Earth and the other planets in the correct order. They use different blocks to make each object recognisable and add signs with short facts, without trying to recreate the enormous real distances. This supports the line of inquiry into Earth’s place in the solar system. Each pair leads classmates through its finished build using Minecraft’s block-building, signs and movement controls.

Students make a short iMovie sky report explaining one tool or method people use to observe the sky, such as eyes, binoculars, telescopes or space telescopes. They record themselves presenting a drawing or classroom model, then arrange the clips and add a clear title. This connects directly to the line of inquiry into tools and methods we use to observe the sky. The class finishes with a set of short, shareable reports created with iMovie’s video recording, clip trimming and title tools.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|Sharing the Planet.d: Students view two communities in Google Maps, such as Melbourne and a remote Australian community, and look for rivers, reservoirs, roads and visible water infrastructure. They use the map, satellite view and Street View to discuss unequal access to water without assuming that every visible water source is safe to use. Pairs compare distances between homes and nearby water sources using the distance information shown on the map. They present a short screen-guided comparison to the class, explaining what the maps show and what they cannot tell us.

Students program a Bee-Bot to move across a teacher-prepared floor grid showing a reservoir, treatment plant, storage tank and homes. They enter and test directional steps to model the transferral of water from its source to where people use it. When a route does not reach the correct square, students clear the program, change the sequence and test it again. Each pair presents a successful route and explains each stage of the water journey while the Bee-Bot travels.

Students complete a simple class survey about everyday water use, such as showering, drinking, washing dishes and watering plants. This supports the central idea that water is a limited resource that is essential to life and helps students consider their responsibility as global citizens. They submit choices using picture-supported multiple-choice questions and then examine the automatic class charts with the teacher. The class records two practical water-saving actions based on patterns shown in the responses.

Students code a short ScratchJr animation showing a drop of water travelling from a natural source to a home or school. They choose or draw backgrounds, add characters and use movement and message blocks to show stages such as collection, treatment, storage and use. This directly explores the transferral of water from source to use. Each pair presents its finished animation and explains how changing the order of the code would change the water journey.

Students create a Seesaw page comparing water access for two children, such as one using a nearby tap and another travelling to collect water. They use the built-in drawing and text tools to show the distance, containers and ways water is used, then add a voice recording explaining the differences. This connects directly to unequal access to water and communities affected by water access. Students publish the page to their class journal and listen to a partner’s explanation before leaving a simple spoken or written response.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|How We Express Ours.d: Students use Book Creator to make a short digital picture book about how they see and understand their local world. They explore the line of inquiry about how texts and images work together by pairing brief descriptions with drawings, photos or page backgrounds. Each student publishes a shareable book with a clear beginning, middle and end. The simple page templates, text boxes, drawing tools and voice recording make the task manageable for Year 3.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short animation showing an everyday place changing through their imagination, such as a classroom becoming a jungle. This connects to the central idea that creativity allows people to express their understanding of the world. Pairs plan, move paper shapes or classroom objects a little at a time, capture each frame, and present a finished animation. The camera frame capture and playback controls let students test their sequence and fix movements that appear too fast or jumpy.

Students use Sketchbook to create a digital artwork called “My World Through My Eyes” for the How We Express Ourselves unit. They investigate how technology influences our creativity by trying different brushes, colours, layers and erasing choices, then discussing how these options changed their original idea. Each student presents a finished artwork alongside a short written artist statement added to the image. Sketchbook’s drawing brushes, colour picker and layers are the everyday features that power the task.

Students use PicCollage to make a visual poster showing several ways people use technology to express creativity, such as digital drawing, photography, animation and music-making. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the ways people use technology to express creativity. Students arrange selected images, add short captions and choose a layout that helps the viewer understand their message. PicCollage’s grids, image placement, text and sticker tools make the poster concrete and achievable in one or two lessons.

Students use Explain Everything to present how one image can communicate different ideas when it is paired with different words. This directly explores the line of inquiry about how texts and images work together. Students place or draw one image on several slides, add a different caption to each version, and record a short explanation of how the meaning changes. The slide canvas, drawing tools, text boxes and built-in voice recording allow each student to publish a simple narrated presentation.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|How We Organise Our.d: Students ask classmates which school needs are helped by digital systems, such as borrowing library books, ordering lunch or sharing notices, and enter the answers in an Excel table. They sort the information into categories and create a simple column chart using Excel’s table and chart tools. This directly explores the central idea that needs can be met with digital systems. Each group presents its chart and explains which digital system meets the most common class need.

Students use Padlet to build a class board showing examples of digital systems used at school and the needs they meet. Each pair adds a short post with a title, explanation and image, then leaves one helpful and respectful comment on another post. This explores how ideas and information can be organised and shared in safe online environments. The finished board becomes a shared class collection, powered by Padlet’s post and comment features.

Students create a one-page Canva poster called “Being a Responsible Digital Citizen” for younger students. They include practical reminders about protecting personal information, using kind words, asking before sharing and telling an adult when something feels wrong. This directly supports the line of inquiry about being a responsible digital citizen. Students use Canva’s poster templates, text boxes, icons and images, then present their finished poster to the class.

Students use Explain Everything to map how one familiar digital system meets a need, such as an online lunch order moving from a family’s choice to the school and canteen. They draw boxes and arrows for the information going in, how it is organised and what comes out, then record a short spoken explanation. This directly explores what digital systems are and how they work in an organised way. The final product is a narrated system diagram made with the tool’s drawing, text, arrow and recording features.

Students use Seesaw to make a short digital safety response to a classroom scenario, such as receiving an unkind message or being asked to share a password. They draw or type what they would do, then record their voice explaining why their choice is safe and responsible. This addresses the line of inquiry about being a responsible digital citizen. Students publish the response to the class space using Seesaw’s drawing, text and voice-recording tools, ready for teacher feedback.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|Sharing the Planet.d: Students examine several soil samples and use Microsoft Excel to record colour, texture, particle size and how quickly water drains through each one. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals. Pairs enter their results in a simple table and create a column chart comparing the samples. The everyday spreadsheet cells and chart tool help them turn observations into a clear class data display.

Students use Google Maps to view a quarry, a mine and a protected natural area in Australia, switching to satellite view or Street View where it is available. They compare visible features and discuss the line of inquiry that Earth's resources are vital and must be used responsibly. Small groups present a short live map tour, pointing out evidence of resource use, changed landscapes and land care. The ordinary zoom, satellite view and Street View controls make distant places visible without students needing accounts or editing a map.

Students use Book Creator to make a class field guide about the diversity of soils, rocks and minerals. Each pair creates a page describing one sample's observable properties, a common use and one way that resource could be used responsibly. The finished book includes labelled pictures, short written explanations and recorded student narration, ready to share with another Year 3 class. Book Creator's page templates, text, image and audio tools keep the task manageable for this age group.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to explore where selected Australian resources such as gold, iron ore, clay and coal are found. They add simple map annotations showing resource locations and nearby land or water features, then explain how the Earth's geology shapes the way people use particular places. Each group presents its annotated map and identifies one question about responsible resource use. The map layers, zoom controls and annotation tools allow students to build and share a clear geographic picture.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short model showing soil and rock layers before, during and after a resource is removed. They move small amounts of classroom modelling material frame by frame to show both landscape change and a realistic repair action such as replacing topsoil and replanting. This connects directly to the line of inquiry that Earth's resources are vital and must be used responsibly. The app's camera capture, frame-by-frame playback and simple titles turn the model into a shareable stop-motion explanation.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|How the World Works.d: Students use Stop Motion Studio to photograph an ice cube at regular intervals as it changes from a solid to a liquid. This directly explores how heating and cooling change state and shows why careful observation helps us understand the physical world. Pairs arrange the photographs into a short stop-motion film and add simple labels such as solid, melting and liquid. The app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features make the slow change easy to see. Students present their films and explain what stayed the same and what changed.

Students investigate the observable properties of classroom solids and liquids, testing features such as shape, flow, texture and whether each material can be poured. They use Book Creator to make a short digital materials guide with one page for each item they test. Each page includes a photo, written observations and a recorded explanation of why the material is a solid or liquid. The built-in page templates, camera and voice recording tools support students to combine their evidence in one place. The finished books can be shared with classmates as a reference during the unit.

Small groups test which everyday covering, such as foil, fabric or paper, best slows the melting of an ice cube. This connects scientific thinking with the everyday problem of keeping something cold. Students enter their covering, prediction, observations and melting time into a Microsoft Forms survey prepared by the teacher. The automatic response charts help the class compare results and look for patterns across all groups. Students use the class data to present a recommendation supported by evidence.

Students use Explain Everything to show what happens when water is cooled into ice and then warmed back into liquid water. This directly addresses how heating and cooling change state. On separate whiteboard pages, they draw and label the solid, melting and liquid stages, then record themselves explaining the observable changes. The drawing, annotation and voice-recording features let students point to evidence while they speak. Each student finishes with a short narrated explanation that can be played to a partner or the class.

Students photograph safe examples of solids and liquids around the classroom, such as a wooden block, water, glue and a metal spoon. This supports the line of inquiry into the observable properties of solids and liquids. They use PicCollage to sort the photographs into two labelled sections and add short property words such as keeps its shape, flows or can be poured. The photo layout, text and sticker features help Year 3 students organise their observations clearly. Groups present their finished classification collage and explain any example that was difficult to place.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|Where We Are in Pla.d: Students use Google Maps to explore Australia and neighbouring regions, switching between the world map, satellite view and Street View. They compare how borders, coastlines, roads and landmarks help define places, linking directly to the line of inquiry about how Australia and neighbouring regions define places. In pairs, students prepare and present a short live walkthrough showing one Australian place and one nearby regional place. The everyday zoom, distance and Street View features make the comparison manageable for Year 3.

Students create a short digital book about one Australian state or territory and the features that give it a unique identity. Each page can cover its location, capital city, natural features, landmarks and something people value about the place, connecting directly to the line of inquiry about states and territories having unique identities. Students publish a book with labelled maps, pictures, short text and a recorded spoken introduction. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing, image and audio tools keep the task simple and contained in one place.

Students build a class gallery showing different ways land and place are represented and valued. Each pair adds a post about one place, including a simple map or image, a short description and an explanation of why that place matters to people. The finished Padlet becomes a shareable class collection connected directly to the central idea that land and place are represented and valued in different ways. Padlet’s post, image, audio and comment features allow students to contribute and respond without creating a full presentation.

Students place Sphero BOLT on a large floor map of Australia and code it to travel between selected states and territories. They use measured distances and compass headings, then test and debug the route so the robot stops at the correct places. Each group presents its completed route and explains how location, direction and distance help represent Australia, linking to how Australia defines places. Sphero BOLT’s movement commands, compass heading and programmable LED matrix are central to the task, with the lights used to display a simple symbol or colour at each stop.
