Students record a short podcast episode explaining why a selected place or area of Country is important to First Nations peoples, using respectful information provided during the unit. They connect their explanation directly to the line of inquiry about First Nations connections to Country and include the relevant Nation or language group name where this has been confirmed. Each group publishes a two-minute episode with an introduction, two or three key ideas and a closing acknowledgement that Country is more than a location on a map. Canva’s recording, trimming and simple audio timeline features support a clear Year 3 recording without specialist equipment.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital book about health and wellbeing, with one page each for sleep, food, movement, relationships and calming strategies. This directly explores what it means to be healthy and actions that maintain a healthy mind and body. Each page includes a simple explanation, an everyday example and a drawing or recorded spoken message. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and voice recording make the finished class health guide easy to create and share.

Students use Microsoft Forms to collect class data about everyday health and wellbeing choices, such as sleep routines, active play, water and screen breaks. They examine the automatic charts and discuss the line of inquiry about choices and their impact on health. Each pair records two findings and one realistic action the class could try. The simple question builder and automatic response charts are the key features used for this task.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|Who We Are.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
Glen Waverley|Year 3|Who We Are.d: Students choose a character and record a short health and wellbeing message explaining one action that supports a healthy mind or body. Their message must name the choice, explain its likely impact and give a practical example, directly addressing choices and their impact on health. Adobe Express turns the recorded voice into a short animated character video that students can present to the class. The ready-made characters and voice-driven animation keep the task manageable for Year 3 students.

Students add posts to a shared Padlet about actions that maintain health and wellbeing, organised under headings such as healthy body, healthy mind and healthy relationships. Each student publishes one action, explains why it helps and adds a suitable picture or drawing. Students then read classmates’ posts and leave one respectful comment that identifies a choice they could try themselves. Padlet’s shared board, columns, posts and comments support a clear class collection linked to actions that maintain a healthy mind and body.

Students code a micro:bit to act as a simple health and wellbeing reminder. Pressing button A displays a movement symbol, while pressing button B displays a calm-breathing symbol, and students test and debug both sequences. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about actions to maintain a healthy mind and body, because students must explain when each reminder could be useful. The micro:bit’s buttons, LED grid and simple block coding power the finished working reminder.

Glen Waverley|Year 4|How We Organise Our.d: Students create an annotated map showing services that help a community live fairly and safely, such as schools, hospitals, parks, police stations and public transport. This directly explores the central idea that communities create services to help people live together. They add symbols, labels and short notes explaining who each service supports, then present their finished community service map to the class. The simple map layers, drawing and labelling tools make the task manageable for Year 4 students.

Students use Microsoft Forms to create a short survey about which classroom or community rules people believe are most important for fairness and safety. This explores how leadership impacts communities because leaders need to listen before making decisions. Classmates complete the survey, and students present the automatic response charts and explain one rule they would recommend to a leader. The familiar multiple-choice, short-answer and response summary features power the activity.

Students make a short digital book profiling a real school, community or civic leader and the strengths that help that person guide others. This directly addresses effective and influential leadership and the strengths that help leaders guide others. Each book includes a title page, key decisions, examples of community impact and a recorded spoken reflection about what makes the leader effective. Book Creator’s page templates, text boxes, image tools and built-in audio recording keep the task straightforward.

Students respond to several teacher-posted community leadership situations, such as deciding how to share a park fairly or improve safety near a school. For each situation, they post what a fair leader should do and explain how the decision could impact the community. Students then read and comment on classmates’ ideas before the class presents a shared leadership advice wall. Padlet’s posts, columns and comment feature allow everyone to contribute and compare responses in one place.

Students design a public information poster explaining one community rule, law or service and how it helps people live together fairly and safely. This connects directly to the unit’s central idea and asks students to communicate as responsible community leaders. Their finished poster includes a clear heading, a simple explanation, an example and a practical action for community members, and is published for a class gallery. Adobe Express templates, text boxes, icons and image tools make it easy to produce a clear Year 4 poster.

Glen Waverley|Year 4|How the World Works.d: Students create and complete a class survey about the materials used in everyday products such as lunch boxes, drink bottles and food packaging. This directly explores how the design and use of products can have an impact on the natural world. They use the question builder and automatic response charts to collect data and compare reusable, recyclable and single-use items. Each group presents one chart and a practical change supported by the class data.

Students use Tinkercad to design a simple 3D prototype of a product that could replace a commonly discarded item, such as a reusable bag tag or a clip for closing food packets. This connects to material solutions for a sustainable future by asking students to design a small, useful product intended for 3D printing in plastic rather than pretending to test different materials on screen. They build the model with basic shapes, resize and align the parts, and add simple text where useful. Students finish with a printable 3D design and present how its shape and repeated use could help reduce waste.

Students make a short stop-motion film showing the life cycle of an everyday product, from raw material to manufacture, use, reuse and disposal. This addresses how the design and use of products can have an impact on the natural world. Using the built-in camera, frame-by-frame timeline and title tools, they move classroom objects or paper pieces a little at a time and add clear labels. Their finished film presents both the environmental problem and one more sustainable product choice.

Students explore where common product materials such as timber, metals and plastics come from and identify natural environments that may be affected by their production or disposal. This supports the line of inquiry about how research solves problems in the natural world. They use MapMaker’s map layers, drawing and labelling tools to create an annotated map linking selected materials with relevant places and environmental concerns. Each pair presents its map and explains one change in product design or use that could reduce harm.

Students create a short narrated explanation comparing two materials that could be used for the same product, such as paper and plastic packaging or wood and metal furniture. This directly explores how material properties determine their use. They use the drawing, text, image and voice-recording features to show useful properties, likely drawbacks and the effect each choice may have on the natural world. The finished recording becomes a clear two-minute recommendation for which material should be chosen and why.

Glen Waverley|Year 4|Where We Are in Pla.d: Students use Google Maps to view the routes and destinations of a selected historical explorer, then examine important locations in Street View where it is available. They estimate distances, notice physical barriers and discuss how geography influenced the journey. This directly explores the line of inquiry, how people have explored over time. Using the world map, distance information and Street View, each group presents a short guided walkthrough showing the route, key landmarks and one discovery or consequence of the exploration.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital journal about a real journey of exploration. They write dated entries explaining why the person explored, what was discovered and what opportunities or problems followed. This connects the central idea, exploration leads to discoveries, opportunities and new understandings. Students combine pages of text, drawings, images and voice recordings, then publish and read their journal to a partner.

Students enter teacher-provided information about several journeys of exploration into Microsoft Excel, including the date, distance travelled and main purpose. They sort the information by date and create a simple column chart to compare how the journeys changed over time. This supports the line of inquiry, how people have explored over time. The finished spreadsheet and chart give students a clear visual they can present while explaining one pattern they noticed.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short animation showing a journey of exploration and one consequence for the people or place involved. They move paper figures, ships and map pieces a small amount between each photograph, then check and adjust the sequence. This directly addresses the line of inquiry, consequences of exploration. Using the app’s frame-by-frame camera, playback and title tools, each group produces and screens a one-minute explanation of cause and effect.

Students use Padlet to build a shared class wall about reasons for exploration, such as trade, curiosity, resources, science or finding new routes. Each student publishes one post naming a real example, explaining the reason and adding a relevant image or source link supplied by the teacher. This connects directly to the line of inquiry, reasons for exploration. Padlet’s shared posts, columns and commenting tools allow the class to sort examples into categories and respond with questions or connections.

Glen Waverley|Year 4|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital book about spiritual or religious beliefs explored in the Who We Are unit. Each pair includes two belief traditions, showing similarities and differences in celebrations, places, symbols or everyday practices. They publish a six-page book with respectful captions, drawings and recorded explanations, ending with a page about how beliefs contribute to human diversity. Book Creator’s simple page templates, drawing tools and audio recording make the task manageable for Year 4 students.

Students use Google Maps to view significant spiritual or religious places around the world, such as churches, mosques, temples, synagogues and places connected to First Nations spirituality. They explore the map and Street View to compare the buildings, surrounding communities and ways each place is used, supporting the line of inquiry into similarities and differences of spiritual beliefs. Small groups present a guided on-screen tour of three places and explain one careful observation about each location. The everyday map search, zoom and Street View features are central to the activity, with students viewing rather than creating or saving maps.

Students design a one-page infographic explaining how different religions contribute to the diversity of human life. They combine short factual statements with respectful images and headings about areas such as festivals, food, music, service, art or community traditions. Each student publishes and presents an infographic that includes one contribution from two different religions and a clear statement linked to the central idea. Canva’s ready-made infographic templates, text boxes and image library keep the design work realistic for Year 4.

Students record a short comparison of two spiritual or religious beliefs studied during the Who We Are unit. On separate slides, they add pictures and labels showing a similarity, a difference and one contribution each belief makes to human diversity. They then use the recording feature to narrate their thinking while pointing to the evidence on each slide, producing a shareable two-minute explanation. Explain Everything’s slide canvas, pointer and voice recording are the main features used.

Students make a digital collage titled “Beliefs Add to Human Diversity” using examples from the class’s learning about spiritual or religious beliefs. They arrange respectful images and brief captions into sections for celebrations, sacred places, symbols and community contributions. The finished collage shows both shared features and differences, directly addressing the line of inquiry into similarities and differences of spiritual beliefs. PicCollage’s photo layout, text and sticker tools allow students to create and present the work in one lesson.

Glen Waverley|Year 4|Sharing the Planet.d: Students view several teacher-selected First Nations Countries in Google Maps, including the Melbourne area, central Australia and the Torres Strait Islands. They use the map, satellite view, Street View and distance tool to compare landscapes, locations and scale, without treating Country as just a boundary on a map. This directly supports the line of inquiry about the importance of Country to First Nations people. Pairs present a short live map walkthrough showing two places and explaining, from the class learning, why Country includes deep cultural connections as well as land and water.

Students make a short digital book about the diversity of First Nations people using teacher-approved information and images. Each page can focus on a different community, language group, place or tradition, directly supporting the line of inquiry about diversity of First Nations people. They use Book Creator’s page templates, text boxes, image tools and built-in voice recording to combine written explanations with spoken reflections. The finished books are shared with classmates as a class library rather than presenting one community as representative of all First Nations people.

Students complete a teacher-made Microsoft Forms investigation based on short, approved examples of First Nations communities, languages, family connections and traditions. They record which details belong to each example and identify evidence that First Nations peoples are diverse, linking directly to the diversity line of inquiry. The class then studies the automatic response charts and discusses patterns, common misunderstandings and answers that need checking. Small groups present one chart and explain what the collected class data shows about avoiding broad generalisations.

Students record a two-minute spoken reflection about why Country, language and community are significant to the lives of First Nations people. They choose evidence from the class’s teacher-approved learning and explain it in their own words, making a clear connection to the central idea. Using GarageBand’s audio recorder, playback and trimming tools, students rerecord unclear sections and edit their reflection into a polished audio piece. The completed recordings are played in a class listening session, with no copied cultural music or sound effects added.

Students create a one-page visual explainer showing how community, family and traditions are important within one teacher-selected First Nations case study. They organise accurate facts under clear headings and include approved images or simple icons, directly addressing the line of inquiry about community, family and traditions. Canva’s poster templates, text boxes, shapes and image placement tools help students arrange the information clearly. Students publish the finished explainers as a class display and briefly present the evidence behind one design choice.

Glen Waverley|Year 5|How We Express Ours.d: Students investigate how people design for purpose by creating a short survey about a real classroom or playground need. This directly explores how design thinking meets community needs because students collect responses before deciding what to design. They use question types such as multiple choice and short answer, then review the automatic response charts to identify a common need. Each group presents a simple design brief that names the users, the problem and the most important survey evidence.

Students explore effective ways to engage an audience by designing a poster that promotes a useful product or service for the school community. They choose a clear message, arrange text and images, and test whether classmates can understand the poster’s purpose within five seconds. Canva’s ready-made poster layouts, text tools and image library make it practical to create and revise the design in one or two lessons. Students publish their finished posters and explain how their choices help the design reach its intended audience.

Students document how design thinking creates in various ways by developing a digital design journal for a simple solution to a classroom need. They create pages showing the problem, early sketches, feedback, changes and a final proposal, making the unit idea that people design for purpose clear throughout. Book Creator’s page layouts, drawing tools, text boxes and built-in audio recording let students combine written, visual and spoken explanations. Students share the finished book as a clear record of how their idea changed through testing and feedback.

Students examine effective ways to engage an audience by producing a short stop-motion advertisement for a product they have designed to meet an everyday school need. They plan a clear opening, show the product solving the problem, and finish with a memorable message for Year 5 students. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera, playback and simple editing tools allow groups to test pacing and reshoot unclear sections. Each group presents its finished advertisement and gathers audience feedback about which design choices were most persuasive.

Students explore how people design for purpose by creating a short audio identity for a school event, club or community message. This connects to effective ways to engage an audience because students must choose sounds that suit a particular purpose and group of listeners. They use GarageBand’s loops, virtual instruments and voice recording to build a 20-second jingle or audio introduction, then edit the order and volume of each part. Students play their finished audio to the class and explain how the sound choices communicate the intended mood and message.

Glen Waverley|Year 5|How We Organise Our.d: Students use Microsoft Excel to create a simple weekly budget for a fictional person earning income from a part-time job. They allocate money to needs, wants, saving and giving, linking directly to the line of inquiry, “Responsibilities when managing income.” Students produce a completed budget table and a chart showing where the income goes, then present and explain one choice they changed after checking the totals. The everyday features that make this work are spreadsheet cells, simple formulas and charts.

Students use Book Creator to explore the idea that wealth is more than money by creating a short digital book called “What Makes a Life Rich?” They include pages about relationships, health, knowledge, time, community support and money, linking directly to the line of inquiry, “Wealth is more than money.” Each student publishes a book with written explanations, drawings or photos, and a recorded reflection about which forms of wealth matter most to them. The everyday features that power the task are page templates, text boxes, drawing tools and voice recording.

Students use Canva to make an infographic showing several ways people earn and manage income, such as wages, running a small business, saving and budgeting. This directly supports the line of inquiry, “Income is earned and managed in many ways.” Students present their finished infographic to a partner, checking that each example includes a clear explanation rather than just a picture. Canva’s ready-made infographic templates, icons, shapes and text boxes keep the task manageable for Year 5.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short film about a character making choices after receiving income. Their character must balance a need, a want, saving and giving, connecting directly to the line of inquiry, “Responsibilities when managing income.” Students move paper characters and labelled money pieces between frames, then show the finished film and explain the consequences of the character’s decisions. The central feature is the frame-by-frame camera, which lets students turn small physical movements into a clear animated sequence.

Students use Padlet to build a class collection of examples showing how economic systems are part of everyday society. Each pair adds a post about one way income can be earned or managed, then comments on another post with a question or a responsible suggestion, supporting the line of inquiry, “Income is earned and managed in many ways.” The class ends up with a shared digital wall that can be sorted into categories such as employment, business, saving, spending and giving. Padlet’s simple post, image and comment features make it easy to collect and discuss everyone’s examples in one place.

Glen Waverley|Year 6|How We Organise Our.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to map a local human-made system, such as public transport, waste collection or emergency services. They add locations, routes and labels to show how parts of the system connect people and places across the community. This directly explores the central idea of interconnected human-made systems and communities. Using the map’s drawing, marker and measurement tools, each group creates and presents an annotated system map that explains what might happen if one connection stopped working.

Students use Microsoft Forms to investigate how a school organisation works by surveying classmates about a familiar system such as the canteen, library or lunchtime clubs. They write clear questions, collect responses and examine the automatically generated charts to identify what works well and what could improve. This connects directly to the central idea by showing how an organisation’s structure and function affect its community. Each group presents a short evidence-based recommendation using the response summary and charts in Forms.

Students build a small community organisation in Minecraft Education, such as a recycling centre, community health centre or emergency services hub. They create separate spaces for key roles, resources and processes, then add signs explaining how people and information move through the organisation. This explores the central idea by making the structure and function of an organisation visible. Using Minecraft’s blocks, signs and in-world camera, students present a guided tour showing how the parts work together and where delays or problems could occur.

Students use Book Creator to make a digital case study of a chosen organisation, such as the school, local council, charity or public library. They create pages showing the organisation’s purpose, key roles, decision-making structure and connections with the wider community. This directly addresses the central idea about the structure and function of organisations. Using Book Creator’s page layouts, drawing tools, image tools and voice recording, students publish a shareable book with a simple organisation chart and narrated explanation.

Students use Lego Spike Prime to build and code a working model of one process within a human-made system, such as sorting recycling or moving supplies through a warehouse. They assign each part a clear job, test the sequence, record failures and debug the code until the process runs reliably. This connects to the central idea by showing how the structure and function of connected parts affect an entire organisation. Using the Lego pieces, motors and block coding, each team demonstrates its model and explains how a breakdown in one part changes the whole system.

Glen Waverley|Year 6|How We Express Ours.d: Students use Adobe Express to create two versions of an advertisement for the same school event, with each version aimed at a different audience. This directly explores how media targets audiences and uses techniques to engage and persuade. They publish a matched pair of digital advertisements and add a short note explaining their choices of words, images and colours. Simple templates, text tools and the built-in image library make the task manageable in a few lessons.

Students use IMovie to make a 45-second media message persuading Year 6 students to take action on a school or community issue. They focus on techniques used to engage and persuade, including music, pacing, repeated phrases and carefully chosen visuals. Each group presents a finished video and explains the response they hoped to invite from its audience. The timeline, title cards, voice-over recording and built-in soundtracks provide the main tools they need.

Students use Book Creator to build a short interactive guide called “How Media Gets Our Attention”. This supports the critical evaluation of media messages by asking students to examine examples and identify audience, purpose, persuasive language and missing information. Their finished book includes written explanations, recreated sample messages and recorded audio reflections. The page templates, text boxes, drawing tools and audio recording feature allow students to combine their findings in one shareable book.

Students use Kahoot to create a class quiz about spotting persuasive techniques and evaluating media messages. They write questions that ask players to identify intended audiences, emotional language, exaggeration, trustworthy evidence and calls to action. Small groups host their finished quizzes, then discuss which questions produced different responses and why. The multiple-choice question builder, images, timer and live results make audience response visible straight away.

Students use Padlet to run a class media response wall about a set of teacher-provided advertisements and campaign messages. They post a brief evaluation of one message, naming its target audience, persuasive techniques and the response it invites. Classmates add comments that agree, challenge an idea or point out something that may have been left out, creating a shareable record of critical evaluation. Padlet’s post columns, image attachments and comment feature keep the discussion organised and easy to review.

Glen Waverley|Year 6|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to create a short class survey about what influences consumer choices, such as price, advertising, convenience, fairness and environmental impact. This directly explores the line of inquiry about influences on consumer choices. They collect anonymous responses and examine the automatic charts to identify the strongest influences in their year level. Each group presents one chart and explains what it reveals about the connection between people’s choices and natural systems.

Students use a teacher-prepared Excel table to compare everyday products linked to the Sharing the Planet unit, such as new and second-hand clothing or packaged and refillable soap. They sort the information and calculate simple totals for cost, packaging, transport distance and expected useful life. This addresses how consumer decisions impact living things and their habitats by making the costs and environmental effects easier to compare. Students create a column chart and add a short written recommendation for the most responsible choice, using Excel’s formulas, sorting and chart tools.

Students use Google Maps in viewing mode to trace the likely journey of a familiar consumer product, such as a cotton T-shirt, from a growing or manufacturing region to Melbourne. They compare distances, examine satellite views and use Street View where available to notice ports, farms, factories, shops and transport routes. This connects to the central idea by showing the interdependence between human and natural systems behind consumer choices. Pairs give a live map walkthrough to the class, explaining where habitats or communities might be affected along the journey.

Students use Adobe Express to make a one-page consumer guide promoting an alternative such as repairing, borrowing, swapping, buying second-hand or choosing a refillable product. This directly explores alternative models of consumerism that honour a fair and sustainable future. Their guide includes a clear claim, two supporting facts, an image and one realistic action families could take. Students publish and present the finished guide, using Adobe Express templates, text boxes and image tools to communicate clearly.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small sustainable shopping area for the Sharing the Planet unit. Their model includes practical alternatives such as a repair shop, refill station, tool library, second-hand store or community garden, with signs explaining how each choice reduces waste or supports fairness. This addresses the line of inquiry about alternative models of consumerism and their different perspectives. Groups present a walkthrough of their completed world, using Minecraft’s blocks, signs and building tools to show how the marketplace works.

Glen Waverley|Year 6|How the World Works.d: Students build and code a small motor-powered winch to explore energy transfer and transformation in circuits. They change one factor, such as motor speed or the load being lifted, and run repeated tests while keeping the rest of the build the same. Each group presents its working model, code and a simple table of results showing how the change affected the winch. The familiar building pieces, programmable motor and block-based coding make the investigation manageable for Year 6.

Students use Sphero BOLT to investigate how changing programmed speed affects the distance travelled in a fixed time. They write a short program, predict the result, run repeated trials and measure each journey along a marked floor track. This directly practises the scientific method and shows how experimentation can confirm or contest an initial prediction. Groups share their final code, recorded results and a brief evidence-based conclusion, using BOLT’s motors and block-based coding as the main features.

Students create a short stop-motion model showing the relationship between planets and the Sun, including rotation and orbit. They move simple classroom models a small amount between each photograph so the final animation clearly shows the different movements. This supports the line of inquiry about the relationship between planets and the Sun, while giving students a chance to explain what a model can and cannot prove. The frame-by-frame camera, playback and simple titles allow each group to publish a clear scientific animation.

Students use Book Creator to publish a digital laboratory report about a classroom investigation of energy transfer and transformation in simple circuits. They add their question, prediction, method, results and conclusion, including photos taken during each circuit test. This directly supports the scientific method and asks students to explain whether their evidence confirmed or contested their prediction. Book Creator’s page templates, text boxes, built-in camera and voice recording give each group a shareable report without needing a separate presentation tool.

Students collect class data from repeated paper-helicopter drop tests to examine how changing one variable affects falling time. Each group submits its measurements through Microsoft Forms, then the class studies the automatically generated charts for patterns, unusual results and possible testing errors. This connects directly to how experiments lead to new understandings and shows why scientists need repeated trials before making a claim. The response form and automatic charts produce a shared data set that students can present and use to write an evidence-based conclusion.

Glen Waverley|Year 6|Where We Are in Pla.d: Students use Google Maps to explore Street View in two Australian places shaped by different patterns of migration and national development. They compare housing, transport, public services, workplaces and visible cultural landmarks, linking their observations to how human needs drive national development. Pairs then present a live guided walkthrough of selected locations and explain what each place suggests about migration and nation building. The everyday features that power the task are the world map, Street View and distance measurement.

Students enter teacher-provided census data about migration, population growth, housing or employment in Australia into Microsoft Excel. They use the data to investigate the role of migration in nation building and how growing populations create needs for services and infrastructure. Each group produces a labelled table and two clear charts, then presents one evidence-based conclusion to the class. The ordinary Excel features used are cells, sorting, simple formulas and chart tools.

Students create a short recorded explanation showing how one human need, such as safe housing, transport, work or water, has influenced the development of an Australian town or city. They connect their explanation to the central idea that human needs drive the development of nations, while also identifying an impact on Indigenous or colonial populations. Each student produces a three-slide narrated presentation using maps, images, labels and arrows to show change over time. The task uses Explain Everything’s basic drawing, text, image and voice-recording features.

Students build a small Australian settlement at two points in time, showing how needs such as food, water, shelter, transport and employment influenced its development. They must also represent and explain at least one impact of that development on Indigenous people or the local environment, directly addressing the unit’s third line of inquiry. Groups create labelled areas with blocks and signs, then lead classmates through the finished world and justify their design choices. The familiar Minecraft Education features used are building blocks, signs and shared-world exploration.

Students create a class evidence wall about the role of migration in Australian nation building. Each pair publishes one post about a migrant group or migration period, including a short explanation, an image, a source link and an example of a need that influenced settlement or development. Students then comment on two other posts to identify connections, differences or impacts on Indigenous and colonial populations. The activity uses Padlet’s straightforward post, column, image, link and comment features to produce a shareable class collection.

Glen Waverley|Year 6|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital book called “Who I Am”, using words, drawings, photos and voice recordings to share parts of their identity. Each page explores the central idea’s focus on the self, beliefs, values, health or relationships, while allowing students to keep private information out. They finish with a shareable book that includes an identity page, a values page and a reflection on the people or practices that support them. Book Creator’s simple page layouts, drawing tools and audio recording make the task manageable within a few lessons.

Students design an anonymous class survey about everyday habits that support physical, mental and social health, such as sleep, movement, screen breaks and time with others. This directly investigates the central idea’s focus on personal health and human relationships without asking classmates to reveal sensitive details. Students collect responses, examine the automatically generated charts and present two patterns and one practical suggestion to the class. Microsoft Forms’ question choices, response collection and built-in charts power the whole activity.

Students code a simple wellbeing check-in tool linked to the central idea’s focus on mental health and the choices people make to care for themselves. Pressing one button displays a chosen symbol for a calming strategy, while the other displays a symbol for seeking support or connecting with someone. Students test and debug the button actions, then present their working Micro:bit and explain when each strategy could be useful. The programmable buttons and LED grid are the central features used in the task.

Students make a one-page personal wellbeing plan about balancing physical, mental, social and spiritual health in everyday life. They connect their practical choices to the central idea by explaining how habits, values and relationships can shape a person’s sense of self. The finished infographic includes four realistic actions, simple icons and a short statement about one value that guides their choices. Canva’s templates, text boxes, shapes and icon library help students organise and publish the plan clearly.

Students record a two-minute spoken reflection titled “Sounds of Belonging” about a relationship, community or personal value that helps shape who they are. This connects directly to the central idea’s focus on the self, beliefs, values and human relationships. They combine their own narration with a small number of built-in loops, adjust the volume so the words remain clear and export a finished audio piece for a class listening session. GarageBand’s voice recording, tracks, loops and volume controls make the activity achievable without specialist music skills.

St Kilda|Prep|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students create a class book about celebrations and traditions that are important to their families. Each child makes one page with a drawing, a short teacher-supported sentence and a voice recording explaining what happens at the celebration. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about the traditions of our families and communities. The finished book can be played on the classroom screen and shared with families, using Book Creator’s page-making, drawing and audio recording features.

In pairs, students use character puppets to act out a familiar celebration such as a birthday, Lunar New Year or Christmas. They move the puppets and record a short conversation showing what people do and why the event is important. This explores the line of inquiry about how and why people celebrate. Each pair presents a simple recorded puppet scene, using Puppet Pals’ characters, backgrounds, movement and voice recording.

Students code a short animation showing the order of events in a celebration or family tradition. They choose or draw characters, then use movement, speech and start blocks to show three simple moments such as arriving, sharing food and giving thanks. This supports the central idea that people recognise important events through celebrations and traditions. The finished project is a short sequence students can play and explain to the class, powered by ScratchJr’s picture-based coding blocks.

Students make a simple comparison poster about two celebrations. They use PicCollage’s camera option to photograph teacher-provided celebration picture cards, then arrange them under headings such as “same” and “different” with a few labels or stickers. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about the similarities and differences between celebrations. The finished collage gives each child a clear visual poster to present to a partner or the class.

With teacher guidance, students view two places where different celebrations or traditions are important, such as Melbourne and another city connected to class families. They use the world map and Street View to notice landmarks, decorations, gathering places or features of the local community, while understanding that the images may not show a celebration happening that day. This supports the line of inquiry about the traditions of our families and communities. Small groups present a short screen-based comparison by navigating between the two places and sharing one similarity and one difference they noticed.

St Kilda|Prep|How We Organise Ourselves.d: Students use Book Creator to make one page about a role in the school community, such as a teacher, gardener, nurse or librarian. They add a drawing or photo and record themselves explaining the person’s responsibilities, linking directly to the line of inquiry about roles people play. The pages are combined into a class book called Our School Community and shared with another Prep class. The simple page templates, drawing tools and voice recording make this manageable for young students.

Students place picture cards of community places on a floor grid, then program a Bee-Bot to travel from one place to another, such as from the fire station to a home. Before pressing go, they explain which community worker is travelling and what responsibility that person has. Pairs take turns entering directions, testing the route and fixing their sequence, showing how working together helps everyone. The Bee-Bot’s forward, backward, left and right buttons are the central feature of the task.

Students photograph a drawing of a community worker and use ChatterPix Kids to make the character speak. They record a short message beginning with “My role is…” and explain one responsibility in the community, directly exploring roles people play. Each student produces a short talking-character video to present to the class. The simple mouth line and voice recording features let Prep students create the video with minimal help.

Students view the St Kilda neighbourhood in Google Maps and use Street View to look for places where people carry out community roles, such as schools, shops, libraries and emergency services. In small groups, they follow a teacher-chosen route and discuss the responsibilities of people who work at each place. Each group presents a short live Street View walkthrough, explaining how the places and workers help the community. The zoom, map view and Street View features allow students to explore familiar locations without needing to log in or edit the map.

Students use PicCollage to create a simple poster showing one responsibility they have in the classroom community, such as packing away, caring for books or helping a partner. They add a photo or drawing and a short teacher-supported sentence, linking to the central idea that we all have roles and responsibilities in the community. The finished posters are presented to the class and displayed as a shared Classroom Responsibilities gallery. PicCollage’s basic layout, image and text features make the task clear and achievable for Prep students.

St Kilda|Prep|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Seek by iNaturalist during a supervised walk to find and identify plants, insects and other living things around the campus. They use the camera identification feature to explore how people interact with the local environment. Each pair records a small set of identified species in Seek and later opens them to show the class. The class discusses how actions such as leaving plants alone or putting rubbish in bins can help care for these living things.

Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a teacher-made floor map showing a park, pond, trees, bins and pieces of rubbish. They press the forward, backward and turn buttons to plan a route that visits helpful actions and avoids places being harmed. This connects directly to ways in which people can take action and care for the environment. Each group presents its programmed route and explains the caring choices it included.

Students use ScratchJr to make a short animation about how human actions change the environment. They create a simple outdoor background, add characters and code them to drop rubbish, clean it up or care for plants. The movement and speech blocks help students show the effect people have on an environment. Each pair plays its finished animation for the class and explains which action harmed or helped the place.

Students use classroom objects or play materials to build a small habitat and show it changing after people leave rubbish behind. They then move the objects a little at a time to show people returning to clean and care for the habitat. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera turns these small changes into a short movie about the central idea that human actions change the environment. Groups present their finished movie and name one action everyone can take.

Students draw or photograph a tree, animal or other living thing and use ChatterPix Kids to make it speak about Sharing the Planet. They add the talking mouth line and record a short message describing one human action that affects its environment. This supports the line of inquiry about the effect people have on the environment. Each student finishes with a short talking picture that can be played to the class as an environmental care message.

St Kilda|Prep|Where We Are in Place and.d: Students explore the St Kilda campus and nearby landmarks in Google Maps as part of Where We Are in Place and Time. They use the map and Street View to notice where places are, what is nearby and how the area looks from the street, linking to the central idea of orientation in place. In pairs, students choose one landmark and present a short on-screen walkthrough showing how they would travel there from the campus. The everyday map zoom, route viewing and Street View features make the activity manageable for Prep students without needing student logins.

Students create a simple personal history timeline in Seesaw for the unit Where We Are in Place and Time. They draw or add a photo for three moments such as being a baby, starting kindergarten and beginning Prep, connecting directly to the central idea of personal histories. Students record a short voice explanation for each moment and publish the finished timeline to their learning journal. Seesaw's drawing, photo, voice recording and journal features allow students to complete and share the task in one place.

Students make a Then and Now collage about themselves for Where We Are in Place and Time. They place a teacher-provided baby photo beside a recent photo and add simple labels showing what has changed and what has stayed the same, linking to the central idea of personal histories. Each student produces a one-page collage to show during a class sharing circle. PicCollage's photo layout, text and sticker features help Prep students organise their ideas clearly.

Students choose a photo of an object connected to their personal history, such as a favourite baby toy, family recipe book or first school bag, for Where We Are in Place and Time. They add a mouth to the object and record it explaining who used it, when it was important and what memory it holds, connecting to the central idea of personal histories. Each student makes a short talking-object video to present to the class. ChatterPix Kids' simple photo, mouth-drawing and voice recording features keep the task playful and achievable for Prep.

Students draw a simple picture map of their route from the classroom to a familiar place on the St Kilda campus for Where We Are in Place and Time. They add arrows, basic shapes and pictures of landmarks such as a gate, playground or office, linking to the central idea of orientation in place. Students trace the route with a finger and present their finished map to a partner using words such as forwards, turn, beside and near. Freeform's drawing tools, shapes and movable labels make it easy to build and adjust the map.

St Kilda|Prep|Who We Are.d: Students photograph a simple face drawing, add a moving mouth and record the character explaining one emotion. They say what the character might do to build a positive relationship, such as asking to join in or using calm words. This directly explores how our emotions, behaviours and actions promote relationships. The photo, mouth-drawing and voice-recording features create a short talking-character video to share with the class.

Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a floor mat showing basic needs such as water, nutritious food, sleep, movement and care. They press the direction buttons, test the route and fix the sequence if the Bee-Bot reaches the wrong picture. This connects directly to the central idea that people’s basic needs must be met to be healthy. Each pair presents one completed route and explains how the chosen need helps us care for our bodies.

Students create a digital poster called “Ways I Care for My Body” using pictures, stickers, drawings and short labels. They include realistic choices such as drinking water, eating varied foods, sleeping, washing and being active. This supports the line of inquiry into how we care for our bodies. The collage layout and simple text and drawing tools help each child publish a clear poster to show the class.

In pairs, students choose characters and record a short scene about a common Prep relationship problem, such as someone feeling left out. They move the characters and use their voices to show an unhelpful action followed by a kinder choice. This explores how our emotions, behaviours and actions promote relationships. The character-moving, background and voice-recording features produce a short puppet performance the pair can present to classmates.

Students complete a short class survey about basic health needs by selecting answers to teacher-read questions about sleep, water, food, movement and caring adults. They then view the class response charts with the teacher and describe one pattern they notice. This connects to the central idea that people’s basic needs must be met to be healthy. The simple choice questions and automatic response charts create a shared class data display for discussion.

St Kilda|Prep|How the World Works.d: Students make a simple class book about changes they notice in Melbourne’s weather across one week. This connects to the central idea by exploring patterns in the natural world and how weather affects what people wear and do. Each pair adds a page with a photo, a weather drawing and a short spoken observation. Book Creator’s page templates, camera and voice-recording tools make the finished weather book easy to share with families.

Students use playdough or paper pieces to show how a seed grows into a plant. This explores the central idea by looking closely at change and patterns in the natural world. They move the pieces a small amount, capture one frame at a time and replay the sequence to check whether the growth is clear. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera creates a short plant-growth film that students can present to the class.

Students create a simple animation showing daytime changing into night-time. This connects to the central idea by exploring a repeating pattern in the natural world. They choose backgrounds and characters, then use start and movement blocks to make the sun cross the sky before changing to a night page. The finished ScratchJr project is a short coded animation that students can play and explain to a partner.

Students view St Kilda Beach and nearby streets to compare natural features with places built by people. This connects directly to the central idea about the interaction between the natural world and human societies. In pairs, they use satellite view and Street View to find the sea, sand, trees, roads and buildings, then present a short guided walkthrough to the class. Google Maps’ viewing and Street View tools let students explore these places without logging in or creating a map.

Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a teacher-made floor map containing a beach, park, road and buildings. This explores how natural places and human-made places sit together in the local environment, linking to the central idea. Students press the directional buttons, test the route and clear and debug their instructions if the Bee-Bot stops on the wrong square. Each pair finishes by presenting a successful programmed journey and naming the natural and built features it passes.

St Kilda|Year 1|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students photograph a drawn face showing an emotion, add a mouth line and record the character explaining how it feels. This explores different ways to communicate emotions through facial cues, pictures and voice. Each student makes a short talking-face video to present to a partner, who guesses the emotion and explains the clues they noticed. The simple photo, mouth-drawing and voice-recording features make the task manageable for Year 1.

Students create a short class book about how people express their emotions through the way they communicate. On each page, they draw or photograph an emotional expression and record a sentence describing the facial expression, body language or tone of voice. This directly supports the line of inquiry about understanding others' expressions through body language and facial cues. The page templates, drawing tools, camera and audio-recording button help students publish a shareable digital book.

Students code a character to express two different feelings through movement, facial appearance and a short message. They choose simple movement blocks, add speech bubbles and change scenes to show how the character's communication changes when its emotion changes. This connects to the central idea that people express their emotions through the way they communicate. Each pair presents its short coded animation and explains which clues help the audience recognise each feeling.

Students use paper figures or modelling clay to make a character's face and body slowly change from one emotion to another. They take a series of frames after each small movement, exploring how art and movement express feelings. The finished stop-motion film clearly shows the character's changing eyebrows, mouth, posture and gestures for classmates to interpret. The frame-by-frame camera and playback features let Year 1 students create and review a short animation with teacher support.

Students photograph themselves making three safe, teacher-chosen facial expressions and body poses linked to different emotions. They arrange the photos in a collage and add simple labels such as happy, worried or excited, focusing on the line of inquiry about understanding facial cues and body language. Each student presents the completed emotion collage and points out the visible clues in each image. The built-in camera, photo layout and text features provide a straightforward way to make a shareable visual display.

St Kilda|Year 1|How We Organise Ourselve.d: Students use Google Maps to explore where familiar products such as bananas, rice or chocolate come from and view those places using the map and Street View. This directly supports the line of inquiry about where products come from. In pairs, students present a short live map tour showing the product’s place of origin and the distance to Melbourne. The everyday map search, zoom and Street View features make distant production places visible to Year 1 students.

Students use ScratchJr to show the system a product goes through before reaching a consumer, such as wheat becoming bread. They place characters or objects on several pages and code simple movement and speech to show growing, making, transporting and selling. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about the systems products go through. Students finish with a short animated product journey that they can play and explain to the class, using ScratchJr’s blocks, pages and speech bubbles.

Students ask classmates which of three versions of a familiar product they would choose, such as apples, lunchboxes or drink bottles, and enter the results into a teacher-prepared Microsoft Excel table. This supports the line of inquiry about how people choose their products. With teacher guidance, they turn the class totals into a simple column chart and discuss which choice was most popular. Excel’s cells, number entry and chart feature help the class collect, compare and present real choice data.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to make a short film showing a product moving through a simple system, such as an apple travelling from orchard to truck, shop and consumer. They move paper pictures or classroom objects a small amount between each photo and check whether the order makes sense. This directly explores the central idea that systems are involved in preparing products for consumers. The finished stop-motion film is shared with the class, using the app’s built-in camera and frame-by-frame playback.

Students use Seesaw to explain where one everyday product comes from and how it reaches a consumer. They create a page with a drawing of the product journey, add simple labels for each stage and record their voice explaining the order. This connects the lines of inquiry about where products come from and the systems products go through. The result is a clear, shareable learning post made with Seesaw’s drawing, text and voice-recording tools.

St Kilda|Year 1|How the World Works.d: Students create a daily weather journal about the types of weather conditions they observe at school. They draw the sky, choose or write a weather word, and record themselves explaining how the weather affects their clothing, activities or feelings. Over several days, the class reviews the journal posts to notice weather patterns and changes. Seesaw’s drawing, voice recording and class journal features make each observation easy to record and share.

Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a floor grid showing different weather conditions and matching clothing or activities. They enter a sequence using the forward, backward and turn buttons, then test and debug the route if the Bee-Bot lands on the wrong picture. This directly explores how weather impacts our lives through choices such as wearing a raincoat, playing indoors or going to the beach. Pairs present one successful route and explain why their chosen clothing or activity suits that weather.

Students make a short class book called “Weather Affects Our Lives” with one page for each type of weather. On each page, they draw or add a photo, write a simple sentence, and record their voice explaining suitable clothing, food, activities or feelings. The finished book shows clear examples of the central idea that weather affects our lives in different ways. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and voice recording button support a polished book that the class can read together.

Students create a short puppet scene in which two characters experience a particular type of weather. They move the characters, choose a suitable background and record dialogue about what to wear, eat or do in those conditions. The scene connects directly to the line of inquiry about how weather impacts our lives. Puppet Pals’ movable characters, backgrounds and built-in voice recording let pairs present a simple weather story to the class.

Students complete a simple class weather survey by choosing today’s weather, suitable clothing and an activity they would do. The teacher displays the automatic response charts so students can compare answers and discuss how weather affects people’s choices. The class repeats the survey on several days and looks for patterns linked to changing weather and seasons. Microsoft Forms’ picture questions, large choice buttons and automatic charts create a clear class data record to present and discuss.

St Kilda|Year 1|Where We Are in Place an.d: Students use Book Creator to make a class book about family or classroom artefacts that connect the past, present and future. Each child adds a photo of one safe artefact, writes a short sentence about what it tells us, and records their voice explaining why it should be preserved. This directly explores why people preserve stories and artefacts and how they can be shared into the future. The simple page templates, camera, typing and voice-recording features help students create a book that can be read by families or next year’s class.

Students use Google Maps to view Street View around St Kilda and closely examine a preserved local landmark such as Luna Park or the St Kilda Pier area. They look for visible clues about the past, notice newer features nearby, and discuss what has stayed the same or changed. This supports how we learn about the past by examining places and their surviving features. Using the ordinary search, zoom and Street View controls, pairs present a short guided walkthrough to the class and explain the clues they found.

Students use GarageBand to record a short oral history about a family tradition, treasured object or story from the past. They plan two or three sentences, record their voice, listen back and re-record unclear parts before adding a simple opening or closing sound. This connects with how stories and artefacts can be shared into the future. The audio recorder, playback and basic trimming tools allow the class to create a collection of clear, shareable spoken memories.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show how an everyday object has changed from the past to the present, using teacher-provided pictures, drawings or simple models. They move the items a small amount between each photo, then play the frames in order and add short title cards such as “past”, “present” and “future”. This explores the central idea that stories and artefacts help us understand connections between the past, present and future. The frame-by-frame camera and playback features produce a short animation students can present and explain to the class.

Students use ScratchJr to retell a simple story that has been passed from an older family or community member to a child today. They choose characters and backgrounds, then use movement, speech and page-change blocks to place the events in a clear sequence. This directly explores how stories can be shared into the future. The picture-based coding blocks let Year 1 students build, test and debug a short animated story for classmates to view.

St Kilda|Year 1|Sharing the Planet.d: Students make a simple digital book about the physical structures of plants and bees. On each page, they draw or add a photo of one feature, such as roots, petals, wings or antennae, and record a short explanation of how it supports survival. This directly explores the line of inquiry about how features support survival in different environments. The finished books can be read aloud and shared with classmates, using Book Creator’s page, drawing, image and voice-recording tools.

Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a teacher-made floor grid from a hive to different flowers. They press the directional buttons, test the route and correct their sequence if the Bee-Bot reaches an obstacle or the wrong flower. This practical task explores how bees move through an environment to find food and help plants reproduce. Each pair presents one successful route and explains why safe, flower-rich spaces help bees survive.

Students photograph or draw a plant or bee and use ChatterPix Kids to make one of its structures speak. The moving mouth and voice-recording feature let a root, petal, wing or antenna explain how it helps the living thing survive. This connects directly to the central idea that living things have structures that allow them to survive in different environments. Students create and present a short talking picture with one clear scientific fact.

Students use Google Maps and Street View to look at two environments, such as a leafy local park and a busy built-up street near St Kilda. They observe and discuss visible plants, flowers, shelter and human-made features that could help or harm bees and other living things. This supports the line of inquiry into human impact on living things. Using the map view, zoom and Street View controls, students present one helpful feature and one possible problem they noticed.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show how a bee’s body structures help it collect food from a flower. They move a paper bee model a small amount between each photo, showing its wings carrying it to the flower and its legs or mouthparts helping it gather food. This explores the physical structure of plants and bees and how features support survival. The frame-by-frame camera and playback tools produce a short animation that students can show while explaining the science.

St Kilda|Year 1|Who We Are.d: Students use ScratchJr to code two characters playing a simple game and show what happens when one player makes a kind or unkind choice. This directly explores how players’ choices affect relationships in the games we play. They create and present a short animated story with movement, speech and a clear ending. The simple block-based coding, character and speech features make the task manageable for Year 1 students.

Students make a short digital book about the emotions they feel during the games we play, such as excitement, disappointment or frustration. This connects directly to identifying and managing emotions. Each child creates pages with a drawing or photo, a short sentence and a recorded suggestion for managing each feeling. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and audio recording make it easy to publish and share the finished books.

Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a floor grid showing different moments from the games we play, such as waiting for a turn, losing or helping another player. At each chosen square, they explain the player’s responsibility and what a fair choice would look like. This directly explores our responsibilities when playing games. Students present their completed route to the class, using the Bee-Bot’s forward, backward, left and right buttons to enter and test the sequence.

In pairs, students use Puppet Pals to record a short scene about a disagreement during one of the games we play. They show the characters naming their emotions, listening to each other and choosing a way to keep playing fairly. This connects identifying and managing emotions with how players’ choices affect relationships. Students present a recorded puppet show using the app’s characters, backgrounds, movement and voice recording.

Students complete a simple picture-supported class survey about how they feel and what they do in common situations during the games we play. This gathers class information about identifying and managing emotions, such as what helps when someone loses or has to wait. The teacher displays the automatic response charts, and students describe patterns they notice in the class answers. Microsoft Forms’ multiple-choice questions and automatic charts provide a clear, shareable class record.

St Kilda|Year 2|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students make a short digital museum book about artefacts that provide a window into the beliefs and values of a chosen culture. Each page includes a picture of an artefact, a simple caption explaining its use, and a recorded sentence about what it tells us about the culture. This directly explores how artefacts capture history and cultural expression. Book Creator’s page templates, image tools and built-in audio recording help students publish a shareable class museum book.

Students photograph a teacher-provided image of a cultural artefact and use ChatterPix Kids to make it appear to speak. They record a short first-person explanation of who might use the artefact, during which ritual or tradition, and why it matters. This connects directly to the importance of rituals and traditions in How We Express Ourselves. The simple mouth line and voice-recording features produce a short talking-artefact video that students can present to the class.

Students use Google Maps and Street View to explore places where cultural artefacts, rituals and traditions can be seen, such as temples, monuments, museums or festival streets. In pairs, they compare two locations and identify visible clues about the beliefs and values of each culture. This supports the line of inquiry that beliefs and values contribute to a culture. Using the search, zoom and Street View controls, each pair prepares and presents a short guided walkthrough of one location on the screen.

Students create a short soundscape inspired by a cultural ritual or tradition studied in the unit. They choose a small number of suitable loops or virtual instruments, arrange them in order, and explain how the sounds might help people celebrate, remember or belong. This directly explores the importance of rituals and traditions. GarageBand’s loop browser, instrument sounds and track-recording controls allow each group to make and play a one-minute audio piece for the class.

Students create a digital museum poster showing one artefact and what it reveals about a culture’s beliefs, values or history. They arrange a teacher-provided image with a title, three short fact labels and simple decorative shapes or colours connected to the artefact. This addresses the central idea that artefacts provide a window into the beliefs and values of cultures. PicCollage’s ready-made layouts, text boxes and image tools help students publish a clear poster for a classroom gallery.

St Kilda|Year 2|How the World Works.d: Students create a short class book showing how electricity, fossil fuels and solar energy help people in daily life. Each pair makes one page about an energy source and explains one way people can conserve it, linking directly to responsibility to conserve energy and find sustainable sources. They use Book Creator’s drawing, text and voice-recording features to add a labelled picture and a simple spoken explanation. The finished pages are combined into a shareable class energy guide.

Students code a short animation showing an energy transformation, such as sunlight becoming electricity that powers a lamp. They create a simple scene and use movement and appearance blocks to show the energy travelling from the source to an everyday object. This directly explores energy transformation and how energy helps us in daily life. Students run and debug their animation, then present it to a partner and explain each step.

Students place picture cards of energy sources and everyday uses on a floor grid, then program a Bee-Bot to travel from a source to a matching use. They might route it from the sun to a solar panel and then to a house, or from a power station to a light. This helps students talk through how people rely on different energy sources and how energy reaches things we use each day. Using the directional buttons, students plan, test and correct a route before presenting it to the class.

Students use paper pictures and arrows to make a stop-motion film showing one energy transformation, such as electrical energy changing into light and heat in a lamp. They move the pieces a small amount at a time and capture each frame with Stop Motion Studio’s camera button. This makes the line of inquiry into energy transformation visible as a clear sequence. The finished film is played to the class while students explain where the energy starts and what it becomes.

Students complete a simple classroom energy audit by photographing examples of energy being used, such as lights, screens and heating. They use Seesaw’s drawing and voice-recording tools to mark each photo and explain whether the energy use is needed or could be reduced. This connects directly to responsibility to conserve energy and find sustainable sources. Each student publishes a short energy-saving recommendation that can be shared with classmates and families.

St Kilda|Year 2|How We Organise Ourselve.d: Students use Seek to photograph and identify plants, insects and other small animals in the school grounds as part of their study of ecosystems. This directly explores the line of inquiry that an ecosystem has animals, plants and microorganisms. Pairs record their identified species in Seek and then show the class two living things that may depend on each other. The camera-based identification feature makes this a manageable outdoor investigation for Year 2.

Students use Google Maps and Street View to explore two Melbourne environments, such as an urban creek and a protected wetland. They look for visible technology such as roads, drains, bridges, fences and walking paths, linking their observations to the line of inquiry that technology can help or hinder ecosystems. Each pair presents a short live Street View tour, pointing out one feature that may help an ecosystem and one that may hinder it. The familiar zoom, map view and Street View controls allow students to investigate without creating or saving a map.

Students code a short ScratchJr animation showing an ecosystem before and after people introduce a piece of technology, such as a road, rubbish bin or water-cleaning system. This connects directly to the central idea that technology can influence the way ecosystems can survive. They create two scenes, move plant and animal characters, and record simple narration explaining whether the change helps or hinders the ecosystem. ScratchJr’s character, background, movement and voice-recording tools keep the coding task suitable for Year 2.

Students use Microsoft Excel to record class data about items found during a simple schoolyard litter survey, such as plastic, paper and food scraps. They connect the results to the line of inquiry that technology can help or hinder ecosystems by discussing how bins and waste systems affect living things. As a class, they enter the totals into a table and create a column chart to show which type of litter was most common. Excel’s cells and chart tool turn their collected data into a clear visual that they can present to the class.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to make a short film showing how an ecosystem changes when technology is added, such as a drain cover stopping rubbish from entering a pond. This addresses the line of inquiry that technology can cause ecosystems to adapt and evolve, as well as help or hinder ecosystems. Using simple classroom models, they move the animals, plants, water and rubbish a little at a time, then add a spoken explanation of the change. The frame-by-frame camera and playback features let students create and share a clear before-and-after sequence.

St Kilda|Year 2|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Google Maps to view St Kilda and a less built-up Victorian location, switching between the map, satellite view and Street View. They look for roads, homes, shops, parks, trees and open land, then discuss how people’s wants and needs affect the land. Pairs present a short guided screen tour showing three differences and one way people could care for each environment. The familiar zoom, satellite view and Street View controls make the comparison manageable for Year 2 students.

Students use Book Creator to make a short book about how people, plants, animals and environments depend on one another. Each page shows one connection, such as trees providing animal homes, bees helping plants or people caring for waterways. Students add simple sentences, drawings and a recorded explanation, then publish the finished book for classmates to read and hear. The page templates, drawing tools and voice-recording button keep the task simple and concrete.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small neighbourhood that uses land and resources responsibly. In pairs, they include homes, shared green space, food-growing areas and ways to reduce unnecessary land clearing, linking their choices to responsibility to use sustainable resources. They finish by guiding classmates through the world and explaining three building decisions that help people and the environment depend on one another. The block-building tools and first-person walk-through make their ideas visible and easy to present.

Students use ScratchJr to code a simple animation showing an environmental chain, such as rain helping a plant grow, the plant feeding an animal and people caring for the habitat. They program characters to move between scenes and add short speech bubbles explaining each connection. The finished animation presents the unit’s idea that people and environments depend on one another. ScratchJr’s block coding, characters and backgrounds let Year 2 students build and debug the sequence without needing to type much.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short film showing the life of a piece of paper from use to reuse and recycling. They move the paper and labelled classroom objects a little at a time, photographing each step to show how responsible choices can reduce demand for resources and land. The class watches the finished films and students explain where waste was avoided. The app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback controls make the change easy to record, check and improve.

St Kilda|Year 2|Where We Are in Place an.d: Students view a journey from St Kilda to a familiar Melbourne landmark and follow parts of it using Street View. They identify landmarks, road crossings and other possible challenges, linking directly to the line of inquiry about challenges encountered on journeys. Pairs prepare a short live walkthrough in which they show the route, explain its distance and point out one new understanding about the place. The everyday map, directions, distance and Street View features make the journey visible without students needing to log in or edit a map.

Students program a Bee-Bot to complete a physical journey across a teacher-prepared floor grid containing places such as a home, bridge, park and school. Along the way, they must plan around blocked squares, which connects to the line of inquiry about challenges encountered on journeys. Each pair records its planned sequence with arrow cards, tests it, fixes any mistakes and presents the successful journey to the class. The Bee-Bot's forward, backward, left and right buttons provide a simple way for Year 2 students to code and debug the route.

Students make a short digital book about a physical, learning or cultural journey explored during the unit Where We Are in Place and Time. Across four or five pages, they show the starting point, an important challenge and a new understanding gained through the journey. They publish and share a book containing their own drawings, short sentences and recorded narration. Book Creator's page templates, drawing tools and voice recording make it manageable for Year 2 students to combine pictures, writing and speech.

Students create a short puppet performance showing a character taking a journey, meeting a realistic challenge and learning something new.
