This directly explores the central idea that journeys can lead to challenges and new understandings. Pairs choose characters and backgrounds, move the puppets through each scene and record their dialogue as they perform. Puppet Pals' simple character movement, scene backgrounds and voice recording let students produce and present a complete recorded play.

Students use small classroom figures and simple scenery to make a stop-motion film about a journey through different places. Their traveller meets one clear challenge, responds to it and finishes with a new understanding, linking to the unit's central idea. Pairs plan a beginning, middle and end, move the figure a small amount between photos, and then play their finished film for classmates. Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame camera and playback tools make the movement easy to capture and review.

St Kilda|Year 2|Who We Are.d: Students explore Who We Are by photographing a self-portrait, drawing a mouth on it and recording it speaking about one personal strength. This directly supports the line of inquiry into personal identity and strengths. Each student makes a short talking portrait that explains their strength and gives an example of when they use it. The simple photo, mouth-line and voice-recording features make this manageable for Year 2 students.

Students create a short Who We Are story showing a character facing a learning challenge, calming down and trying again. This connects directly to how self-regulation supports learning and how knowing ourselves can build resilience. Students code two or three scenes using movement blocks, speech bubbles and simple character actions, then present their finished story to a partner. ScratchJr’s picture-based coding blocks let students sequence and debug the character’s actions without needing advanced reading skills.

Students use Seesaw to record a Who We Are reflection about a time they managed a strong feeling or kept going with something difficult. This supports the lines of inquiry into self-regulation and building resilience through knowledge of ourselves. Each student creates a drawing and adds a short voice recording explaining what happened, what strategy they used and what they might do next time. Seesaw’s drawing canvas and voice-recording tools make the reflection concrete and easy to share with the teacher or family.

Students make a Who We Are identity collage showing their interests, strengths, important people and things that help them learn well. This connects to personal identity and strengths, as well as the central idea that who we are influences how we interact with others. Students arrange photos or pictures, add short labels and choose colours that represent them, then present the finished collage to a small group. PicCollage’s basic image layout, text and sticker features allow Year 2 students to create a clear, shareable page in one lesson.

Students create a short puppet scene for Who We Are in which two characters have a disagreement, listen to each other and choose a respectful response. This directly explores the central idea that the way we interact with others is influenced by who we are. In pairs, students choose characters and a background, move the puppets while recording their dialogue, and present the finished scene to the class. Puppet Pals’ simple character movement and built-in voice recording make it easy to rehearse and capture the role-play.

St Kilda|Year 3|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students use Adobe Express to create a poster about How We Express Ourselves, choosing words, images, colours and layout to communicate a simple school message. They make two versions of the same message and compare how the correct form can enhance its effectiveness. Each student publishes a finished pair of posters and presents which version is clearer and why. The everyday features are ready-made poster templates, text boxes, images and colour choices.

St Kilda|Year 3|How We Express Ourselves.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
St Kilda|Year 3|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students choose a character and record it delivering a short message for How We Express Ourselves, such as an invitation, warning or friendly reminder. They experiment with wording, tone, volume and pace to explore the features of verbal and non-verbal communication. Each student produces a short animated character video, then classmates explain how they interpreted the message. The key feature is the simple voice recording that automatically matches the character’s mouth movements to the student’s speech.

Students make a short digital book about How We Express Ourselves, with one message communicated through writing, a picture and a voice recording. They ask classmates which form was easiest to understand and use the responses to consider how people interpret messages and bring their own meaning. The finished book includes the three versions of the message and a final page explaining which was most effective. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and built-in audio recording make the task manageable for Year 3.

Students use paper shapes, symbols or classroom objects to create a short stop-motion message about How We Express Ourselves without using spoken words. They test the film with a partner to see whether movement and visual clues communicate the intended meaning, linking directly to the forms of non-verbal and visual communication. Each group publishes a short stop-motion film and presents the choices that made its message clear or confusing. The activity uses the tool’s frame-by-frame camera and playback controls.

Students respond to a shared image or everyday message on Padlet as part of How We Express Ourselves, adding a short written post or audio response explaining what they think it means. They read or listen to several classmates’ responses and notice how people can interpret the same message differently and bring their own meaning to interactions. The class ends with a shared digital wall showing a range of interpretations and a brief reflection from each student. Padlet’s simple post, image display, comment and audio recording features support the whole task.

St Kilda|Year 3|How We Organise Ourselve.d: Students complete a teacher-made survey about everyday online choices, such as whether to share a photo, reply to an unkind message or ask an adult for help. They then examine the built-in response charts and discuss how informed choices can make a positive difference. In pairs, students use Forms to create a short online safety quiz with three ethical choice scenarios and helpful feedback for each answer. They share the finished quiz with classmates and use the results to identify choices the class understands well and choices that need more discussion.

Students use a closed class Padlet to practise how actions and reactions affect others online. The teacher posts simple scenarios, and students add a respectful response before leaving one kind, useful comment on a classmate’s idea. They use Padlet’s post and comment features to create a shared wall of safe and ethical responses. The class reviews the wall and agrees on examples that help everyone feel safe online.

Students make a short stop-motion story about an online choice, such as receiving a mean message or being asked to share personal information. Their story shows two possible reactions and how each one affects other people, directly exploring how choice of action and reaction affects others online. Students move paper characters a little at a time and photograph each frame using Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera. They add a title and present the finished animation with an explanation of the safer, more ethical decision.

Students create a one-page digital guide called “Our Rights and Responsibilities Online” for other Year 3 students. They include the right to feel safe online and practical responsibilities such as asking permission, protecting private information and reporting harmful behaviour. Using Adobe Express templates, text boxes, icons and images, students organise their advice into a clear and appealing page. They publish or present the finished guide to explain how ethical decision making supports online choices.

Students record a short role-play showing how to respond when something online feels unsafe, unfair or unkind. The role-play connects directly to our right to feel safe online and our responsibility to make ethical decisions. Using Seesaw’s built-in video recording and caption tools, students explain the choice they made and name a trusted adult who could help. They post the finished recording to the class journal, where classmates can respond with one respectful suggestion or positive observation.

St Kilda|Year 3|How the World Works.d: Students code a Micro:bit to show temperature readings on its LED grid, then place it in several safe classroom locations and record what they notice. They compare warmer and cooler readings to explore how matter changes states depending on temperature and energy. Each group presents a simple table of readings and explains where heating or cooling might cause a material to change. The built-in temperature sensor, buttons and LED grid make the investigation manageable for Year 3.

Students enter a teacher-provided set of results showing how the temperature of water changes as it cools and freezes. They use the data to explore how matter changes states depending on temperature and energy. Each pair makes a labelled table and a simple chart, then presents the point where the change of state occurred. Excel’s cells and chart tool make patterns in the results easy to see and discuss.

Students make a short digital guide to solids, liquids and gases using examples from home and school. They explain the properties of each state of matter and include a page showing how one material can change state when heated or cooled. Their finished book contains labelled drawings, short written explanations and a recorded spoken summary that can be shared with classmates. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and audio recording support students to combine these ideas clearly.

Students build three particle diagrams for a solid, a liquid and a gas using repeated shapes arranged on a Freeform board. They add arrows and short labels to show how particles move and what happens when temperature and energy increase or decrease. This directly supports the line of inquiry about the three states of matter and how matter changes states. Freeform’s shapes, duplicate tool, arrows and movable notes let students revise their model during class discussion.

Students create a one-page poster about the responsible and ethical use of glass or plastic. They identify one challenge, such as single-use packaging or broken glass, and present realistic actions people can take to reuse, recycle or dispose of the material safely. Each student publishes a clear poster with a heading, short facts, pictures and a practical call to action for the school community. Canva’s poster templates, text boxes and image library make the final message easy for Year 3 students to design and present.

St Kilda|Year 3|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to explore places affected by earthquakes, volcanoes, cyclones or floods. They add simple labels, lines and shaded areas to show the natural disaster, nearby communities and possible safe locations. This directly supports the line of inquiry into the causes and types of natural disasters and their impact on people and the environment. Each pair presents an annotated disaster map using the tool’s map layers and drawing features.

Students create a short digital guide called “Responding with Resilience” for one natural disaster. They explain what happens, how people and the environment may be affected, and practical ways a community can prepare, respond and reconnect. This directly explores how humans respond to natural disasters with resilience and connection. Students publish a shareable book using Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and voice recording.

Students build a small community beside a river and include homes, a school, roads, higher ground and an evacuation meeting place. They create a controlled flood using Minecraft water, observe which areas are affected, and then rebuild or move key structures to make the community safer. This connects to how natural disasters impact people and environments and how people respond with resilience. Groups present their revised community by walking classmates through the build and explaining the changes they made with Minecraft’s blocks and building tools.

Students make a narrated explanation showing how one natural disaster begins and what happens next. They draw a simple sequence, such as heavy rain leading to rising water, flooding, damaged habitats and people needing support. This directly addresses the causes of natural disasters and their impact on people and the environment. Students produce a short recorded presentation using Explain Everything’s drawing, arrow, text and voice-recording features.

Students code a micro:bit prototype that uses its accelerometer to notice shaking and show an alert symbol on the LED grid. They test it with gentle, medium and strong hand movements, record which movements trigger the alert, and debug the code if it responds too easily or not at all. This supports discussion about earthquake impacts and how warning devices can be one part of a resilient response, while making clear that the prototype detects movement rather than predicts earthquakes. Each pair demonstrates its working alert using the micro:bit’s accelerometer and LED grid.

St Kilda|Year 3|Where We Are in Place an.d: Students explore Melbourne and another city using the map, satellite view and Street View, looking closely at roads, buildings, parks, transport and waterways. They compare what they notice to investigate the essential features of a city. Pairs finish by presenting a short guided Street View walkthrough and explaining three similarities and three differences. The everyday zoom, search and Street View controls make it possible to examine real city spaces without students needing to log in.

Students create a short digital book showing how Melbourne has developed through time. Each page covers a different period and combines a picture, a simple caption and a recorded explanation of factors such as transport, population or new buildings. This directly explores the development of cities through time and supports the central idea that many factors shape cities. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing, typing and voice-recording tools help students publish a clear book to share with classmates.

Small groups use blocks, paper shapes or classroom craft materials to build a simple city scene and change it step by step. They photograph each change in Stop Motion Studio to show a settlement developing roads, homes, services, transport and public spaces over time. The finished stop-motion film explains the development of cities through time and shows how several factors shape growth. The app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback controls let students capture, check and improve their sequence.

Students make a one-page poster called “What Does a City Need?” about the essential features of a city. They sort features such as housing, transport, shops, schools, hospitals, parks and water services into clear groups, then add a short explanation of why each group matters. The finished poster can be presented to the class as an argument for which features are most important. Canva’s ready-made poster layouts, text boxes, shapes and image library support a neat result that is manageable for Year 3.

The class builds a shared Padlet about the function of a city, with sections for living, working, learning, travelling, staying healthy and relaxing. Pairs add short posts naming a city place or service and explaining what it does for people. Students then read the wall, comment on one connection between two functions, and present a section to the class. Padlet’s shared posting board, sections and comment feature make everyone’s ideas visible in one place.

St Kilda|Year 3|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital book explaining how two body systems, such as the breathing and circulatory systems, connect and function. This directly explores the line of inquiry, “How our body systems connect and function.” Each student publishes labelled pages with simple explanations and a recorded voice reading of their key ideas. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and voice recording make the task manageable for Year 3.

Students complete a class survey about everyday choices linked to sleep, movement, food, screen breaks and ways to manage strong feelings. The class then examines how these choices affect physical, emotional and mental wellbeing, without naming or judging individual students. Students discuss the automatic charts and present two patterns they notice and one healthy choice the class could try. Microsoft Forms’ simple questions and automatic response charts are central to the activity.

Students collect one week of simple personal wellbeing data, such as hours of sleep, serves of water and minutes of active play, and enter it into a table. This supports the line of inquiry, “Strategies to measure and maintain the health of the human body.” They use the data to create a basic column chart and write a short conclusion about one pattern and one realistic goal. Microsoft Excel’s cells, tables and chart tool allow students to organise, compare and present their measurements clearly.

In small groups, students use paper cut-outs to show food moving through the digestive system or oxygen moving from the lungs into the blood. This helps them explain how body systems connect and function rather than simply naming body parts. They capture a sequence of small movements and present a short stop-motion film with paper labels visible in each important stage. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback feature let students test, fix and replay their model.

Students plan and record a one-minute wellbeing audio guide that teaches a practical strategy such as calm breathing, positive self-talk or preparing for sleep. This connects directly to how our choices affect emotional and mental wellbeing and the strategies we can use to maintain health. Each student produces a clear spoken recording with a short introduction, guided steps and a closing reminder, then plays it for a partner to test whether the instructions are easy to follow. GarageBand’s voice recording, trimming and simple music loops help students create a polished audio guide.

St Kilda|Year 4|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short scene for How We Express Ourselves in which paper characters change colour, position and movement to show a shift in mood. This directly explores how colour and movement communicate character and mood. In pairs, students move their pieces a small amount, capture each frame and test whether the emotion is clear without spoken explanation. They finish with a shareable stop-motion film using the app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features.

Students use the Podcast Equipment to record a short behind-the-scenes interview about preparing a live performance for How We Express Ourselves. This connects to the effort and commitment required to produce a live performance. One student acts as the host while others explain rehearsals, feedback, mistakes and improvements, then the group records a clear final take. They produce a short audio interview using the microphones, headphones and recording controls.

Students use Book Creator to document the creative process of making a multi-disciplinary presentation for How We Express Ourselves. Each page shows one stage, such as choosing a mood, planning colours, selecting music, rehearsing movement and improving after feedback. Students combine drawings, written reflections and built-in voice recordings to explain the choices their group made. They publish a shareable digital process journal using Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and audio recording feature.

Students use Sketchbook to create two digital character portraits for How We Express Ourselves, with each portrait communicating a different mood through colour, line and shape. This directly explores how colour communicates character and mood. They test different brushes and colour combinations, then add a short written label explaining which artistic choices carry the emotion. The finished pair of portraits can be presented to classmates using Sketchbook’s brushes, colour picker and layers.

Students code Sphero BOLT to perform a short movement sequence for How We Express Ourselves that communicates a chosen character and mood. This explores how movement and colour communicate character and mood as part of a multi-disciplinary presentation. In small groups, students program changes in speed, direction, pauses and colours on the LED matrix, then test and debug the sequence until classmates can interpret the intended mood. They present a live robot choreography powered by BOLT’s programmable motors and LED matrix.

St Kilda|Year 4|How the World Works.d: Students use Google Maps to view several real bridges in Melbourne and around the world, switching between the map, satellite view and Street View where available. They compare bridge types and look closely for design features such as arches, towers, cables, beams and supports. This directly supports the line of inquiry into different types of bridges and their design features. Pairs present a short live Google Maps walkthrough, explaining how each bridge appears fit for its location and purpose.

Students use Lego Spike Prime pieces to build a small bridge and a simple coded vehicle that can travel across it. They test whether the bridge stays stable as the vehicle crosses, then change the position of beams, supports or triangular braces and test again. This addresses how engineering features contribute to structural strength and stability, as well as testing and refining designs. Each group presents its final bridge, runs its program and explains which construction change made the biggest improvement.

Students use Tinkercad to design a small 3D bridge prototype with a deck, supports and repeating structural shapes such as triangles or arches. They use the basic shape, resize, align, duplicate and group tools to create a neat model that could be 3D-printed in plastic. This connects to the central idea that engineers choose specific features to make structures stable and fit for purpose, without treating Tinkercad as a strength or materials simulator. Students present their finished digital model or printed prototype and explain the purpose of its main design features.

Students use Geoboard’s pegs and virtual rubber bands to create side views of beam, arch and truss bridges. They compare squares and rectangles with triangular arrangements, then adjust their designs to reduce shapes that could easily change form. This supports the line of inquiry into how engineering principles contribute to structural strength and stability. Students present three saved geoboard designs and explain which pattern they would choose for a bridge and why.

Students use Book Creator to make a short engineering journal about designing, testing and refining a classroom bridge. On each page they draw or photograph their design, record test results, and explain one change they would make before the next test. This directly addresses the line of inquiry into testing and refining designs through experimentation. The finished book uses Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, camera and audio recording to provide a shareable record of the student’s engineering thinking.

St Kilda|Year 4|How We Organise Ourselve.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to map community needs and the not-for-profit organisations that respond to them around St Kilda. This directly explores how not-for-profit organisations respond to community needs. They add simple labels and annotations for places such as food relief centres, animal shelters and community support services, then identify areas where help is easy or difficult to access. The map view, scale and annotation tools help students create a shareable community support map. Pairs present their map and explain one need they think deserves more attention.

Students collect class survey data about which community needs, such as homelessness, food relief, animal welfare or environmental care, they believe local not-for-profit organisations should prioritise. This connects to our responsibility to take action and make a difference. They enter the results into a simple Excel table and create a column or pie chart showing the class responses. Excel’s cells, basic totals and chart tool make the findings clear and easy to present. Students use the chart to recommend one realistic class action supported by the data.

Small groups create a digital profile of one not-for-profit organisation and explain its purpose, who it helps and how it responds to a community need. This directly addresses the function and purpose of not-for-profit organisations. Each group makes a short book containing headings, typed information, student drawings or photos, and a recorded explanation. Book Creator’s page templates, text, image and audio recording tools keep the task manageable for Year 4 students. The finished books become a class library that students can read and discuss.

Students record a short community awareness announcement about a need addressed by a not-for-profit organisation. This supports the line of inquiry about our responsibility to take action and make a difference. They write and record a clear message that names the need, explains how the organisation helps and suggests one safe action families could take. GarageBand’s voice recording, trimming and simple music loop features allow students to produce a polished one-minute audio message. The class listens to the finished recordings and discusses which messages are clear, accurate and persuasive.

Students build a visual explanation showing how a not-for-profit organisation turns community support into practical help. This explores both the function of not-for-profit organisations and how they respond to community needs. On a series of slides, students draw and label a simple sequence such as donations being collected, sorted and delivered to people who need them. Explain Everything’s drawing, text, slide and voice recording tools let students narrate each step in their own words. They present the finished explanation to a partner, who checks whether the organisation’s purpose and actions are easy to understand.

St Kilda|Year 4|Who We Are.d: Students create a short class survey about the strengths and qualities of a leader in the Who We Are unit. They write clear multiple-choice questions, collect responses from classmates and examine the automatic response charts. This directly explores the line of inquiry, the strengths and qualities of a leader. Each group presents one chart and explains what the class data suggests about effective leadership, using the everyday survey and chart features in Microsoft Forms.

Students make a digital leadership handbook for the Who We Are unit, with one page for each important role, responsibility or quality. They add short examples showing how a leader can help a group to function effectively. This connects directly to the roles and responsibilities of effective leadership. Students publish and present their handbook using Book Creator’s simple page, text, drawing, image and voice-recording features.

Students work in small production teams to record a short podcast episode called What Makes a Helpful Leader? They take on clear roles such as host, interviewer, timekeeper and sound checker, then interview one another about the purpose of leadership. The finished recording includes examples of how leaders help groups to function effectively. Students play their episode for the class, using the microphones and audio-recording controls that are central to the podcast equipment.

Students work in teams to build a small community meeting place in Minecraft Education for the Who We Are unit. Before building, they assign and rotate roles such as team leader, designer, builder and checker, then test which leadership actions help the group work effectively. This gives them a practical way to explore the roles and responsibilities of effective leadership. Each team presents a walkthrough of its completed build and points to signs placed in the world that explain each member’s responsibility, using Minecraft’s shared building blocks and signs.

Students work in teams to build and code a simple LEGO model that can move an object from one point to another. They rotate the team leader role between planning, building, coding and testing rounds, noticing which actions help the group to function effectively. This directly investigates the purpose of leadership and the responsibilities of an effective leader. Each team presents its working model and explains one change it made after testing, using the LEGO pieces, motors and block-coding tools in Lego Spike Prime.

St Kilda|Year 4|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Google Maps to view several places connected to different First Nations communities and examine the landscape through satellite view and Street View where available. They compare distances, waterways, coastlines and other visible features while exploring the diversity of Country across Australia. This connects to the line of inquiry about the significance of connection to Country, while making clear that Google Maps does not show all cultural boundaries or knowledge. Pairs finish by presenting a short live map walkthrough in which they locate two places and explain what they noticed using the zoom, distance and Street View features.

Students use Adobe Express to create a one-page profile of a First Nations language group studied through reliable, teacher-provided sources. Their page includes the language group's name, location, several carefully checked facts and a statement explaining that First Nations language and culture are diverse across Australia. This directly supports the line of inquiry about the diversity of language and culture across First Nations communities. Students publish and present their finished page using the tool's templates, text boxes and image layout features, without copying artworks or cultural symbols they do not have permission to use.

Students use GarageBand to record a two-minute audio reflection about what they have learned from a First Nations speaker, interview or approved classroom source. They explain one idea about connection to Country, one example of custodial responsibility and one question they still have. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about listening to and learning from Indigenous perspectives. Students edit pauses and repeated sections, add a spoken introduction and export a clear audio reflection using GarageBand's voice recording and track editing features.

Students use Padlet to build a class learning wall titled "Listening to First Nations Perspectives". Each student publishes a short post that accurately paraphrases an idea from an approved First Nations source, names the source and explains why the idea matters. This supports the line of inquiry about listening to and learning from Indigenous perspectives rather than speaking on behalf of First Nations people. Students then add one thoughtful question or connection to a classmate's post using Padlet's post, comment and attachment features, creating a shareable class collection.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to make a short animation showing practical ways people can care for a local waterway, park or coastal area as part of custodial responsibility. Using simple paper shapes or classroom objects, they animate actions such as removing litter, protecting habitat and staying on marked paths, then add brief titles explaining each action. This connects to the line of inquiry about connection to Country as custodial responsibility and is based on advice from approved local First Nations sources. Pairs present a finished 30-to-45-second film created with the app's frame-by-frame camera, playback and title features.

St Kilda|Year 4|Where We Are in Place an.d: Students view the routes and key locations linked to the age of exploration, including Europe, the Cape of Good Hope and Australia. They use the map, satellite view, Street View and distance tool to explore why journeys were difficult and how location shaped explorers’ choices. This directly supports the line of inquiry about the age of exploration and the reasons explorers set out on their journeys. Pairs present a live map walkthrough showing one route, its approximate distance and three important landmarks or geographical features.

Students create a short digital book about how Australia changed through European arrival. They make pages showing life before arrival, early encounters and later changes, including both Aboriginal and European perspectives based on class sources. Book Creator’s page templates, text, drawing, image and voice-recording features let students combine evidence with clear explanations. Each student publishes a shareable book that connects directly to the line of inquiry about different perspectives on the consequences of exploration.

Students enter teacher-provided information about several exploration journeys, such as dates, distances, journey lengths and numbers of ships. They use a simple table and column chart to compare the journeys and look for patterns in the age of exploration. This supports the line of inquiry about why explorers set out and helps students see how exploration and discovery shaped the world. Groups present one chart and explain two conclusions they can support with the recorded data.

Students record a two-minute historical news report about European arrival in Australia and its consequences. Working from researched facts, they include two viewpoints, such as an Aboriginal person describing disruption to Country and a European arrival describing their aims and experiences. GarageBand’s voice recording, trimming and simple music features help students produce a clear audio report without needing specialist equipment. The finished recording is shared with the class as evidence of learning about different perspectives on exploration.

Students build a class evidence wall about the consequences of exploration by adding short posts drawn from teacher-approved sources. Each post includes a fact, the perspective it represents and a brief explanation of whether it shows change, benefit, harm or a mixture of consequences. Padlet’s columns, post boxes, images and comment feature allow classmates to compare and respond to different viewpoints in one shared space. The completed wall becomes a class display that directly addresses how Australia changed through European arrival and why perspectives on that change differ.

St Kilda|Year 5|How We Organise Ourselve.d: Students use Book Creator to explain how a familiar product, such as chocolate or a cotton T-shirt, moves from raw material through manufacturing to the consumer. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the production of goods from raw materials through manufacturing to consumer. Each pair makes a short digital book with one stage per page, including captions, drawings and recorded narration. The simple page templates, drawing tools and audio recording make the production journey clear and easy to share with the class.

Students use Microsoft Forms to investigate how people make decisions when exchanging currency for goods and services. In small groups, they create a short survey asking classmates to choose between products with different prices, quality, packaging or ethical claims. The tool automatically collects responses and displays charts, which students use to present two conclusions about consumer choices in a functioning economy. The everyday question types and automatic response charts keep the data collection manageable for Year 5.

Students use Canva to create an honest advertisement for a product sold in a class marketplace. This connects to ethics and responsible decision-making by requiring them to include a fair price, accurate product information and a clear statement about where the product comes from. Each student publishes a one-page advertisement and presents how it informs rather than misleads the consumer. Canva’s ready-made poster layouts, text boxes and image library help students organise the information clearly.

Students use Google Maps to view the real journey of a selected good, such as bananas travelling from a growing region to Melbourne shops. They explore the world map, compare distances and use Street View to examine places such as farms, ports, warehouses and shopping areas where available. This supports the line of inquiry about how goods move from raw materials through production and distribution to the consumer. Each group presents a live map walkthrough, using the distance tool and Street View to explain the main stages and why transport adds time and cost.

Students use Sphero BOLT to model an automated delivery route through a marketplace supply chain. They code the robot to travel between marked stations for raw materials, factory, warehouse, shop and consumer, then test and debug the route so each delivery arrives accurately. This makes the organisation of goods within a marketplace visible and connects directly to production and distribution from raw material to consumer. Students present their working route and explain how the block-coding controls, compass heading and motor movement represent an organised delivery system.

St Kilda|Year 5|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students use Adobe Express to design a campaign poster that challenges a stereotype linked to hobbies, jobs, appearance or gender. This directly explores how people overcome stereotypes to express themselves and inspire change. Each poster includes a clear message, a respectful image and one practical action the audience can take. Students use the ready-made poster templates and simple text and image tools, then publish their finished posters for a class gallery.

Students create a digital class book about how social norms and stereotypes can influence the way people express themselves. Each pair makes a short fictional story showing an assumption being made, its impact on a character, and how the character or community responds. This connects directly to the impact of discrimination, prejudice and assumptions on individuals and communities. Students use Book Creator’s pages, text, drawing and voice-recording tools to publish a book that classmates can read and listen to.

Students build a shared Padlet wall called “Where Do Stereotypes Come From?” to investigate how stereotypes and social norms form and persist in society. They add short examples from familiar areas such as toys, sport, clothing, advertising and family expectations, then explain the message each example may send. Classmates respond with comments that question assumptions or suggest a more inclusive message. The activity uses Padlet’s post, image, column and commenting features to create a shared evidence wall for class discussion.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to make a one-minute animation about a character who is judged because of a stereotype and chooses to express themselves confidently. The story must show the assumption, its effect on the character and one action that helps create change. This directly explores how people overcome stereotypes to express themselves and inspire change. Students move simple paper figures or classroom objects frame by frame, then use the app’s capture, title and playback tools to present the finished animation.

Students build a small Minecraft Education exhibition called “Beyond the Label” about social norms and stereotypes. In separate display spaces, they show how a stereotype can form, how prejudice can affect a person or community, and how someone can challenge the assumption. Students add signs with short explanations and practical messages encouraging fair treatment and individual expression. They use Minecraft’s blocks, signs and shared world to build the exhibition and lead classmates through a live walkthrough.

St Kilda|Year 5|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to investigate how communities interact with a chosen natural environment, such as a river, coastline or forest. They add map features and labels showing conservation areas, community facilities, land uses and places facing environmental pressure. This directly explores how community values shape the management of the natural environment. Each group presents its completed annotated map and explains one management decision it would recommend, using the map’s layers, drawing and labelling tools as evidence.

Students use Microsoft Excel to record and compare a class set of data about water use, waste production or biodiversity observations linked to Sharing the Planet. They organise the figures in a table, calculate totals or averages, and create a column or pie chart using Excel’s everyday spreadsheet and chart tools. This supports the line of inquiry into the need for conservation and environmental stewardship by helping students identify where change is most needed. Each pair presents one chart and a practical conservation action supported by its data.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital book about ways First Nations land management practices can drive positive environmental change. Using teacher-provided information, they create pages explaining practices such as cultural burning, seasonal knowledge and caring for waterways, while making clear that practices vary between Countries and communities. They combine text, drawings, images and recorded narration using Book Creator’s simple page and audio tools. The finished books are shared with classmates as a Year 5 guide to respectful and effective environmental stewardship.

Students code a Micro:bit to collect light and temperature readings from several agreed locations around the school grounds during a Sharing the Planet investigation. They use the built-in light and temperature sensors, buttons and LED display to take repeated readings and compare conditions in shaded, planted and paved places. This connects to the central idea that communities interact with the environment in different ways and helps students consider how school grounds could better support people and other living things. Each group demonstrates its working program and presents the readings shown by the Micro:bit, along with one realistic environmental improvement.

Students use Sphero BOLT to model how people might move through a protected natural environment without entering sensitive habitats. They arrange a simple floor map with marked paths, habitat zones and conservation areas, then code BOLT to travel from an entrance to a destination while staying on the approved route. This explores the need for conservation and environmental stewardship by showing how access can be managed to reduce harm. Students test and debug their route using BOLT’s movement commands and compass heading, then present a successful run and explain the community values behind their path choices.

St Kilda|Year 5|How the World Works.d: Students investigate global problems linked to the UN Sustainable Development Goals, such as access to clean water, food security or climate change. They use MapMaker’s map layers and annotation tools to mark affected places and add short notes explaining the problem in each location. This directly supports the line of inquiry about the Sustainable Development Goals and the global problems they address. Each group presents its annotated world map and explains one pattern it noticed.

Students collect class data about a changing need in society, such as reducing lunch waste, saving water or using less electricity. They enter their results into an Excel table and use the chart feature to turn the data into a clear column or pie chart. This supports the central idea that inventions and initiatives respond to the changing needs of society by giving students evidence for a possible solution. Each group presents its chart and a short recommendation for an invention or initiative that could address the need.

Students build and code a small working invention that responds to a real-world need, such as an automatic barrier, a warning system or a device that moves an item from one place to another. They use the building pieces, motors and block-based coding to make the model perform a simple, repeatable action. This directly supports the line of inquiry about using the design thinking process to create innovations that respond to real-world needs. Teams test and debug their invention, then demonstrate the finished model and explain which need it addresses.

Students research one invention, such as the telephone, bicycle or refrigerator, and show how it changed over time to meet society’s needs. They use Adobe Express templates, text boxes and image tools to create a one-page visual timeline with key versions, dates and short explanations. This directly supports the line of inquiry about how inventions have changed over time to meet the demands of society. Students publish or present their finished timeline and identify the social need behind each major change.

Students choose one UN Sustainable Development Goal and design a practical school initiative connected to it, such as a food-waste campaign or a water-saving plan. They use Canva’s poster templates, headings, icons and page layout tools to explain the problem, their proposed action and how success could be measured. This connects the Sustainable Development Goals line of inquiry with the central idea that initiatives are a response to changing needs. Each group presents its finished campaign poster as a proposal for the class or school community.

St Kilda|Year 5|Where We Are in Place an.d: Students use Google Maps to explore places shaped by colonisation, such as Melbourne, Hobart and London, and compare their locations, distances and visible landmarks. This supports the line of inquiry into the reasons, methods and impact of colonisation by showing the long sea journeys and strategic coastal locations involved. In pairs, students use the world map, distance tool and Street View to prepare and present a live walkthrough of one important route and place. Their presentation explains what the map reveals and what it cannot show about the experiences of the people who were colonised.

Students make a short digital book about how colonisation transformed society and culture in one country they have studied. They create paired pages showing different perspectives, such as a coloniser’s written record alongside an account based on the experiences of First Peoples. Using Book Creator’s page templates, text, drawing and voice-recording features, students add dates, evidence, captions and spoken explanations. The finished books are shared as a class library that shows why the lasting impact of colonisation can be understood differently by different people.

Small groups build two simple versions of the same place in Minecraft Education: one representing life before colonisation and one showing changes made during or after colonisation. The task connects directly to how colonisation transformed society and culture, including changes to land use, buildings, movement and access to important places. Students use the ordinary building blocks, signs and non-player characters to label evidence and explain whose perspective each part represents. Each group leads classmates through its finished world and explains which changes had lasting impacts and which details are supported by class learning.

Students create a narrated cause-and-effect board explaining the reasons, methods and impact of colonisation in one country. They arrange key events on slides, draw arrows between causes and consequences, and add short labels showing effects on land, language, government and daily life. Explain Everything’s drawing, text, image and voice-recording features allow students to talk through their thinking while pointing to evidence on the screen. The finished recording becomes a clear two- to three-minute explanation that can be played to classmates for questions and feedback.

Students create a class survey about the responsibility of colonisers and the perspectives of those colonised, using claims drawn from the unit’s shared evidence. They write a small set of multiple-choice and short-answer questions, then classmates complete the form and explain one response with evidence. Microsoft Forms collects the answers and produces automatic response charts, which students examine for patterns, disagreements and viewpoints that may be missing. Each group presents the charts and a short conclusion about how evidence influenced the class’s views on responsibility.

St Kilda|Year 5|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital identity book about how values and beliefs shape who they are and how they interact with others. Each page includes a value, a real-life example of that value guiding an action, and a reflection on how another person may think differently. They publish a shareable class library of books that shows how values, beliefs and actions contribute to a diverse society. Book Creator’s simple page layouts, text, drawing and voice-recording features let students choose how they communicate their ideas.

Students complete an anonymous class survey about safe and respectful choices in common online and in-person situations. The class examines the automatic response charts to discuss their responsibility to manage emotions and be safe online and in person. Small groups then present one finding, such as which strategies classmates prefer when a message makes them upset, without identifying individual students. Microsoft Forms’ question types and automatic charts make it practical to collect and compare class data in one lesson.

Students design a one-page guide called “Pause, Choose, Respond” for managing strong emotions during online and in-person disagreements. Their guide connects directly to the responsibility to manage emotions and be safe, with three clear steps, an example situation and respectful words someone could use. Students publish the finished guides for display near classroom devices or include them in a class wellbeing collection. Canva’s ready-made poster layouts, text boxes, icons and colour tools help Year 5 students organise the advice clearly.

Students build a shared class advice wall about resilience, respect and positive relationships in a diverse community. Each student posts one realistic friendship challenge, then replies to a classmate with a respectful action, a helpful sentence and a resilience strategy. The class reviews the wall together and presents a short list of responses that support people with different values, beliefs or experiences. Padlet’s post and comment features make everyone’s examples and responses visible in one moderated space.

In small groups, students build a compact shared community space that welcomes people with different values, beliefs and needs. They include practical features such as a quiet area, a gathering place and clear pathways, then add signs explaining how each choice supports respect and positive relationships. Groups present a guided walk through their build and explain how their design shows that values, beliefs and actions contribute to a diverse society. Minecraft Education’s blocks, signs and shared worlds allow students to build, label and present the space without specialist coding.

St Kilda|Year 6|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students investigate a global issue such as plastic pollution by mapping where it is produced, transported and affecting communities or oceans. This directly explores the line of inquiry that global issues are caused by interconnected factors that require collective solutions. Using the base map, drawing and annotation tools, students add labelled locations and connecting routes based on a small set of teacher-provided facts. They present their completed issue map to explain where action by governments, businesses and communities could make a difference.

Students enter teacher-provided data about a global issue, such as food waste, access to clean water or threatened species, into an Excel table. They use simple formulas and charts to check how different chart types or selected data can change the impression given to an audience. This directly addresses the line of inquiry that presentations in the media can reflect the perspective of the author rather than the truth. Each group produces two contrasting charts from the same data and presents which design is more accurate and responsible.

Students examine two short media reports about the same global issue and identify differences in facts, language, images and viewpoint. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about perspective and how media presentations may reflect the author rather than the truth. Using Book Creator's pages, text boxes, image placement and voice recording, students build a short media comparison book with their evidence and conclusions. They finish with a page explaining the responsible choices a reader should make before sharing either report.

Pairs plan and record a three-minute podcast episode that raises awareness of a chosen global issue and suggests one realistic action listeners can take. This supports the central idea that effective communication can inspire action, as well as the line of inquiry about responsible media choices. Students use Canva's recording, audio editing and timeline tools to combine a spoken introduction, key facts, an interview-style section and a clear call to action. They publish a finished episode that can be played to classmates, who give feedback on its accuracy, tone and persuasiveness.

Students create a one-page awareness campaign about a global issue they have studied, such as fast fashion, habitat loss or unequal access to education. This directly explores the lines of inquiry about how messages use different elements and how design choices influence effectiveness. Using a simple Adobe Express template, students adjust headings, images, colour, spacing and short blocks of text to guide the viewer towards a clear action. They publish the finished campaign page and briefly explain how each design choice strengthens the message without exaggerating the facts.

St Kilda|Year 6|How We Organise Ourselve.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to explore how federal, state and local government decisions affect people in different parts of Australia. They add labelled markers and notes for examples such as Parliament House, state transport projects and local parks, directly addressing the line of inquiry about how government decisions impact citizens at three levels. Each group produces an annotated digital map showing which level of government is responsible for each example and who is affected. The everyday map layers, search, markers and annotation tools make the task manageable for Year 6 students.

Students collect class survey data about which government-funded services they use, such as schools, public transport, libraries, sporting facilities and health services. They enter the results into a simple spreadsheet and create charts to examine how government decisions impact citizens at federal, state and local levels. Each pair presents one chart and a short evidence-based statement about which services have the widest impact on their class. Excel’s table, basic formula and chart features power the activity without requiring advanced spreadsheet skills.

Students create a short digital handbook explaining the rights and responsibilities of Australian citizens and their obligations as global citizens. They include pages on voting, following laws, speaking respectfully, helping the community and considering how choices affect people beyond Australia, linking directly to the Equality and Citizenship line of inquiry. Each student publishes a shareable handbook containing written explanations, recorded narration and simple illustrations. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and built-in audio recording keep the task practical and accessible.

In small groups, students record a three-minute current affairs podcast about a realistic government decision, such as funding public transport, changing a local park or introducing an environmental rule. Students take the roles of host and affected citizens, then explain which level of government is responsible and how the decision could affect different people. The finished podcast presents contrasting viewpoints and connects clearly to the central idea that the way a country is governed impacts citizens’ lives. Canva’s recording, trimming and audio timeline tools allow students to produce and share the episode in one place.

Students build a compact civic precinct that shows key institutions and functions of Australia’s democratic system of government. Their model includes clearly labelled spaces representing federal parliament, state parliament and local council, with signs explaining one decision made at each level and how citizens can have a say. Groups guide classmates through the finished world and explain how the three levels differ and work together. Minecraft Education’s blocks, signs and shared-world building features make the institutions visible and easy to discuss.

St Kilda|Year 6|How the World Works.d: Students code Sphero BOLT to represent Earth rotating beside a fixed classroom light that represents the Sun. They use the programmable movement and 8x8 LED matrix to mark a location on Earth, then stop the robot at set points to show sunrise, midday, sunset and night. This directly explores the line of inquiry about how movement of the Earth and Sun causes the predictable pattern of day and night. Each group presents and explains its working coded model, including where the model is useful and where it is not scientifically accurate.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short animation showing the Moon moving around Earth and the changing phases seen from Earth. They move simple classroom models a small amount between each photo, keeping a fixed light source as the Sun. This addresses the line of inquiry about predictable patterns caused by the movement and positions of the Earth, Moon and Sun. Groups publish a labelled animation with titles for the new moon, quarter moons and full moon, using the app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback tools.

Students make a short digital book comparing a scientific explanation of a night-sky pattern with one carefully chosen Indigenous cultural perspective studied in class. They use separate pages to explain what each perspective communicates, rather than treating a cultural story as a scientific theory. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about how different cultures, including Indigenous knowledge systems, interpret the night sky in meaningful ways. Students publish a book containing typed explanations, drawings and recorded narration using Book Creator’s page, drawing and audio tools.

Students build a simplified three-dimensional model of the Earth, Moon and Sun in Minecraft Education. They place the bodies in clear relative positions, add a tilted axis to Earth and use signs to explain rotation, orbit, seasons and the limits of their model. This supports the line of inquiry about the structures, positions and relationships of the Earth, Moon and Sun being represented through models. Each group leads classmates through its finished world using Minecraft’s building blocks, signs and in-world movement.

Students record a three-minute astronomy podcast explaining one predictable pattern such as seasons, tides or moon phases. They organise the episode as a clear question, a scientific explanation and a short section correcting a common misunderstanding, linking to the central idea that Earth, Moon and Sun relationships shape life on our planet. Pairs produce a shareable audio episode with spoken parts, a brief introduction and a simple closing. They use GarageBand’s voice recording, trimming and built-in music tools to assemble the final podcast.

St Kilda|Year 6|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Google Maps to explore Street View around St Kilda Beach, Albert Park and a less developed coastal area, looking for vegetation, wildlife habitat, roads, buildings and rubbish. They compare the places to investigate the line of inquiry about the consequences of human actions on the balance of nature. Each group presents a short live Street View walkthrough showing three examples of human impact and one practical action that could protect the area. Street View, satellite view and the distance tool help students examine each place closely without needing to create or save a map.

Students create a Microsoft Forms survey about everyday actions that affect nature, such as food waste, transport choices, recycling and water use. They collect anonymous class responses to explore our responsibility to care for and protect the natural world. Groups use the automatic response charts to identify one positive pattern and one area where the class could improve, then present a realistic class action based on the data. The question tools, response collection and automatic charts make the investigation manageable within two lessons.

Students make a short digital book explaining how humans, animals and the environment depend on one another in a chosen ecosystem. This directly addresses the line of inquiry about interdependence and shows how one human action can affect several parts of the ecosystem. Each book includes labelled drawings, short explanations, a recorded spoken reflection and a final page suggesting a protective action. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and built-in audio recording allow students to combine their ideas in one shareable book.

Students use paper cut-outs or classroom objects to create a stop-motion sequence showing a balanced ecosystem before and after a human action such as land clearing, pollution or overfishing. They then add a final section showing how responsible action could help restore the balance of nature. The finished film clearly presents a chain of consequences involving humans, animals and the environment. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback controls let students capture, check and improve the sequence as they work.

Students design a one-page public information poster about a local environmental issue connected to Sharing the Planet, such as protecting coastal habitats or reducing plastic waste. The poster explains how people’s actions affect the balance of nature and gives three realistic actions the school community can take. Students present their finished poster to the class and explain how their choices connect to our responsibility to protect the natural world. Canva’s poster templates, text boxes, graphic elements and simple chart tools help students organise evidence into a clear, shareable message.

St Kilda|Year 6|Where We Are in Place an.d: Students use Freeform to organise evidence about human migration into a cause-and-consequence map. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the causes and consequences of migration. They add short notes for challenges, risks and opportunities, then connect these to outcomes for individuals and societies. Freeform’s sticky notes, shapes and connecting lines make the relationships easy to arrange and revise. Each group presents its finished board and explains one important chain of cause and consequence.

Students enter a supplied set of migration data into Microsoft Excel and compare changes across countries or time periods. This supports the line of inquiry about changes in societies as a result of migration. They use rows and columns to organise the figures, then create a clear column or line chart. Excel’s simple tables and chart tool allow students to turn numerical evidence into a shareable visual. Pairs present their chart and explain one pattern the data shows and one question it raises.

Students build a small town area in Minecraft Education showing how human migration can change a society over time. This directly addresses the line of inquiry that migration results in a more diverse society. Their build might include homes, places of worship, shops, community spaces and signs explaining how different groups have contributed. Minecraft Education’s block building and signs let students create and label a manageable three-dimensional model. Groups guide classmates through the finished world and justify their design choices using evidence from the unit.

Students publish a set of short migration case-study posts on Padlet, each based on evidence explored during the unit. This connects to the line of inquiry about the positive and negative impact of migration on an individual. Each post includes the person’s reason for moving, one challenge, one opportunity and one lasting impact, with careful wording that separates facts from reasonable conclusions. Padlet’s post and comment features allow the class to build a shared gallery and respond with thoughtful questions. Students finish by commenting on two cases and identifying a similarity and a difference.

Students create a one-page visual explanation in Canva showing how a particular migration movement responded to challenges, risks and opportunities. This links directly to the central idea that human migration is a response to challenges, risks and opportunities. They combine a short timeline, key facts, simple icons and brief captions, then finish with a statement about the consequences for migrants and the receiving society. Canva’s templates, text boxes and drag-and-drop graphics make the page practical to complete in a few lessons. Students publish the finished page and present a two-minute explanation to the class.

St Kilda|Year 6|Who We Are.d: Students create a digital guide called “How We Thrive” about safe interactions, online safety, wellbeing and positive relationships. This directly supports the central idea that understanding ourselves, our relationships and our wellbeing empowers us to thrive. Each student publishes a short book with practical advice, realistic scenarios and a personal wellbeing plan to share with classmates. They use Book Creator’s simple page templates, text, drawing, image and voice-recording features to explain their ideas clearly.

Students build a short class survey about the connections between emotions, behaviour, learning, interactions and goals. They write respectful multiple-choice and rating questions about fictional or general situations rather than asking classmates to reveal private experiences. After classmates respond, students use the automatic response charts to identify patterns and present two evidence-based suggestions for improving classroom wellbeing. The everyday features driving the task are question forms, response collection and automatically generated charts.

Students code a Micro:bit as a simple wellbeing pause tool for moments when someone feels stressed, distracted or frustrated. This explores the active role we play in achieving and maintaining our wellbeing. Pressing one button starts a short breathing count on the LED grid, while the other displays a student-designed reminder such as a symbol for pause, move or ask for help. Students test and debug their code, then demonstrate the finished tool and explain when it could be used safely.

In small groups, students record and edit a short video showing the recognisable features of safe and healthy interactions. Their video presents one everyday Year 6 disagreement twice: first with an unhelpful response and then with calm language, listening, boundaries and repair. Students publish a two-minute comparison video and present the relationship strategies shown in the improved version. They use iMovie’s built-in video recording, trimming, titles and voice-over features to make the contrast easy to understand.

Students enter a week of fictional check-in data for a Year 6 character, including sleep, mood, focus, social connection and progress towards a goal. This helps them examine the line of inquiry about connections between emotions, behaviour, learning, interactions and goals without sharing personal information. They create graphs, look for patterns and add a short written explanation of two changes that may help the character thrive. The task uses Excel’s everyday table, simple formula and chart features.

Elsternwick|Prep|Where We Are in Place a.d: Students create a three-page book about their own past, showing themselves as a baby, when they were little and now. This supports the line of inquiry about reflecting on and recording our past, and the central idea that discovering our past helps us know more about ourselves today. Each child makes a simple personal timeline with a drawing, photo and short recorded sentence on each page. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tool and audio recording make the task manageable for Prep students.

Students program a Bee-Bot to travel across a floor mat showing three life stages: baby, little and now. This directly supports the line of inquiry about putting personal events in order and discussing what comes first, next and last. In pairs, students plan the steps, enter the directions and present their completed journey while explaining how a person changes over time. Bee-Bot’s forward, backward, left and right buttons provide a simple, hands-on way to practise sequencing.

Students use paper drawings or classroom figures to make a short animation showing a person changing from a baby to a Prep student. This connects to the central idea that discovering our past helps us know more about ourselves today. Each pair produces a short, shareable animation with three clear stages in the correct order. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback button let students capture small changes and immediately check their sequence.

Students take turns answering one class question about the past, such as “How have you changed?” or “What was special when you were little?” This supports the line of inquiry about personal stories and histories while creating the planned class time capsule. The class ends up with a short question-and-answer video that can be shared with families and viewed again in later years. Apple Clips’ simple video recording and title tools help the teacher combine each child’s brief response into one clear presentation.

Students record a short spoken memory about something they did when they were younger, with the teacher offering a sentence starter such as “When I was little…” This supports the line of inquiry about how we can record and share our past. Each child creates a brief audio keepsake that can be played to the class as part of a listening gallery of different personal stories. GarageBand’s Audio Recorder and large record and play controls make it practical for Prep students working with an adult or partner.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|Who We Are.d: Students create a short class book about everybody having rights and responsibilities. Each pair makes one page showing a familiar right, such as being safe or included, and a matching responsibility, such as using kind words or taking turns. They add a simple drawing, a sentence and a recorded explanation, then present the finished book to the class. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and voice-recording button make this manageable for Year 2 students.

Students use PicCollage to sort everyday examples linked to the difference between needs and wants. They place teacher-provided pictures into two labelled sections, then add a short caption explaining one choice that was difficult to sort. Each pair publishes a clear needs-and-wants poster and talks the class through its decisions. The simple grid layout, text labels and picture-moving tools are the main features used.

Students make a classroom object speak about what helps build a respectful relationship. They photograph an object such as a shared pencil tub, lunch box or playground ball, draw a mouth and record a short message about sharing, listening or including others. The finished talking pictures are presented as quick reminders of our responsibility to value the rights of others. ChatterPix Kids’ photo, mouth-drawing and voice-recording features keep the task simple and playful.

Students program a Bee-Bot across a floor grid of classroom relationship scenarios, such as inviting someone to play, grabbing equipment or taking turns. Their goal is to navigate only to examples of a respectful relationship, clearing and debugging the sequence when the robot reaches the wrong square. Each group presents its final route and explains why the chosen actions respect the rights of others. The Bee-Bot’s forward, backward, left, right, clear and go buttons provide all the programming needed.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|Who We Are.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
Glen Waverley|Year 2|Who We Are.d: Students animate a character giving advice about a common Year 2 relationship problem, such as being left out of a game or having someone take a turn. Their short script names the right involved and suggests a respectful responsibility, directly supporting the idea that humans should value the rights of others. They choose a character and background, record their voice, and present the finished animated message to the class. Adobe Express uses the voice recording to animate the character’s mouth and movements, so students can focus on clear, kind advice.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|Where We Are in Pla.d: Students create a short digital book for Where We Are in Place and Time showing three stages of their personal history, such as being a baby, starting school and life today. They add a family photo or drawing to each page and record a simple sentence explaining what has changed and what has stayed the same. This connects directly to the line of inquiry that personal history shapes the present. The finished books can be shared with classmates and families, using Book Creator’s page templates, drawing, photo and voice-recording features.

Students use Google Maps to explore the Glen Waverley area during Where We Are in Place and Time. They view familiar places in Street View, identify landmarks and discuss clues showing whether buildings or spaces may be old, new or changed over time. This supports the line of inquiry about evidence and its significance in a place. Pairs present a short guided Street View walkthrough to the class, using the search, zoom and Street View features to show the landmarks they noticed.

Students work in pairs to build a simple then-and-now model of a local place for Where We Are in Place and Time, such as a street, school or park. One side shows how they think the place may have looked in the past, while the other shows features found there today, based on class evidence provided by the teacher. This connects to the line of inquiry about connections between the past and present within a place. Students present their model by moving through it and explaining their choices, using Minecraft Education’s blocks, signs and camera controls.

Students make a short animation showing how a familiar place has changed over time for Where We Are in Place and Time. They move simple paper buildings, trees, roads or people a small amount between each photo to show a past scene changing into a present-day scene. This demonstrates the central idea that exploring the past helps us to understand the present. The class watches the finished animations, created with Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features.

Students choose a photograph of an old household or school object linked to Where We Are in Place and Time, such as a telephone, toy or classroom item. They draw a mouth on the object and record it explaining what it was used for, what evidence reveals its purpose and what people use today instead. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about evidence and its significance in a place. Students share the finished talking-object clips, using ChatterPix Kids’ photo, mouth-drawing and voice-recording features.

Glen Waverley|Year 4|How We Express Ours.d: In the How We Express Ourselves unit, students choose an artwork, song or performance and create a two-page response explaining what message they think it conveys. This directly explores the language used to respond to The Arts, using words such as mood, colour, rhythm, movement and contrast. Each student publishes a short digital art-response book containing an image, written observations and a recorded spoken reflection. Book Creator’s simple page templates, text boxes, image tools and audio recording make the task manageable for Year 4 students.

In the How We Express Ourselves unit, small groups use classroom objects or paper shapes to make a short stop-motion sequence that expresses an idea such as belonging, change or conflict without spoken words. This explores ways forms of expression convey messages and asks students to think carefully about movement, colour, position and timing. Students capture and adjust frames, test the sequence, and present the finished animation while classmates explain the message they understood. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback controls are the key features used in the task.

In the How We Express Ourselves unit, pairs record a two-minute arts discussion in which they describe an artistic expression and respond to each other’s different interpretations. This supports the line of inquiry into the language used to respond to The Arts and shows how responding can promote thinking. Students plan an opening, give evidence for their views, record their voices and publish a short podcast episode with a simple title page. Canva’s audio recording, page design and presentation tools keep the process contained in one familiar workspace.

In the How We Express Ourselves unit, students create a digital artwork that communicates a chosen feeling or message without using written words. This directly explores ways forms of expression convey messages and develops creative and critical thinking as students make deliberate choices about line, shape, colour and texture. Students save their finished artwork and present it to a partner, who describes the message they receive before the artist explains their intention. Sketchbook’s brushes, colour picker, eraser and layers allow students to experiment and revise without needing advanced drawing skills.

In the How We Express Ourselves unit, students respond to a teacher-posted collection of artworks, music clips or performance images by adding short observation and interpretation posts. This addresses the central idea that responding to different artistic expressions can promote thinking, because students compare how the same work can prompt different ideas.
