Each student publishes one response using a clear claim and supporting detail, then adds a thoughtful comment to a classmate’s interpretation. Padlet’s shared board, post and comment features make everyone’s responses visible for a practical class discussion.

Glen Waverley|Year 5|How the World Works.d: Students build and code a simple LEGO grabbing mechanism inspired by a bird beak, claw or insect mouthpart. They test how well it picks up LEGO pieces of different shapes, linking directly to how structural features and adaptations help living things survive. Groups debug their code and adjust the mechanism before presenting which food type their design would suit best. The familiar building pieces, motor and block coding are the key features that make the task work.

Students code Sphero BOLT to travel through several light and dark locations and record readings from its ambient light sensor. They compare the data to explore how light can be measured and used in science and technology. Each group produces a labelled data table in the Sphero coding project and demonstrates a program that changes the LED matrix when the light level crosses a chosen point. The ambient light sensor, block coding and programmable LED matrix are the everyday features at the centre of the task.

Students explore landforms and waterways in National Geographic MapMaker to find places where weathering and erosion are likely to change Earth’s surface. They use the map’s drawing and annotation tools to mark a river bend, coastline or steep slope and explain where material may be worn away or deposited. Each pair creates an annotated map with short explanations and presents its prediction to the class. The map layers, zoom controls and annotation tools allow students to connect land shape, water and surface change.

Students create a short digital field guide about the structural features and adaptations of three living things. Each page includes a labelled drawing, a written explanation of how one feature supports survival, and a recorded spoken summary. The finished books directly address how structural features and adaptations help living things survive and can be shared with classmates. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and audio recording make the field guide manageable for Year 5 students.

Students make a narrated explanation showing how light travels and how it is used in a familiar technology such as a periscope, torch or reflective road sign. They draw and move arrows to show the path of light, then record themselves explaining what happens when light meets different materials or surfaces. The final product is a short animated presentation connected to how light is used in science and technology. Explain Everything’s drawing, object movement and voice-recording features let students make their thinking visible without specialist equipment.

Glen Waverley|Year 5|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to investigate how communities interact with a local natural environment, such as Gardiners Creek or Port Phillip Bay. They add markers and labels showing habitats, community use, environmental pressures and places needing conservation. This directly explores the need for conservation and how community values inform management of the natural environment. Using the map, layers and annotation tools, each group produces a shareable conservation map with three practical recommendations.

Students use Google Maps and Street View to compare two natural places that communities manage in different ways, such as an urban creek and a national park. They view paths, signs, roads, vegetation and visitor facilities, then record evidence about access, protection and human impact in a teacher-provided table. This connects to the central idea that communities interact with the environment in different ways. The everyday map, satellite view, Street View and distance tools help students present a short evidence-based comparison to the class.

Students create a Microsoft Forms survey asking classmates which actions and values should guide the care of a local natural environment. They collect responses about issues such as habitat protection, recreation, rubbish, pets and access, then examine the automatic charts. This directly investigates how community values inform management of the natural environment. Each group shares a summary of the survey results and recommends one conservation action supported by the collected data.

Students build a small Minecraft Education model showing how a community could restore and care for a damaged creek, wetland or bushland area. They use blocks and signs to include habitat zones, protected areas, paths, rubbish controls and spaces for responsible community use. This explores ways environmental stewardship can drive change while balancing different community needs. Each group presents a guided tour of its completed world and explains how three design choices support conservation.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital field guide called Our Community as Environmental Stewards. Each page explains one realistic action people can take, such as planting local species, reducing litter, protecting habitat or using waterways responsibly. This directly connects to ways environmental stewardship can drive change. Using page layouts, text, drawing and built-in audio recording, students publish a shareable book that includes evidence, explanations and a spoken call to action.

Glen Waverley|Year 5|Where We Are in Pla.d: Students explore a resource town such as Ballarat and trace its links to Melbourne and nearby transport routes while studying how resource discovery shaped Australia. They use the map view, distance tool and Street View to identify mines, roads, railway lines, housing and civic buildings that show the growth of a society. This directly supports the line of inquiry about the significance of resource discovery in the development of societies. Pairs finish by presenting a live Google Maps walkthrough that explains three pieces of visible evidence and the distances between key places.

Students enter a small teacher-provided set of historical data showing population or migration changes before, during and after an Australian gold rush. They use spreadsheet cells, simple formulas and charts to look for links between resource discovery, population growth and economic development. This directly explores the central idea that the discovery of resources has impacted the growth and development of nations. Each group produces a labelled chart and adds short written conclusions explaining the pattern shown by the data.

Students build a small model of a nineteenth-century resource settlement, including the resource site, transport links, housing, businesses and an area representing existing Indigenous connections to Country. They use blocks, signs and books within Minecraft Education to show how exploration and settlement changed land use and affected different groups. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about the effects of exploration and settlement on Indigenous and colonial populations. Groups present a guided walkthrough of their completed model, explaining whose needs were met, whose were not, and how the settlement grew.

Students create a short visual report about a migrant group that moved because of a resource discovery, such as people travelling to the Victorian goldfields. They use page templates, text boxes and images to explain reasons for migration and contributions to cultural, social and economic growth. This directly addresses the line of inquiry about the impact of migration on the growth of societies. Students publish and present a clear five-page report containing a map image, key evidence, a migrant perspective and a concluding statement.

Students make a short stop-motion film showing how the discovery of a resource changed a place over time. Using simple models and paper scenery, they record frame-by-frame scenes of the place before discovery, the arrival of settlers, the growth of a town and an effect on Indigenous people. This directly examines the effects of exploration and settlement on Indigenous and colonial populations. Students use the frame capture and playback features to test and improve their sequence, then screen the finished film with a brief spoken explanation.

Glen Waverley|Year 5|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital guide about managing changes associated with puberty, using clear language and trusted facts discussed in class. This directly supports the line of inquiry about managing changes associated with puberty and the central idea that knowledge and strategies help us manage change. Each student makes several pages covering one common change, a helpful strategy and a trusted person who could provide support. They use Book Creator’s page templates, text, drawing and voice-recording features to make the guide easy for Year 5 students to understand.

Students respond to teacher-posted scenarios about group chats, gaming, sharing photos and receiving unkind messages. This explores the line of inquiry about managing behaviours in digital situations, with students identifying safe, respectful and practical responses. They publish a short response to each scenario, then add a constructive comment that builds on a classmate’s idea. Padlet’s shared board, post and comment features allow the class to collect and compare strategies in one teacher-moderated space.

In small groups, students create a short stop-motion scene showing a friendship facing change, such as a new student arriving or friends developing different interests. The task connects to establishing, managing and maintaining relationships by showing both an unhelpful reaction and a more accepting response. Each group produces a finished scene with simple objects or paper characters, captions and recorded dialogue. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera, text and audio features let students build and explain the relationship scenario clearly.

Pairs record a short advice podcast about managing change in friendships, digital situations or puberty. This supports the central idea that managing change requires acceptance, knowledge and strategies. Students plan a question, record an interviewer and an advice-giver, then edit the episode to include an introduction, two practical strategies and a closing message. GarageBand’s voice recording, trimming and track controls allow students to produce a clear audio episode within one lesson sequence.

Students design a one-page decision guide for a realistic digital situation, such as being excluded from an online game or being asked to share someone else’s photo. This directly addresses managing behaviours in digital situations by helping students pause, consider consequences and choose a safe response. Their finished guide shows a simple sequence such as stop, check, choose, act and seek help, with an example for each step. Canva’s poster templates, text boxes, shapes and icons make it practical to create and present a clear visual guide.
